author: CNT Valladolid
title: Vivienda y antifascismo en tiempos de Desokupa
content:
El miércoles 21 de octubre, como parte de las jornadas de inauguración del nuestro nuevo local en Valladolid, se celebró un debate sobre el tema de la vivienda desde tres perspectivas complementarias: la del

Sindicato de Vivienda de Valladolid

, la del Sindicato de Inquilinas (por parte de

Javier Gil

, autor del libro

Generación Inquilina

, que se vendió durante el acto) y la de

Sistema 161

, grupo de investigación de entramados reaccionarios.


Gracias a los ponentes se perfiló una detallada imagen del problema de la vivienda mostrando que éste es consustancial a un capitalismo que año tras año ha ido deviniendo en un capitalismo rentista en lugar de productivo, especialmente en el Estado español. Lo que la clase trabajadora arañamos a los empresaurios como sueldo, se lo devolvemos teniendo que pagar precios de vivienda inflados por la especulación.


La inversión en vivienda está siendo la tabla de salvación de un capitalismo en crisis, sin tener en cuenta costes humanos de los aumentos de rentabilidad, y eso ha convertido a la vivienda en una palanca estratégica para el cambio social.


Apoyando y sosteniendo este sistema encontramos desde empresas de desokupación encargadas de llevar a cabo brutalmente los desalojos de la nueva clase rentista, hasta todos los gobiernos del Estado españoi, que no han contribuido a dar salida a esta situación e incluso la han empeorado con medidas legislativas que favorecen los desahucios.


La impunidad de las empresas de Desokupa -cuyo sórdido árbol genealógico pudo consultarse en una exposición simultánea a la mesa redonda- es un nuevo ejemplo de que “los ricos siempre han llevado mal que los pobres tengan derechos”; estas empresas son un nuevo nicho de negocio que facilita a la clase rentista saltarse la ley, y que opera gracias a la tolerancia policial y a las campañas favorecedoras de determinados medios.


Quedó claro que el silenciamiento no sólo del historial delictivo de los componentes de estas empresas, sino de sus vínculos tangibles con el negocio inmobiliario -adquiriendo los pisos que desahucian- es algo que los medios de comunicación masiva ocultan por, en el mejor de los casos, negligencia.


Pero el rechazo generalizado a los desahucios que se va extendiendo en la población está restando espacio a esta propaganda, y convocatorias como la de huelga general por la vivienda están desmantelando un espacio público en el que los debates fomentados por la ultraderecha ocupaban el lugar de la discusión de problemas reales.


Es significativo que una semana de acampadas por la vivienda hayan provocado un adelanto de elecciones que no han producido dos años de manifestaciones ultras frente a las sedes del PSOE pidiendo lo mismo, pero también está claro que hay que ir más allá de las elecciones.


Dada la ausencia de una representatividad de la clase obrera en los sistemas parlamentarios habituales en la que ésta vea sus intereses de clase expresados y llevados a cabo, se impone la necesidad de reconstruir una acción política al margen de estos cauces habituales.


Necesidad que se percibe también en todas las movilizaciones por la vivienda, que han abandonado la posición anti-organización que tuvo peso en algunas acampadas del 15M. Las acampadas y movilizaciones por la vivienda no están siendo una repetición del 15M, sino un paso hacia una articulación de una nueva forma de política desde la base.


Una nueva forma de acción política que pasa por hacer nuevas formas de sindicalismo – más combativo y autogestionado- y por fortalecer un nuevo sentido común compartido, y que sean un dique contra las soluciones autoritarias a la pérdida de rentabilidad de los negocios capitalistas.


La entrada

Vivienda y antifascismo en tiempos de Desokupa

 apareció primero en

CNT Valladolid

.


La entrada

Vivienda y antifascismo en tiempos de Desokupa

 se publicó primero en

Confederación Nacional del Trabajo

.

author: webadmin
title: Quorn Hunt Humiliated: Terrierman Arrested As Sabs Disrupt Opening Meet.
content:
Legendary animal liberationist Barry Horne honoured by Northants Sabs.


Just weeks after publishing damning footage of the

Quorn Hunt killing a fox and training hounds

 to attack, saboteurs descended upon their prestigious opening meet – and completely ruined it.


Quorn Killers and Horne Haunts Quorn. Banners proudly displayed by Northants Sabs at the Quorn killers opening meet, 6 November, 2026. Image: Northants Hunt Sabs.


The day saw violence and abuse by the hunt, and resulted in the arrest of a terrierman who attempted to flee from police.


The day was dedicated to Barry Horne, a legendary activist who made the ultimate sacrifice for animal liberation.


Barry was involved in numerous daring rescue operations, helping to free animals destined for experimentation. He died following a series of hunger strikes intended to pressure Tony Blair’s Labour government over its promise to hold an inquiry into vivisection.


Barry Horne, 17 March 1990, rescuing 82 beagle puppies and 26 rabbits from Harlan Interfauna in Huntingdon. The site is now associated with MBR Acres Ltd, and the long-running Camp Beagle protests against the breeding of dogs for laboratory experiments for the petrochemical, chemical and pharmaceutical industries.


The government reneged on its promise, and animal rights activists reacted with fury in Barry’s name, and thousands more animals, including cats, rabbits and guinea pigs were liberated by activists during his hunger strikes.


Barry was also formerly a member of Northants Hunt Sabs. He died on November 5, 2001. His death radicalised and mobilised countless more animal liberations in his name.

In September 2026 multiple dogs were liberated from the MBR site

.


On Friday 6 November 2026, a day after the 25th anniversary of Barry’s death, the Quorn Hunt held their opening meet at its kennels in Kirby Bellars, Leicestershire.


The day did not quite go as they may have planned.


The Quorn Hunt October 2026, kill a fox and use the body to train the hounds. Notice the huntsman blowing for the kill over the hounds as they tear the body apart. Image: Northants Hunt Sabs


On the back of the horrendous footage released only weeks earlier, Northants Hunt Sabs, including personal friends of Barry’s, turned out to stop the Quorn Hunt from killing on their watch.


Part time whipper-in and terrier ‘man’ Mickey Vaughn practising for the regional gurning championship.

Image: Northants Hunt Sabs.


Northants Sabs truly smashed the day, hunt tempers flared as sabs arrived at the meet with banners and flags speaking truth about ‘trail hunting’.


Vaughan bravely attacking a woman. Image: Northants Hunt Sabs


True to form, the hunters natural default for violence saw sabs attacked and pushed to the ground. Sabs stood their ground following the violent outburst and the hunt was soon put back in their box.


Vaughan being put back into his box. Image: Northants Hunt Sabs


Sabs stayed on the hunt throughout the day, leaving huntsman Joe Tesseyman struggling to find opportunities to hunt foxes with saboteurs on his case.


Huntsman Joe Tessyman on the run from sabs and police alike. Image Northants Hunt Sabs


Then, near Cream Gorse, the hunter became the hunted.


A Quorn terrierman was spotted leaving the covert on a quad bike, with officers from Leicestershire Police’s Rural Crime Team in hot pursuit.


The hot pursuit began with a terrierman fleeing from police after leaving the covert. Image: Northants Hunt Sabs


Mickey Vaughan, the terrierman and occasional whipper-in, attempted to slow the pursuing officers down by positioning his horse in the road. Police moved him aside and continued after the terrierman on the quad.


The quad overturned, and the terrierman was spotted running up Pasture Lane with a police officer hot on his tail behind.


You can’t park that there, mate. Image Northants Hunt Saboteurs.


Clearly a runner he was not.


He was promptly caught, cuffed and arrested.


At first I was all like… Image: Northants Hunt Sabs


We couldn’t possibly comment on what the arrest relates to and will not speculate, but lets hope they throw “obstructing an officer” at him whilst they are at it. Same goes for Vaughan who attempted to prevent the officer from pursuing the masked terrierman.


Then I was like… Image: Northants Hunt Sabs


Meanwhile the mounted field dwindled out, no doubt many of whom left thoroughly embarrassed by the thuggish behaviour of this supposed-prestigious hunt …

title: Eastern Visayas farmers suffer from El Niño
content:
TACLOBAN CITY – “All the crops I planted, even if they are supposed to withstand heat, all died because of the extreme drought caused by the El Niño.”

Gil Gacus, a farmer from Samar, stressed this point at the October 28 forum at the University of the Philippines Tacloban titled “Istorya Pankalibungan: A Forum on Climate Change and Environmental Challenges.”

The event was attended by members of organizations of fisherfolk and farmers, environmental defenders, development workers from Leyte and Samar, youth groups, and students from different universities in Tacloban. Farmers from Magsasaka at Siyentipiko para sa Pag-unlad ng Agrikultura (MASIPAG) shared the impact of Super El Niño on their crops.

Gacus said that the lack of a reliable irrigation system adds up to farmers’ burdens. “We have irrigation canals but there is little to no water due to drought so our crops end up dying.”

Jeremias Maligmat, a farmer from Leyte, stressed the need for government action now that farmers are suffering from the effects of El Niño. He also criticized Marcos Jr.’s lack of urgency and genuineness to help them. “He [Marcos Jr.] is asking us to use pails to collect rainwater, but how will we collect it if there is no rain?”

“If Marcos is genuine about helping farmers, his government should focus on addressing the challenges on irrigation and invest in machinery that could pump out underground water to help us farmers during times like this,” Maligmat said.

Maligmat added that on top of the environmental challenges and outright neglect from the government, landlessness is also a major problem faced by farmers. “The government should address these challenges affecting us farmers if they are so genuine about helping us as we are the ones producing food for the country.”

Roque Regis of Save Kanbatok Advocacy criticized the government’s reaffirmation to continue the halted construction of the Causeway Project in Cancabato Bay. “Since the construction of the Causeway started last 2023, there have already been recorded, irreversible damages to the bay. It destroyed the then thriving ecosystem of the bay by obstructing the natural flow of water.”

Regis said that some of his fellow fisherfolk have stopped from fishing due to the deteriorating state of the Bay. “These so-called developmental projects like the causeway project do not benefit the community or the poor, but instead benefit the rich who embezzle money through these projects.”

“Fisherfolk like Mano Roque struggled heavily, so much so that the fish, crabs, and other seafood they catch, if they have any at all, shrunk in size over the years since land was dumped on Cancabato Bay to build that Causeway,” said Jerx Aliposa of Save Kankabato Advocacy.

“Instead of coming up with solutions to address their concerns like providing subsidies and investing on technologies that could help them, the government would always think of developmental projects like the causeway project, with little to no regard of their repercussions to our communities,” Aliposa said.

Nemesio Baldesco of Tinambacan Environmental Advocates Coalition (TEAC), a network of environmental defenders from Calbayog City in Samar, said that their group opposes the Gemini Wind Power Project by Vena Energy in their city. “[I]t will greatly affect the biodiversity of our forests and will pollute our sources of clean water.”

Although their group and other advocates succeeded in getting at least five wind turbines removed from Pan-as Hayiban watershed, Calbayog’s protected landscape, Nemesio said that the project is yet to be abandoned. “Their [Vena Energy] alternative route is to install the turbines outside the watershed but still within our forests where it could still disrupt the biodiversity and result in the cutting down of hundreds of trees.”

WATCH : Envi advocates oppose Gemini Wind Project in Samar

Ronnel Arambulo, Vice Chairperson of Pambansang Lakas ng Kilusang Mamamalakaya ng Pilipinas (PAMALAKAYA), stressed the importance of collective action as well as the youth’s participation to oppose projects that damage the environment and livelihoods of farmers and fisherfolks. “Let us not allow our schools to become producers of brains that will only be used by the rich to forward their anti-poor agenda.” Ronnie Manalo, secretary-general of the Kilusang Magbubukid ng Pilipinas (KMP), called on the farmers to fight for their rightful claim on the P45-billion funds allocated for El Niño. “Let us mobilize our …

author: Bulatlat Contributors
title: Lawyers condemn human rights violations vs protesters
content:
The National Union of Peoples’ Lawyers (NUPL) condemned the arrest, restricted legal access, and prolonged detention of more than 300 protesters apprehended during demonstrations at Liwasang Bonifacio and Sucat People’s Park ahead of the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit.

During a press conference at the Liwasang Bonifacio on November 17, the lawyers’ group stressed that human rights violations were committed against the detained protesters.

Legal counsels assisting the detainees criticized law enforcement authorities for allegedly delaying their access to clients, filing sweeping criminal complaints, and leaving them in detention over a long non-working holiday period.

Ephraim Cortez, president of NUPL, denounced police authorities for requiring clearance from higher authorities before allowing legal counsels to confer with their detained clients.

He said, “A lawyer’s access to their clients cannot rely upon clearance from higher-ranking officials, as this is our clients’ right to counsel.”

Cortez added that the detention already exceeded the 18 hours allowed by the law. “Those arrested are innocent. They were just protesting. They should be released.”

The protesters were taken into custody during standoffs at the Liwasang Bonifacio and Sucat People’s Park.

Lawyer Mary Jane Real said that arresting demonstrators inside Liwasang Bonifacio violates the law on public assemblies. She stressed that Liwasang Bonifacio is a freedom park. “You cannot be arrested for protesting here, because we have the freedom to protest in this place.”

According to Real, the nine individuals arrested in Manila are facing multiple charges including illegal assemblies, direct assault, resistance and disobedience to a person in authority, tumults and other disturbances of public order, and violations of the Public Assembly Act.

Real also raised alarm over procedural delays caused by the ASEAN Summit work suspension in Metro Manila, noting that even if bail is recommended, detainees remain behind bars since there will be no court personnel to process release orders.

“The inquest concluded yesterday… We are currently awaiting the prosecutor’s decision, but since today is a holiday, no action can be taken until everyone returns to the office on Thursday,” Real said. “Consequently, even posting bail is not possible, as there is no one available to sign the necessary documents.”

On the other hand, lawyer Zoe Caballero of Sentro Para Sa Tunay Na Repormang Agraryo

denounced the reported P9-million cumulative bail required for the detained protesters, most of whom are farmers, workers, and students from the Southern Tagalog region.

“They themselves have nothing to eat, so where are they supposed to get the P9 million? If they actually had P9 million, they wouldn’t have marched all the way to Manila just to make their voices heard,” Caballero said. “Now, we’re being told: ‘Yes, you have the right to speak, but this is the price you must pay to say what needs to be said.’ It turns out you have to be wealthy just to be heard.”

Real urged the public to stand in solidarity with the detained demonstrators, stressing that their protests against Pax Silica are meant to protect ordinary Filipinos from worsening poverty and hunger. “If we don’t oppose this, all we’ll get here in this ‘Pax Silica’ is hunger and poverty. These people, they are the ones making sacrifices so that we may uphold our rights.”

“We have a responsibility toward them; we must help them gain their freedom, because they risked their own lives and peace so that we could be free,” Real said. (AMU, DAA)

author: Lindsay McCabe
title: Changes to coronial legislation to broaden next-of-kin determinations
content:
Readers please be advised that this article mentions First Nations people who have passed away, including children.


On Tuesday 22nd September 2026, the Minns Labor Government announced changes to the

Coroners Act 2009

 NSW, specifically, the section of the legislation that instructs coroners to determine and appoint a Senior Next-of-Kin. This followed a statutory review of the Act, and is in response to one of the many recommendations made by the review. 


When a person’s death is reported to the coroner, a Senior Next-of-Kin is appointed. The Senior Next-of-Kin has the exclusive authority to make decisions regarding the person who has died while they are in the care of the coroner. For example, the Senior Next-of-Kin can object to a post-mortem examination being conducted. Being appointed Senior Next-of-Kin also means that the coroner has an obligation to provide mandatory notifications about the progress of a coronial investigation to the Senior Next-of-Kin. When, where and how a person is laid to rest is also under the authority of the Senior Next-of-Kin. 


Who is appointed as Senior Next-of-Kin is decided by a strict legal framework. The

Coroners Act 2009

 (NSW) s 6A states that the Senior Next-of-Kin must be the deceased person’s spouse or de facto partner; if they have no spouse or de facto partner, then any of the adult children of the deceased person can be appointed. If the person has no adult children, then the person’s parent/s may be appointed. 


This appointment-flow hierarchy has been problematic for Mob for many years, across many jurisdictions. It does not take into account our kinship systems, laws, or spiritual beliefs. One of the earliest challenges of the Senior Next-of-Kin hierarchy involved

two Aboriginal parents

 who could not agree on where to bury their deceased adult child. The mother wanted to hold a Catholic ceremony and burial in Darwin; the father however wanted to have a burial on their homelands, Bardi Country, and provided the Court with supporting information outlining the cultural obligations to do so. The Court ruled in favour of the mother. 


In

2016

, the NSW Supreme Court was asked to rule on a matter where the Senior Next-of-Kin appointment had been challenged. In this matter, the coroner had appointed a deceased man’s de facto partner as the Senior Next-of-Kin, as per the legislation. This allowed the partner, a Gumbaynggirr woman, to make arrangements for the deceased man’s burial to take place in Bowraville. The man’s sister however, wanted the man to be taken home to Weilwan Country and to be buried alongside his ancestors. The Court ruled in favour of the man’s de facto partner, citing common law precedent. Further, because the de facto partner of the deceased man established her de facto status to the Court, she held ‘administrative priority’; in other words, she had the highest right as per the legislation. 


More recently, in 2024, the Supreme Court of NSW decided on a dispute between a deceased man’s de facto partner and mother who could not agree on where to bury him. The de facto partner of the man insisted he wanted to be buried in La Parouse; his mother wanted to take him home to his father in Cherbourg, Wakka Wakka Country, where he could be buried on Country. The Court held in favour of the man’s de facto partner, accepting that she was the deceased man’s de facto partner at the time of his death. 


So, who is appointed Senior Next-of-Kin when a person dies has significant ramifications for where, when, and how a person is returned to Country. 


There have however been instances where the appointment of Senior Next-of-Kin has affirmed cultural responsibilities and laws, albeit outside of NSW. In

1999

, the non-Aboriginal spouse of a deceased Aboriginal man sought to bury them in Port Augusta. The deceased man’s father wished to bury him in Oodnadatta, where other members of the family had been buried, and on Yankintatjara Country. Several affidavits were presented to the Court, highlighting that, according to cultural responsibilities and practices, the head of the family should be empowered to make these decisions, not the spouse. The deceased’s spouse, on the other hand, argued that the children of the deceased would not be able to visit their father’s grave if it were located 700kms away in Oodnadatta. Significantly, the Court ruled in favour of the father of the deceased man, allowing him to take his son home, and to be buried according to …

author: Unknown
title: Agnes Grundel - Novemberminnen
content:
Författare

: Agnes Grundel

Titel

: Novemberminnen

Källa

: Allarm november 1916


 Ett år har förflutit sedan vår kamrat, frihetskämpen Josef Hillström slöt sina av förtryck betyngda ögon, för att aldrig mera skåda den värld som fråntog honom allt - ja till och med rätten att leva. I den värld där han strävade att frigöra människorna, var hans egen frihet osäker. I det samhälle där han agiterade med varje gnista av sin outtröttliga energi, var hans liv icke tryggat.


Varför?

 Jo: Därför att han hade hjältemod nog att trotsa, att opponera sig mot våldets blodtörstige tyranner, som alltid mördat och stympat, bränt och krossat alla dem som försökt vrida makten ur deras järnklor, samt ersätta människornas lidande med lycka.


 Alla dem som i någon mån försökt att förbättra mänsklighetens förhållanden, alla dem som vågat fråga: med vad rätt kunna dessa legaliserade ogärningsmän tvinga mig att arbeta för dem, samt bestjäla mig produkten av mitt arbete, alltid ha de fått falla offer för den s. k. rättvisan. Sådana män äro farliga för förtryckarna, enär de ha förmågan att väcka andra och få dem att göra gemensam aktion mot förtrycket, därför måste de rödjas ur vägen.


 Josef Hillström var en av de oböjlige. Ingenting förfärade honom, in i dödens käftar trotsade han dem alla. De togo hans unga kraftiga, förhoppningsfulla liv, men hans skändligt utgjutna blod ropar på hämd, från alla delar av jorden juder det som av en tordönsstämma:

hämnd

. Så länge här finnes en slav, komma hans brännande odödliga ord och eldiga entusiasm inspirera miljoner till verksamhet.


 Josef Hillström har ej levat förgäves, oaktat han dog i blomman av sitt liv. Det säges han var en drömmare, kanske så, enär hans idé ännu ej hunnit bliva förverkligad, men han drömde ej när han i sina sånger gav slavarna råd huru att bekriga sina svurna dödsfiender. Det var realisten Joe Hill vi minnas och vörda.


 Joe Hill drömde om en bättre värld där arbetaren skördar fulla produkten av sitt arbete, där nyttiga medborgare styra samhället till allas bästa, där list, lögn, våld och bedrägeri ej längre triumferar, där små barn vårdas som praktfulla blommor.


 Att han lärde slavarna att förverkliga detta, däri låg Joe Hills brott. Någon invände hånfullt att han gick i döden för en kvinnas skull. Ja alltid ha frihetshjältar förhånats av den okunniga massan. Vi minnas kanske Robert Emmet, Irlands store frihetskämpe, en Voltaire, Thomas Payne m. fl.


 Samtidigt som Joe Hill mördades i SAlt Lake hade de samhällsbevarande här i staden konferens varvid en av de viktigaste frågorna för dagen var:

hur skola vi kunna fördriva I. W. W. männen ur U. S. A.

 Detta visar att dessa herrar tycka sig redan nu se hur deras makts sista dagar börja randas. De mötas för att uppgöra planer huru att på bästa sätt tillintetgöra denna organisation. En av deras planer är väl känd och praktiseras ofta, den att mörda de aktive ledande männen. För denna metod föll vår präktige Joe Hill, för samma försöka de få de tre kamraterna i norra Minnesota: Joe Smidt, Carlo Tresca och Sam Scharlet. Allt beror på er arbetare om de även i detta fallet skola lyckas. Skola vi låta våldets bödlar döda våra bästa och aktivaste kamrater. Nej. Låt oss visa att vi äro män och kvinnor med ett för rätt och frihet klappande hjärta och med mod att handla.


 Vi kunna ej bättre vörda Joe Hills minne än att följa hans sista uppmaning till världens arbetare:

Organisera.

author: Jenny Brown
title: Labor Mobilized for ‘Many vs. Mighty’ Midterms
content:
Something different was in the air as the labor movement mobilized for the midterms.


More than usual, unions were willing to support insurgent candidates who refused corporate donations and bucked the Democratic Party establishment. They championed a Bernie Sanders-style list of working-class issues: Medicare for All, a higher minimum wage, union rights, immigrant rights, stopping war, and taxing the rich. Many are union members themselves. And they won.


United Auto Workers President Shawn Fain called the election “the many versus the mighty.”


In Michigan, the UAW was a key backer of the victorious Abdul El-Sayed, who earlier defeated the party’s depressing primary choice for U.S. Senate.  “You had a lot of rich people who tried to… buy a seat, to buy these races,” Fain told

Michigan Advance

. “Michiganders… are telling these people they’re not for sale.”


Logger and union member Troy Jackson won a Senate seat against 30-year incumbent Republican Susan Collins in Maine after the UAW and the Maine AFL-CIO helped defeat the establishment choice in the primary there. In Ohio, labor stalwart Sherrod Brown faced a river of crypto lobby cash but recovered the Senate seat he lost in 2024.


In Texas, the Communications Workers (CWA) mobilized for union-member candidates up and down the ticket, asking candidates to commit to a

“Contract with Working Texans.”

 Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa signed on—she’s a labor lawyer, member of Texas State Employees Union/CWA, and the first Democrat elected Texas governor since 1990.


Various union members and leaders are headed for Congress. Ironworker Brian Poindexter won in Ohio. Pennsylvanians elected firefighter and union president Bob Brooks. Forest Service smokejumper and local union vice president Sam Forstag won in Montana. VA nurse and union member Mitchell Berman beat a Republican incumbent in Wisconsin.


In New York, UAW members and Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) congressional candidates Claire Valdez and Darializa Avila Chevalier defeated establishment Democrats in the primary, then romped November 3.


Richard Ojeda, a champion of the West Virginia teachers’ strike of 2018, won a Congressional seat in North Carolina, beating the head of the National Republican Congressional Committee. "We were elected to elevate the lives of working people across this country,”

said Ojeda

. “We're coming in LASER FOCUSED on the mission. Help people. Hold anyone who has hurt people accountable. Tax the billionaires. The end.”


Others lost, but came way closer than expected. In Nebraska, Kellogg’s strike leader and independent Dan Osborn came up short (44-50) for U.S. Senate. He faced ferocious attack ads, with $24 million in ‘independent’ spending. In Florida, former SEIU organizer and DSA member Angie Nixon defeated the establishment Democrat in the primary and almost won (48-50) a Senate race the pundits had written off. She got zero support from the national Democratic Party.


CORPORATE DEMS UNDER FIRE


Now some unions have come out swinging, demanding more from the party. The Machinists (IAM) sent a letter

urging Senator Chuck Schumer to resign as party leader

. OPEIU

did the same

.


The IAM “is through with any member of leadership, in any political party, who stops one iota short of being a ferocious, unyielding and unbending champion of working people,” said President Brian Bryant. “This means… sweeping economic policy changes that will recalibrate the vast, immoral, economic injustice in this country.”


The United Electrical Workers concurred: “The credit for these wins belongs not to the Democratic Party—whose leadership has offered at best tepid resistance to the Republican agenda over the past two years—but to the working people across the country who have spent the last two years organizing and fighting back in their communities and workplaces.”


UE set out an ambitious agenda

: a $25 minimum wage, Medicare for All, dismantling ICE, taxing the rich, protecting Social Security, and passing labor law reform including the PRO Act and card-check recognition for speedier union recognition. National Nurses United said voters expect a stop to health care cuts, stat.


President Trump can veto most bills Congress passes, but Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders

insisted

 on November 9 that Congress needs to do its job and pass a bold working-class agenda. If Trump vetoes the bills, that’ll raise the stakes in 2028 to elect a president who will sign them …

author: Mehran Khalili
title: What’s next for Europe’s autumn of protests?
content:
This article

What’s next for Europe’s autumn of protests? 

 was originally published by

Waging Nonviolence

.


It was a Wednesday afternoon in late October, and several marches were converging on Syntagma Square in Athens, the epicenter of Greek protest. There were teachers on strike, university students who’d camped in the square overnight, and high schoolers holding painted banners that read “From Greece to France, we’re fighting for modern schools.” Parents pushed strollers through the growing crowd, their toddlers looking on in wonder.


But not everyone was there for the same reason. Groups of black-clad young men ducking in and out of the march, faces covered, were play-fighting each other in a way that looked like a rehearsal. Riot police were lining the side streets, watching over it all with the bored expression of men waiting for their shift to end. And photojournalists were circling, hoping for the youths and the police to meet in a burst of violence that would pay for their day.


The violence didn’t happen this time. According to the

police count

, 10,000 people marched peacefully through central Athens. Afterwards, people hung around, arguing about politics and passing water bottles in the autumn sun. 


I keep thinking about those bored riot police, though, because they seemed to understand what organizers sometimes don’t: A government that has seen a lot of marches knows how to wait one out. The question for the teachers and students in Athens — and in Paris, Milan, Brussels, Lisbon, Madrid, Berlin, Vienna, Tirana and every other city caught up in Europe’s autumn of protest — is how to make saying no cost their governments more than saying yes.


An autumn of anger


The energy in Europe’s streets is bigger than many realize.  Young people have been protesting in at least nine European countries this autumn, most of them since mid-September. 


In France, a walkout over the lack of teachers at one high school in Créteil in September

spread to hundreds of schools

 within weeks. By mid-October, about 550,000 people (by the

government’s own count

) were marching in cities and towns across the country. In Spain and Portugal, the anger is about housing. Protesters set up camps in

Madrid’s Puerta del Sol

 and

Lisbon’s Rossio,

 and on Nov. 11, Spain’s tenants’ unions, backed by the big trade unions, held the country’s

first general strike in 14 years.

 It came after Maricarmen Abascal, an 87-year-old widow in fragile health, was forcibly removed from the Madrid apartment she had lived in for most of her life. She

died in hospital

 two weeks later.


Demonstrators march for the right to housing  after the eviction of  an 87-year-old woman from the home where she had lived for around seventy years in Madrid, Spain. (Wikimedia Commons)


The grievances overlap without being the same. It’s about schools in France and Greece, university tuition in

Belgium

 and

Albania

, university budgets in

Austria

, military conscription in

Germany

, and rent in Portugal and Spain, where the average rent is now

98.7 percent

 of what a young person earns in a month. But running beneath most of them is a familiar story: governments that say there’s no money for schools, or for people who are struggling, always, somehow, manage to find it for something else, often weapons.


In France, Germany and

Italy

, protesters have made that link. France’s

2027 budget

 adds $7 billion for defense and just $1.2 billion for schools, while

cutting 1,588 teaching posts

. In Germany, young people marched in more than 30 cities on Oct. 31, angry, as

Al Jazeera reported

, that military spending is rising while education funding is cut. 


The protests have achieved some modest wins. On Oct. 26, France’s government promised to

replace Parcoursup

, the hated university admissions system, cap first-year high school classes at 28, and add 500 teaching posts. And in Serbia, a student movement that began after a railway station canopy

collapsed in Novi Sad two years ago

 turned itself into an electoral list and, on Oct. 25,

beat Aleksandar Vučić, Serbia’s strongman of 14 years

. 


Sign Up for our Newsletter


We’ll send you a weekly email with the latest articles.


Facts like these are why, in my organizing circles, there’s a lot of talk of a “European wave.” I think we should be careful with that phrase, though, because it suggests a level of coordination and a plan that doesn’t — yet — exist. The reporting I …

author: infolibre
title: Fossil Tech: Η νέα συμμαχία των BigTech με τους Big Oil και πώς οδηγεί τον πλανήτη σε κατάρρευση
content:
ΦΩΤΟ: Μια εικόνα από drone δείχνει το υπό κατασκευή εργοστάσιο xAI του Elon Musk στο Southaven του Μισισιπή. Το δεύτερο κέντρο δεδομένων του, που ονομάστηκε Colossus 2, είναι διπλάσιο σε μέγεθος από το προηγούμενο (Kevin Wurm_Reuters).


Από τις

Naomi Klein

 και

Astra Taylor (*)


Ένα απόσπασμα από το

τελευταίο βιβλίο

 των

Naomi Klein

 και

Astra Taylor

 με τίτλο

END TIMES FASCISM – And the Fight for the Living World,

το οποίο

παρουσιάστηκε

 μία ημέρα πριν την επίσημη κυκλοφορία του από την καναδική Globe and Mail.  Στο συγκεκριμένο απόσπασμα θίγεται ένα ζήτημα με το οποίο γνωρίζουμε όλοι ότι θα βρεθούμε αντιμέτωποι. Το 

 πώς ο αδηφάγος

εξορυκτισμός

  σε αγαστή συνεργασία με την τεχνητή νοημοσύνη επιδεινώνει την κλιματική κρίση σε μια πραγματικά μοιραία στιγμή για τον πλανήτη.


* * * *


Όταν ο Elon Musk δημιούργησε το xAI το 2023, βρέθηκε στη θέση που απεχθανόταν περισσότερο: πίσω. Οκτώ χρόνια νωρίτερα, είχε βοηθήσει τον Sam Altman να ιδρύσει την OpenAI, πριν από την πολύκροτη και αμφιλεγόμενη διαμάχη τους. Τώρα η OpenAI κυριάρχησε στον τομέα, αφήνοντας τον πλουσιότερο άνθρωπο του κόσμου να προσπαθεί να καλύψει τη διαφορά. Από την οπτική γωνία του, έπρεπε να κατασκευάσει τον μεγαλύτερο υπολογιστή που είχε γνωρίσει ποτέ ο κόσμος, και έπρεπε να το κάνει γρήγορα.


Θα το ονόμαζε Κολοσσό. Το όνομα αποτίει φόρο τιμής σε μια

τριλογία

 μυθιστορημάτων επιστημονικής φαντασίας των δεκαετιών του 1960 και του 1970, στην οποία ένας αυτόνομος υπερυπολογιστής που ονομάζεται Κολοσσός στρέφεται εναντίον της ανθρωπότητας και εκτοξεύει ένα πυρηνικό όπλο εναντίον της Σοβιετικής Ένωσης. Αυτή θα έπρεπε να ήταν η πρώτη ένδειξη ότι ο κ. Musk και η μηχανή του μπορεί να μην ήταν ιδανικοί γείτονες.


Τον Μάρτιο του 2024, αφού εξέτασε τις επιλογές του, ο πλουσιότερος άνθρωπος στον κόσμο δήλωσε: «Θα μετακινηθούμε γρήγορα στο Μέμφις». Έτσι τουλάχιστον

θυμάται

 ο Ted Townsend, πρόεδρος του Εμπορικού Επιμελητηρίου του Greater Memphis, τη στιγμή που ο κ. Musk αποδεχόταν το δελεαστικό πακέτο. Αυτό περιελάμβανε μεγάλη προσφορά για ένα τεράστιο άδειο εργοστάσιο που κάποτε παρήγαγε συσκευές και απασχολούσε περισσότερους από 700 εργάτες. Και όπως

ανέφερε

 η ProPublica, το Εμπορικό Επιμελητήριο παρείχε επίσης μια ειδική πενταμελή «ομάδα ειδικών επιχειρήσεων xAI» για να διασφαλίσει «υπηρεσία θυρωρού όλο το 24ωρο» και την «απρόσκοπτη εκτέλεση των σχεδίων ταχείας επέκτασης της εταιρείας».


Το Εμπορικό Επιμελητήριο ήταν αποφασισμένο να αποδείξει ότι μπορούσε να κινηθεί με «αστραπιαία ταχύτητα» για να γίνει «ένας παγκόσμιος κόμβος όπου η ταχύτητα συναντά την ισχύ».


Υπό αυστηρές συμφωνίες εμπιστευτικότητας, η κατασκευή του υπολογιστή ξεκίνησε σχεδόν αμέσως και ο κ. Musk αργότερα

 θα καυχιόταν

 ότι ολοκλήρωσε σε 122 ημέρες αυτό που θα χρειαζόταν στους ανταγωνιστές του δύο χρόνια. Η κύρια χρήση του Colossus θα ήταν να εκπαιδεύσει τον Grok, το «αντι-αφυπνισμένο» chatbot που τώρα ενσωματώνεται στην πλατφόρμα κοινωνικής δικτύωσης X του Musk, πρώην Twitter, καθώς και τη γεννήτρια εικόνων του Grok, η οποία σύντομα θα έβαζε τον δημιουργό του σε μπελάδες επειδή του επέτρεψε να γδύνει γυναίκες και κορίτσια χωρίς τη συγκατάθεσή τους.


Το «Τέρας που Τρώει Ηλεκτρικό Ρεύμα» κατά Τραμπ


Λίγους μήνες νωρίτερα, ο Ντόναλντ Τραμπ είχε περιγράψει σωστά την Τεχνητή Νοημοσύνη ως

«ένα τέρας που τρώει ηλεκτρικό ρεύμα» (

κάτι που το εννοούσε ως κομπλιμέντο). Στον Κολοσσό, με τις σειρές λευκών «υπολογιστικών δωματίων» και τους χοντρούς μαύρους σωλήνες ψύξης από κάτω, αυτό το τέρας ήταν στην πιο αδηφάγο φάση του. Το ερώτημα ήταν: τι είδους ηλεκτρική ενέργεια θα έτρωγε αυτό το τέρας;


Ο κ. Musk – διάσημος για τα ηλεκτρικά αυτοκίνητα, τις μπαταρίες και τα ηλιακά πάρκα της Tesla – επέλεξε τον τύπο ηλεκτρικής ενέργειας που μπορούσε να προμηθευτεί πιο γρήγορα και με την υψηλότερη ισχύ. Αυτό σήμαινε μεθάνιο, ένα εξαιρετικά ισχυρό ορυκτό καύσιμο. Και όχι σε μικρές ποσότητες: σε ένα σημείο, για να διατηρήσει σε λειτουργία τον πρώτο υπερυπολογιστή και τις περίπου 300.000 μονάδες επεξεργασίας γραφικών, ο κ. Musk

λειτουργούσε

 35 τουρμπίνες μεθανίου, οι οποίοι συνολικά παρήγαγαν αρκετή ενέργεια για να τροφοδοτήσουν περίπου 280.000 σπίτια στο Μέμφις.


Οι τεράστιες, βρυχώμενες τουρμπίνες ήταν ουσιαστικά φορητές βιομηχανικές γεννήτριες, το είδος που χρησιμοποιείται συνήθως σε μια απομακρυσμένη τοποθεσία χωρίς γραμμές ηλεκτροδότησης. Συνδέοντας αυτά τα μηχανήματα, ο κ. Musk ουσιαστικά κατασκεύασε αυτό που η

Αμάντα Γκαρσία,

title: Ozgur Ozel: "Em di Komîsyona Çavdêriyê de cih nagirin"
content:
Serokê Parlamentoyê Numan Kurtulmuş di çarçoveya hevdîtinên ji bo avakirina Komîsyona Çavdêriyê de,  li Enqereyê çû serdana Serokê Giştî yê Partiya NÛ Ozgur Ozel.


Ozgur Ozel piştî hevdîtina bi Kurtulmuş re daxuyaniyeke çapemeniyê da û helwesta partiya xwe ya li ser Komîsyona Çavdêriyê eşkere kir.


Ozgur Ozel destnîşan kir ku desthilat di warê demokratîkbûnê de gavên pêwîst navêje û xala 7emîn a rapora Komîteya Parlamentoyê ya ji bo demokratîkbûnê nayê bicihanîn.


Sedemê redkirinê


Ozel ragihand ku sîstema qeyûman berdewam dike, qeyûm li ser 3 kanalên televîzyonê hatine danîn û biryarên Dadgeha Destûra Bingehîn û Dadgeha Mafên Mirovan a Ewropayê nayên bicihanîn.


Ozel ev yek wekî sedemên cihnegirtina partiya xwe ya di nav Komîsyona Çavdêriyê de destnîşan kir.


Ozgur Ozel da zanîn ku Partiya NÛ dê ji ber van sedeman endaman nede Komîsyona Çavdêriyê ya ku biryar e li Parlamentoyê were damezirandin.


Serokê Giştî yê Partiya NÛ rexne li helwesta hikûmetê girt û diyar kir ku desthilat tenê jibo parastina pêgeha xwe gavên siyasî diavêje û got:


"Tekane tiştê ku di berjewendiya vî welatî de ye, rawestandina vê desthilatê ye. Hinekan tenê ji bo ku desthilata xwe bidomînin her tişt kir. Bila kes li ser pişta me hesaban neke"


Ji bo qonaxên piştî vê yên pêvajoyê, bila kes me tevlî hesabên xwe yên şexsî neke û liser pişta me hesaban daneyne. Ji niha û pê ve bila kes bi hizirkirina li ser me hesaban neke. Bila li gorî hebûn an nebûna me hesabên xwe bikin. Kes nikare kesî bixapîne. Dema hûn li wan deriyan dixin, hûn dê wan sozên ku we berê dabûn bînin bîra xwe. Ez dibêjim em di nava vî karî de nînin."


Serokê Parlamentoya Tirkiyeyê Numan Kurtulmuş di çarçoveya hewldanêndamezirandina Desteya Çavdêriyê de bi serok û nûnerên partiyên AK Partî, MHP, DEMPartî û Rêya Nû re jî hevdîtin kiribû.


Ev deste li gorî Yasaya Çarçoveyê ya Tebaxa 2026an li Parlamentoya Tirkiyeyê têavakirin û ji bo şopandina gavên pêvajoya aştiyê û bêçekbûnê hatiye plankirin lê belêredkirina Partiya NÛ dê bandorê li ser hevsengiya nûnertiya partiyan a di nava desteyêde bike.


"Em di nava vî karî de nînin"


Serokê Partiya NÛ Ozgur Ozel di berdewamiya axaftina xwe de got:


"Ji niha û pê ve eger hûn li cihekî deriyê Partiya NÛ bixin, dema hûn tên li wî derî dixin,hûn dê wan sozên ku we berê dabûn bi cih bînin; ne sozên ku we dane Partiya NÛ lê ez behsa wan sozan dikim ku we li ber komîteyê di girtenameyan de xistine bin îmzeyan. Ez ji wan kesên ku gotin 'em dê di demokratîkbûnê de her tim bi hev re bin' û pişt reparçe dikin re dibêjim. Ez ji wan kesên ku teslîmî burokratên Koşkê bûne re dibêjim. Ez ji wan kesên ku bi zext û zordariyê hewl didin tiştekî bikin re dibêjim, em di nava vîkarî de nînin. 


Ew kesên ku dixwazin em di nava van karan de bin, divê pêşî wan sozên ku di dîrokê dedane vî welatî bi cih bînin. Rapor li wir e, komîte li wir e. Ji niha û pê ve ew kesên ku bi serê xwe lîstikademokrasiyê dilîzin, bila kerem bikin bilîzin. Li wir we partiyeke mixalefetê ya 'meqbûl' jî dît; mixalefeta majesteyan!


Heta ji we tê bi kar bînin. Mixalefeteke ku hatiye hilbijartin, di hilbijartinan de bi serketiye, li kolanan bi deh hezaran kes li pey dimeşin û bi milyonan mirovan li meydanankom dike, dê rewabûnê nede wî zemînê ku hûn lê ne. Bi mixalefeta majesteyan re hûn dikarin li ser kîjan rêyê bixwazin bimeşin."


(AEK/AY)

author: Unknown
title: Riflessioni di alcunə giovani italianə sullo sciopero generale dell’11 di novembre a Barcellona
content:
Riceviamo e pubblichiamo un racconto sulla giornata di sciopero a Barcellona da parte di alcune compagne che vivono lì.


Mezzanotte dell’11 di novembre, qualche secondo dopo l’inizio dello sciopero generale per la casa. Nel cielo di Barcellona compaiono fuochi d’artificio da vari punti della città, seguiti da cori e canti, per festeggiare l’inizio della giornata. 

La libertá è quando comincia l’alba in una giornata di sciopero generale

 dice una strofa di una poesia di Joan Margarit, che circola nei giorni precedenti.  Qualche ora dopo, verso le 3.30/4, escono di casa lə primə compagnə per raggiungere a piedi i primi blocchi stradali delle principali arterie viarie della Catalogna. 

A Barcellona i principali obiettivi sono le varie 

ronde

, tangenziali con una funzione simile al raccordo anulare romano, che abbracciano tutta la cittá. Il livello di tensione con lə conduttricə di moto e macchine, determinatə a raggiungere i propri posti di lavoro, sono delle piú variegate. Nella 

ronda del mig

 a Lesseps tutto procede senza particolari problemi; ad uno dei tagli della 

ronda litoral

lə manifestantə, bardatə, si stendono sull’asfalto per dormire e recuperare le poche ore di sonno. In vari punti della Catalogna le macchine investono lə scioperanti procurando feritə; molte sono lə manifestantə che, visto il grande numero di persone, si autogesticono e separano per bloccare altre uscite o entrate della stessa arteria. Le reazioni sono delle piú diverse, tra chi tira fuori la sdraio felice di non andare a lavorare a chi ha un crollo psicotico quasi gritando tra le lacrime: “E il mio diritto di andare a lavorare dov’è? Io muoio se non vado a lavorare!”. Rispettando una buona tradizione catalana, quella de 

elfoc i la rauxa

, i primi fuochi della giornata riempono l’aria periferica barcellonina, bloccando persino l’entrata di zone logistiche strategiche come quella di Mercabarna e del porto di Barcellona.


L’adesione allo sciopero è storica, l’84% secondo le principali sigle sindacali. In Spagna non si vedeva uno sciopero generale cosí da almeno quattordici anni. 

Nonostante il tempo passato, si nota la tradizione 

vaguista

 della città con un programma giá ben collaudato: blocchi stradali a prime ore dell’alba, poi, mentre alcuni di questi si mantengono fino all’ora di pranzo come a Lesseps, iniziano i picchetti informativi (e meno informativi) per i vari quartieri. È evidente una differenza molto grande tra gli scioperi italiani e quelli di Barcellona. Qui la storia sindacale è molto differente. Mentre in Italia una delle tradizioni politiche piú forti, quelle dell’autonomia, nasce propriamente come movimento extraparlamentare e contro i principali sindacati (basta pensare alla ben nota cacciata di Lama alla Sapienza), qui sindacati come la CNT hanno avuto un ruolo centrale giá dalla resistenza antifranchista nel ‘36 . Oggi rilevante è soprattutto il ruolo della CGT, nata da una scissione della CNT, che mantiene viva la tradizione di sindacalismo anarchico e combattivo.


Se negli scioperi di dimensioni minori, come quelli per la Palestina, l’obiettivo dei 

cercavila

 di quartiere erano le filiali delle note multinazionali pro-israele, nella giornata dell’11 sono stati segnalati tutti i negozi aperti al grido di 

esquirol

 (crumiro). 


A Gràcia, quartiere ribelle fino a 10 anni fa ed oggi mangiato dagli expats e svuotato della maggior parte delle sue occupazioni, ci sono tre diversi picchetti che si muovono avanti e indietro per le strade principali, costringendo a chiudere piú o meno gentilmente ogni serranda. Piano piano gli animi si vanno scaldando e la fantasia cresce: piante ornamentali di hotel tirate per terra, farina sulle casse dei supermercati, immondizia all’entrata dei negozi, scritte, manifesti e pressioni in ogni porta illuminata o aperta. I lavoratori lasciano le proprie attivitá con piú o meno buona volontá, la maggior parte chiudono poco prima che arrivi la piccola manifestazione, alcuni si nascodono al buio mentre altri litigano e si confrontano con lə manifestantə, a cui viene tirata farina, uova e costretto con la forza a chiudere il negozio. Vengono risparmiate farmacie e altri servizi minimi, particolare accanimento avviene contro i negozi piú gentrificatori. Un lavoratore, mentre trasporta un pallet di prodotti a un supermercato, scappa alla vista del picchetto e i prodotti vengono distribuiti tra tuttə, dal succo ai pannolini. In altri quartieri il confronto è piú violento …

author: ROAPE
title: Statement of the Finishers Revolutionary Movement
content:
At the beginning of this year, young Ugandans (activists, researchers, academics and lawyers) came together under one roof to confront a question that could no longer be postponed: what becomes of Uganda after the sham elections of January 2026?


With the possibility of Muhoozi Kainerugaba succeeding his father, we gathered around a simple conviction: Uganda must not be handed from one generation of the same ruling family to another. Succession is not liberation. Changing the face at the top while preserving the same machinery of patronage, militarism and corruption is not the future Uganda deserves.


Under the name Finishers Revolutionary Movement, we committed ourselves to organizing Ugandans to reject this succession project and to take up the unfinished work of national democratic liberation.


What we stand for


The Finishers is more than a name. It is an idea: that Uganda’s liberation cannot remain an unfinished historical promise, and that our generation has a responsibility to finish the task. That means we will:


End dictatorship.


Dismantle systems of patronage and impunity.


Reclaim democratic power for the people.


Build a country capable of true economic independence.


What have we done


Since the beginning of the year, we have been organizing, teaching and rallying people to confront injustice and corruption and to recover the spirit of resistance that every generation of Ugandans has inherited. We have reminded our people that oppression survives not only through the violence of the state, but also through fear, silence and the belief that nothing can change.


Because political freedoms in Uganda have been brutally restricted, we have had to organize with caution. Much of our work has been quiet and covert, because even the ordinary act of bringing Ugandans together has become dangerous.


Why we write in mourning


In the last month, the state has descended on the Finishers with an iron hand. Three of our comrades have been arrested or disappeared.


Praise Aloikin 

was arrested, later released on court bail, and continues to face the state through an ongoing court case.


Byakika Abubaker 

and 

David Musiri 

have been taken, and their whereabouts remain unknown.


We mourn them. We fear for them. We are angry.


Yet we refuse to let their disappearance become the disappearance of an idea. The state may arrest a Finisher. It may abduct a Finisher. It may intimidate a Finisher. But it cannot arrest the hunger for freedom that brought us together.


We are Finishers. We are not terrorists. We are young Ugandans who looked at the country we are inheriting and decided we cannot remain spectators to its destruction. We chose to organize. We chose to resist. And we choose to continue.


Our demands


That the state immediately disclose the whereabouts of Byakika Abubaker and David Musiri, and return them safely to their families.


That the state end enforced disappearances and abductions of Ugandans for their political beliefs and organizing.


That the state stop criminalizing the right to organize, assemble and hold political ideas.


That Praise Aloikin be afforded a fair process, and that the case against her be dropped.


Our appeal to the people of Uganda


Do not leave the Finishers alone. Protect your own. Protect the people who are standing up for the country we all claim to love.


When a Finisher is taken, ask where they are. When a family is left searching for a disappeared son or daughter, stand with that family. When the state attempts to criminalize an idea, refuse to repeat its lies. When fear tells you to look away, remember that the person taken today could be your neighbour, your child, your brother, your sister, or you tomorrow.


The Finishers belong to the people, and so does the idea. You do not have to carry our name to carry it. You do not have to stand where we stand to believe that dictatorship must end. You do not have to be an activist to understand that Uganda cannot be inherited like a family estate


Our resolve


We do not know what the state will do next. We know only that repression is meant to make us disappear one by one, to isolate us from each other and to convince Uganda that resistance is futile. We refuse that outcome.


The disappearance of our comrades has deepened our grief, but it has also clarified our resolve. We will remember those who have been taken. We will stand with their families. We will demand their return. And we will continue the …

author: Farai Shawn Matiashe
title: Electrification in Africa means closing the energy access gap and reducing energy poverty
content:
At the United Nations climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, the COP31 presidency is pushing for a global target to increase electricity’s share of final energy consumption to

35% by 2035

, a central pillar of the conference.


The COP31 Turkish presidency proposed the global electrification target at the 2026 Bonn Climate Change Conference in June to encourage countries and businesses worldwide to electrify transport, buildings, and industry using renewable energy, helping to accelerate the shift away from fossil fuels.


But as delegates gather in the Mediterranean country for the climate summit known as Conference of the Parties 31 (COP31), the target risks overlooking the different energy realities Africa faces unless they place energy access and development at its centre.


For industrialised economies, electrification is all about replacing existing fossil fuel systems, while in Africa, some countries still want to build electricity infrastructure and distribution networks.


The new target, up from the current global rate of electrification of about 20%, comes at a time when Africa faces energy poverty and a huge electricity access gap.


About 600 million people lack electricity access, with half of them living in three countries, namely Nigeria, Ethiopia and the Democratic Republic of Congo,

according

 to the International Energy Agency.


Sub-Saharan Africa accounts for roughly 85% of the global population lacking electricity.


The 35 by 35 risks widening existing energy inequality


Dr Chigozie Nweke-Eze, founder of the Integrated Africa Power (IAP), an enterprise focused on solving energy and infrastructure deficits across the African continent, said the proposed 35 by 35 target risks overlooking the different energy realities Africa faces.


Some of the solar panels which are part of a solar mini grid in Hakwata Chipinge in Zimbabwe. Photo by Farai Shawn Matiashe.


“There is a fundamental distinction between the energy transition in industrialised economies and that in many African countries,” he said.


“There is also a risk that a global target expressed as the share of electricity in final energy consumption could obscure inequalities between countries.”


Nweke-Eze said a global increase in electricity consumption does not mean improved energy access for populations that remain disconnected from the grid.


“Nor does it automatically address the affordability and reliability of electricity for households and small businesses,” he said.


In industrialised economies, electrification is largely about replacing petrol and diesel vehicles with electric vehicles, and industrial gas boilers and household gas heaters with electric heat pumps.


For Africa, it means it must build entirely new energy systems to support its expanding population and development aspirations. The continent is simultaneously attempting to shift towards renewable energy that is both cleaner and more sustainable.


Nweke-Eze said electrification cannot happen at scale without adequate generation capacity, transmission and distribution networks, reliable electricity supply, and affordable connections.


But Nweke-Eze said that Africa should be an integral part of the 35-by-35 ambition, with the target adapted to the continent’s unique energy context, recognising its diverse starting points and prioritising pathways that expand energy access and address the needs of underserved communities.


Another initiative

launched

 at COP31 is the Global Rooftop Solar Declaration, which aims to double the number of solar-powered households globally to 300 million by 2030. Endorsed by a cross-continental coalition including Kenya and Nigeria, the initiative offers a practical pathway to addressing Africa’s energy access gap by accelerating the deployment of household solar, particularly in communities underserved by centralised electricity grids.


It focuses on overcoming barriers such as high upfront costs, complex permitting processes and skills shortages that can slow the adoption of decentralised

solar solutions

.


This, Nweke-Eze argued, also requires a broader understanding of how progress towards electrification is measured. Africa should not be judged solely against the pace at which industrialised economies replace fossil-fuel technologies, but also by how effectively its countries expand electricity access, develop productive energy infrastructure and improve the quality of energy services.

author: Fabrizio Floris
title: The Sahara was never a border
content:
In July, Algeria and Mali reinstated their ambassadors and reopened their airspace to each other, more than a year after Algerian forces shot down a Malian drone near the border town of Tin Zaouatine.

Al Jazeera reported the thaw

; Agence France-Presse (AFP)

added

 that rebel advances in northern Mali had accelerated it, and that restoring cross-border security cooperation was a priority. In September, Algeria’s prime minister was

received in Bamako with military honors

. 

The reconciliation is about a border that both governments say they cannot control.

Farther east, on the Algeria–Niger frontier, the same logic works differently. The Niger-based NGO, Alarme Phone Sahara, counted more than 34,000 people

expelled from Algeria to Niger in 2025

, a record, up from 31,404 in 2024 and 26,031 in 2023. Migrants who are not Nigerien are left at a desert spot known as Point Zéro and they walk about 15km to Assamaka.

Both stories treat the Sahara as a line to be secured: a front to be held, a space to be cleared of the wrong people. Judith Scheele’s

Shifting Sands: A Human History of the Sahara

 (2025) is a sustained argument that this is the wrong picture. An anthropologist at the

École des hautes études en sciences sociales

, Scheele

combines historical archives, including many Arabic-language accounts, with decades of fieldwork

 and interviews with Saharans themselves. Edward Said taught us that places are imagined before they are governed; Fernand Braudel, that seas link as much as they divide. Scheele applies both lessons to a desert.

Scheele’s Sahara is a human world. The book moves from a city-building civilization in Libya’s Fezzan, contemporary with the Roman Empire, through the caravan trades that carried gold, salt, textiles, and enslaved people to the borderlands of Algeria, Mali, Niger, Chad, and Libya that she knows from her own travels.

The caravan of gold and spice is the image that outsiders inherited, and Scheele asks readers to separate Saharan from trans-Saharan trade: the second is the part that crosses the region and so leaves traces in archaeological sites and in sources written beyond it. Most Saharan trade, she suggests, was in staples, the cereals, dates, salt, cloth, dried meat and skins that groups such as the Arba’a and the Tubu carried. The fabled gold was something the explorer René Caillié never saw in Timbuktu.

The trade in staples survives, and it remains, in Scheele’s phrase, “relatively democratic”: anyone with a four-by-four, some capital and enough cousins along the road can become a carrier or trade on their own account, and negotiate with Malian customs officials. She also notes that the advance of trade routes, and the political rivalries that followed in the Maghreb, pushed North Africans deeper into the desert until they had little choice but to become trans-Saharan traders. Mobility, here, was as much pressure as opportunity. In northern Mali, she visits al-Khalil in 2009 and finds its trade booming. The oldest permanent house there dates from 1993 and began as a store for arms for the separatist rebellion of the early 1990s. Commerce, rebellion and settlement, in the Sahara, are often built with the same walls. What these cases share is a desert that is never empty. It is inhabited not by permanent settlements alone but by routes, encounters, negotiations, and obligations.

Scheele applies the same method to the subjects that dominate the headlines. Slavery, racism, religious militancy, terrorism and desertification each get their own treatment, and in each case, as a

reviewer for


Foreign Affairs


notes

, she shows how familiar narratives often grow out of outsiders’ fantasies of the desert as an inhospitable, impermeable barrier. She does not romanticize that circulation. The same routes carried enslaved people, reproduced racial hierarchies and concentrated wealth in few hands. Nor did colonial rule invent every division: Saharan societies had their own rivalries and territorial distinctions. But colonial administrations hardened them into borders drawn around distant capitals, and began to treat older routes as marginal, illicit, or dangerous. Independent states inherited that architecture, and with it a contradiction: communities keep depending on cross-border movement, while official policy reads that movement as a failure of control.

This is why emptiness is never an innocent description. Calling an inhabited space empty lets existing relationships …

author: WoMin
title: Women Unite to Defend the Congo Basin Against Extractivism – A Call for Climate Justice at COP31
content:
As world leaders gather in Antalya, Türkiye, for the 31st UN Climate Change Conference (COP31), taking place from 9–20 November 2026, women from the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), the Republic of Congo and Cameroon are raising an urgent message: there can be no climate justice without defending the Congo Basin, protecting community territories and recognising the leadership of women on the frontlines of environmental struggles.


The Congo Basin is one of the world’s most important ecological treasures, acting as the “

second lungs

 of the Earth”, after the Amazon, which is being decimated. Spanning over four million square kilometres across six countries, its forests, rivers and peatlands play a vital role in regulating the global climate, protecting biodiversity and sustaining millions of people. For Indigenous Peoples and local communities, the forest is not simply a natural resource; it is their home, heritage, identity and source of life.


Yet this vital ecosystem faces growing threats from mining, logging, oil and gas extraction, deforestation and expanding infrastructure. Across the Congo Basin, rising demand for minerals is increasing pressure on forests and community territories.


Recent investigations have

documented

 mining concessions overlapping with community forests in the DRC, gold-mining-related

forest destruction and water pollution

 in the Republic of Congo, and

concerns over the impacts

 of the Lobé-Kribi iron-ore project on forests and livelihoods in Cameroon.


This exposes a growing contradiction: while governments promote renewable energy as a solution to the climate crisis, the extraction of minerals needed for the energy transition can create new threats to forests, water resources and the communities that depend on them.


For women in the Congo Basin, this is not an abstract debate. It means polluted rivers, disappearing food sources, loss of agricultural land and declining access to forests.


Women on the frontlines expose the cost of extractivism


To strengthen collective resistance, women and community organisations from the DRC, the Republic of Congo and Cameroon came together for a

cross-border solidarity exchange

 to share stories of resistance, expose the impacts of extractivism and develop strategies to defend the Congo Basin.


Over three days, organisations including

Centre d’Encadrement pour la Promotion de la Femme et la jeune fille

 (CEPF),

Dynamique des femmes pour le développement

 (DYFED),

Green Development Advocates

 (GDA), and the Association pour le Respect des Droit des population autochtones et du développement rural et du Droit de l’homme (ARPA2DH)

shared their experiences and struggles. Testimonies from women in Lessoukou, Mayoko, Mangi, Bongonde and Bandzonko revealed the devastating impacts of mining and forest exploitation.


In Lessoukou, 17 of the community’s 24 villages are reportedly occupied by mining companies, threatening access to ancestral lands and traditional livelihoods. Élisé Matsanga, an Indigenous woman from Lessoukou, shared:


“

Agriculture once enabled us to feed our families and send our children to school. Today, because of corporate activities and the loss of access to our lands, we can no longer farm as we used to. We have lost our livelihoods

.”


In Mangi, Tshopo Province, Nyota described how communities are excluded from decisions affecting their territories while rivers become increasingly polluted.


“

We are forced to walk up to three kilometres to find safe drinking water, and sometimes even our children have no choice but to drink polluted water. Our lands, forests and rivers are our sources of livelihood, yet we watch helplessly as they are destroyed

.”


In Bandzonko, Republic of Congo, Odile, the village chief,

described how mining pollution

 has forced women to walk up to 15 kilometres in search of water, exposing families to serious health risks. In Bongonde, Équateur Province, Annie Mboyo, a community woman,

highlighted the disappearance

 of mushrooms, caterpillars, wild fruits and fish, resources that have traditionally sustained community food systems. Meanwhile, in Mayoko, Oko Jeanine, another community woman, denounced the lack of consultation and the destruction of agricultural fields by mining companies.


“

These lands belong to us. They are our heritage, our livelihoods and our identity. How can companies demand that we obtain permits to cultivate our own land while they extract …
