author: Keelan Jacobs
title: Inuit-led program to replace Child First Initiative with $575M in proposed funding
content:
After years of relying on a federally administered program to help Inuit children access essential health, education and social services, Inuit leadership is preparing to take greater control over how those supports are delivered 


Inuit Tapiriit Kanatami (ITK) President Natan Obed and Indigenous Services (ISC) Minister Mandy Gull-Masty released the

 Pirutsiagutiit National Framework

 at a news conference on Parliament Hill Wednesday. 


The framework sets the direction for Pirutsiagutiit — meaning “resources for growing well” in Inuktut — which launches April 1, 2027, and replaces the interim Inuit Child First Initiative.


Budget 2026 proposes $575 million over five years, beginning in 2027-28, to renew the existing initiative and fund the transition. The four Inuit treaty organizations — Inuvialuit Regional Corporation, Nunavut Tunngavik Incorporated, Makivvik and the Nunatsiavut Government — will co-develop regional approaches with Canada and determine how supports are delivered within their respective treaties and self-government agreements.


“Inuit children have long faced barriers to accessing the health, education and social supports they need to thrive,” Obed said. “Pirutsiagutiit marks an important shift from an interim approach toward a program grounded in Inuit self-determination, with Inuit treaty organizations playing a central role in shaping how supports are delivered. This is about more than improving access to services; it is about ensuring Inuit have a meaningful say in the well-being and future of our children.”


Crown Indigenous Relations and Northern Affairs Minister Rebecca Alty, ITK President Natan Obed and Indigenous Services Minister Mandy Gull-Masty at a press conference in Ottawa Wednesday (November 18th, 2026). Photo by: Keelan Jacobs/APTN


Gull-Masty described the program as the product of years of joint work. 


“Pirutsiagutiit reflects years of working together with Inuit Tapiriit Kanatami and Inuit treaty organizations to build a program shaped by Inuit knowledge, leadership and priorities,” she said. “This new program is an important step toward Inuit leading decisions about the care and services their children need, in ways that reflect their own communities and cultures.”


The announcement builds directly on the Inuit Child First Initiative, launched in 2018 through the Inuit-Crown Partnership Committee as a temporary measure while a permanent, Inuit-specific approach was developed. 


According to the news release issued by ITK and Indigenous Services Canada, over the eight years it’s been operating, the initiative has helped Inuit children access more than 330,000 health, social and educational products, services and supports. Similar categories of supports remain eligible under Pirutsiagutiit, with service coordination focused on navigation and case management to reduce duplication and help families use existing programs.


Each treaty organization will verify eligibility based on its own membership criteria. The program is available to eligible Inuit children across Canada, regardless of where they live, provided the child is recognized by one of the four organizations and is under the age of majority in their province or territory. Detailed regional criteria and delivery models will be finalized before launch; further information is expected in spring 2027.


Leaders from the four regions welcomed the framework while underscoring that implementation remains the real test. 


Inuvialuit Regional Corporation chair and CEO Erwin Elias called it “a starting point, not a result” and said the organization will continue working with Indigenous Services Canada toward launch, expecting the federal government to follow through for Inuvialuit children. 


Nunavut Tunngavik Inc. President Gloria Uluqsi stressed that too many families in Nunavut still face barriers and that the program must give Inuit a greater role in decisions affecting their children. “Too many Inuit families in Nunavut continue to face barriers to getting these services.” She continued “ Pirutsiagutiit is an important step toward addressing these gaps”


Makivvik President Pita Aatami framed the shift as “an exciting step forward, giving Inuit a stronger role in shaping the services and support we provide to our children and families”  adding that communities “know our strengths, and we know what our children need to succeed.”


Crown-Indigenous Relations Minister Rebecca Alty and Liberal MPs Lori Idlout …

author: Daron Letts
title: Kotierk family competes on Family Feud Canada
content:
Wednesday night’s episode of

Family Feud Canada

 on CBC features the Kotierk family of Nunavut competing for up to $30,000 in cash prizes.


“It was a lot of fun,” said team captain Kunuk Kotierk, who caught up with Nunatsiaq News ahead of the episode’s première. “We did it on a whim.”


The whim was his.


This past spring, he submitted an application for himself and four family members to compete on the show.


The rest of the Kotierk team includes Kunuk Kotierk’s uncle

David Joanasie

, aunt

Emily Joanasie

, aunt

Jessica Kotierk

, and mom

Aluki Kotierk

.


On each episode, two families of five face off to determine the most popular answers to survey questions.


The application process included three interview stages, held weeks apart, leaving some in the family to doubt whether they would be selected.


“I had confidence the whole way that we were going to make it,” Kunuk Kotierk said. “I was like

—

 this is a sure thing.”


The family practised over the summer by watching

Family Feud

 reruns while trying to out-guess the on-screen contestants, he said.


“We also would look up a lot of

Family Feud

-type questions online,” he added.


His sibling, Siku Rojas, the team’s understudy, played the role of show host Gerry Dee during these sessions.


“And then ‘lo and behold, we end up getting flown to Toronto and filming for a weekend,” Kunuk Kotierk said. “When we came on for our episode, everything was lit up, and it looked magical.”


The show is co-produced by CBC and Zone3 and shot in the national broadcaster’s downtown Toronto studio. The family was put up in a nearby hotel.


During the taping, Rojas sat in the audience.


“It was really surreal,” Rojas said about watching the family on set. “It’s edited, so I am excited to see what they keep in the show.”


Their brother shares that curiosity.


“Me and my family like to talk a lot and so we were definitely chatty with Gerry Dee,” he said. “There was moments where he would go off script and it was like, ‘Oh this is something only we can see because this is not going to be on the show.'”


Wednesday’s episode is titled

Who’s the Sexiest Game Show Host?


The Kotierks are the third Nunavut

family on the show.

Their episode airs at 7:30 p.m. Wednesday on CBC and is also watchable on the CBC Gem app.

author: Savannah Peters, The Associated Press
title: As Deb Haaland elected first Indigenous woman governor in ‘US,’ other Pueblo women still face hurdles
content:
Prior to her election as Governor of ‘New Mexico,’ Democratic nominee Deb Haaland answers questions during an interview at her campaign headquarters in ‘Albuquerque’ on Oct. 9.

Photo by Susan Montoya Bryan/AP


This story is published through the

Global Indigenous Reporting Network

 at The Associated Press, and appears here with permission and minor style edits.


On the morning of Kawaika (

Laguna Pueblo

)’s annual Feast Day, Ashley Sarracino knelt in her family home holding clothespins between her teeth. 


She straightened her niece’s black cotton manta, a traditional one-shouldered dress, and tied a sash around her waist. 


On these days, Sarracino is a caretaker, dressing relatives for the harvest dance and helping feed up to 150 guests. And as a former member of the Pueblo Council, she knows how to balance those traditional responsibilities with official duties. 


“To me, those things aren’t in conflict at all,” she said. 


Yet even as another Kawaika woman, former “U.S.” Interior Secretary Deb Haaland, is set to become the first

Indigenous woman state governor

, women with leadership aspirations such as Sarracino say they are swimming upstream in their Pueblo communities. 


READ MORE:


In Nevada, Indigenous land protectors face off with a Canadian mining company


Sarracino said she was forced off the council after alleging she was paid less because she was a woman, a claim Pueblo officials deny. 


In some of the

19 Pueblos

 in “New Mexico,” including Kawaika, tribal law and customs do not allow women to hold top government positions. 


Haaland told The Associated Press she was once nominated to serve on her Pueblo council but did not make it past a primary. She quipped it was “easier to raise $1 million and run for Congress” than succeed in Pueblo politics. 


“It’s still a man’s world in a lot of Pueblo communities, and certainly in mine,” she said. 


Ashley Sarracino, right, and her sister Lindsay Sarracino prepare food for the annual Feast Day celebration on Oct. 17 in Paraje, a village within Kawaika (Pueblo of Laguna), ‘New Mexico.’

Photo by Roberto E. Rosales/AP


A fight over women’s place in tribal leadership 


Sarracino was offered a road map familiar to ambitious young Indigenous people: Leave the reservation to get an education, then return home to serve your community. 


She built a career in non-profit work and political organizing, including as chair of her county’s Democratic Party. 


In 2022, Sarracino was nominated by a Pueblo Elder to run for council secretary. She finished second but was appointed to the post after a resignation. 


“Finally, I had an opportunity to use my skills to help my own community,” she said. 


While reviewing budget documents, Sarracino discovered she was being paid US$14,000 less than her male predecessor. She asked the Pueblo governor for an explanation, sparking a bitter dispute that would end her tenure on council. 


The council says Sarracino was paid less because she lacked experience and that she abandoned her post. 


But Sarracino insists she was ousted and that the pay discrepancy reflects sexist attitudes embedded in tribal law. 


Since 1996, the Pueblo’s election code has allowed women to run for council treasurer and secretary, but it does not explicitly allow them to serve as governor or lieutenant governor. 


Its constitution, last amended in 2012, refers to the governor as “he” and “him.” 


READ MORE:


Across the border, Indigenous fears spike amidst ‘U.S.’ immigration crackdown


Sarracino’s dispute landed in tribal court but was dismissed this year on sovereign immunity grounds and she’s exhausted her appeals. 


The case took a toll on her mental health. She said it’s been bittersweet to watch Haaland make political history. 


“We all know she would never have the same opportunity here,” she said. 


Yet Haaland’s ascent could help change attitudes at home. 


Emily Hunt, who became Kawaika’s first woman elected official in the late 1990s with legal help from Haaland, believes the Pueblo will someday nominate a woman governor. 


“Whether I’ll see it in my lifetime, I don’t know,” Hunt said. 


Ashley Sarracino poses at her home on Oct. 17 in Paraje.

 Photo by Roberto E. Rosales/AP


Pueblo governance is varied and complex 


Some Pueblos retain traditional theocracies, with government roles appointed by ceremonial Elders and reserved for men. 


Charlotte Little, a citizen of Katishtya (

San Felipe Pueblo

), said …

author: Unknown
title: World of Hurt: Abolitionist Reflections on the Root Causes of Harm
content:
What causes people to harm others? Reactionaries label certain individuals—or, worse, entire demographics—inherently harmful to justify their own efforts to inflict harm via vigilante attacks, policing, and the court system. Others suggest that experiencing harm can lead some to harm others, as suggested by the common catchphrase “Hurt people hurt people.” Here, we examine this popular notion and propose a more useful framework for understanding the root causes of harm.


Today, a ruling class headed by billionaires and aspiring autocrats is making

the celebration of violence

 central to their narratives and policies, openly campaigning against empathy itself. In this context, the question of what causes harm—and how to interrupt it without reinforcing cycles of hurt and oppression—has become increasingly urgent.


World of Hurt


Abolitionists

 who envision a world without

police

 or

prisons

 often face questions about how to address serious forms of interpersonal harm.

Mutual aid

 and resource redistribution may reduce behaviors that arise as a consequence of lack of access to basic needs. But how can we understand those who seem to hurt others out of cruelty or disregard? If we don’t accept the idea that some people are monsters who must be locked up to keep the rest of us safe, how can we make sense of their actions?


Defenders of the criminal legal system frequently cite rape and abuse to justify prisons and imprisonment. In response, abolitionists have devoted considerable energy to developing

alternative approaches

 to addressing sexual violence. Groups such as Generation Five have proposed

principles for responding to child sexual abuse

 through transformative justice frameworks. By focusing on one of the most stigmatized forms of harm, they aim to cut to the root of

carceral thinking

 in order to reimagine safety and justice.


But creative responses beyond the state are not enough. To end sexual violence, we also need to understand its root causes.


Feminist activists coined the term “

rape culture

” to describe how social norms and institutions enable sexual harm. In addition to these structural effects of gender and power, others argue that past experiences of harm shape the behavior of individuals who go on to harm others. One of the most common ways to articulate this principle appears in the phrase “

Hurt people hurt people

.”


Let’s take a closer look to see where this popular saying came from, how it is used, and its implications for an abolitionist understanding of harm.


The Trajectory of a Slogan


From

self-help books

 and

therapist blogs

 to the

writings of abolitionist activists

, “hurt people hurt people” has become an influential account of the psychology of violence. It suggests that some people harm others not because they are pathological monsters, but because they too are victims whose unresolved trauma shapes their hurtful actions.


The precise origins of the phrase are opaque, but it has been in circulation

at least since the 1950s

. It seems to have begun trending in the 1990s in therapeutic and pop psychology circles. A popular 1993 Christian self-help book titled

Hurt People Hurt People

 promised to support readers in healing from painful past relationships “with empathy and biblical insight.” In recent years, this phrase has been repeated by everyone from megachurch pastor Rick Warren to Hollywood actor Andrew Garfield to the stripper con artist character Destiny in the movie

Hustlers

 to

the metal band Mudvayne

. It appears most widely in discourse about therapy, self-help, trauma, and religion.


On the surface, “hurt people hurt people” might seem an odd slogan for radical critics of the

prison industrial complex

. As a maxim of folk wisdom that spans mainstream, religious, feminist, and radical circles, we should consider carefully whether it aligns with our values.


In some ways, it makes sense that abolitionists would find this formulation promising. It humanizes people who cause harm, whereas dehumanizing them paves the way for carceral responses. It attributes the roots of harmful behavior not to inherent depravity, but to contingent circumstances that can be changed. It resonates with the lived experiences of some people who are struggling to heal and to be accountable for hurting others. It seems to offer a hopeful pathway towards a world without sexual violence by intervening in support of those who have been harmed in order to …

author: Valerie Anne
title: LGBTQ+ Representation in Television Hits Devastating Lows
content:
As I’m sure you’ve noticed, LGBTQ+ representation in media is at the lowest it’s been in over a decade.

GLAAD’s latest Where We Are in TV study showed some bleak results that reflect the state of the country due to the hateful administration we live under and the wealthy conservatives who own most of the media conglomerates. Trans representation took the biggest hit, going from 33 characters to a measly SEVEN, and since three of them were on shows that were cancelled and four are from limited series, none of those seven will be returning next season. NONE. Devastating.

Twenty-five percent of LGBTQ+ characters have left our screens since last year, which brings the stats to their lowest point in over a decade. Cable television hit a 16-year low. BLEAK.

Streamers have more queer representation than cable and broadcast characters put together, but we have lost almost 100 characters from streamers as well, so even that isn’t great news. And combining streaming, cable, and broadcast, of all LGBTQ+ characters, 44% of them are characters of color, which is the lowest percentage since GLAAD’s 2017-2018 report.

Pride points out that it seems wild to imagine because some of the buzziest shows of the last few years feature queer characters: The Hunting Wives, Hazbin Hotel, Pluribus, Stranger Things, Heated Rivalry. I don’t think this show made it into the count, but we also have Sterling Point and now The Body. Queer people show up for shows that feature them, and queer people are great at telling unique stories. Alas, too many higher-ups lean on outdated Christian ideals and won’t invest in us in an effort to silence us.

This is especially wild because, while it reflects what the political times want you to believe (that queer people are outsiders, among other things), it doesn’t reflect the actual statistics. Every generation reports identifying as gayer than the last, so representation should also be at a steady increase to reflect reality, not a drastic decrease.

The actual numbers of LGBTQ+ characters on broadcast and cable shows are harrowing to look at. There are dozens of characters on any given TV show, and dozens of shows on each network, and yet the highest number among them is HBO with 15 characters. The second-highest is a big drop down, with Fox and Starz coming in with 10 characters each.

The numbers start off a little more promising for streaming, with 116 on Netflix, but then they also start dropping dramatically, with 68 on Prime Video and then again a steep drop to Hulu with 24.

I’m sure you, like I have, felt the shift even before you saw these numbers. Here at Autostraddle, we used to have to have a weekly TV roundup because there were so many queer characters on cable and broadcast shows that we couldn’t keep up with individual recaps. We used to do Pop Culture Fix twice a week to keep up with the news coming at us from all angles. And now there aren’t enough recurring characters for a weekly roundup and barely enough news for 10-15 links a week in a pop culture roundup.

It’s disheartening to see these numbers go down more and more every year when we were in such a steady incline for so long, but the fact is: We’re still here. We’re still out here writing well-rounded characters and telling our stories and watching and supporting the LGBTQ+ characters we DO still have on TV. We will not go quietly into the night. We will keep shouting and keep showing up for the queer shows doing it right until these numbers make sense again.

More queer pop culture news (that’s less depressing)

+ Phoebe Bridgers was the musical guest on this weekend’s SNL

+ Former wee lesbian (on Derry Girls) Nicola Coughlan doubles down on her pro-trans, anti-Harry Potter stance and we love her for it

+ Beanie Feldstein had nothing but lovely things to say about working with Ariana Grande on Focker-In-Law

+ Kate McKinnon and Queen Latifah are among those listed to be part of the NBC100 Live Celebration next month

+ Sarah Paulson and Holland Taylor have no plans to marry; Sarah Paulson doesn’t even like the idea of someone calling her a “wife”

+ The Hunting Wives stars Brittany Snow and Malin Akerman play fuck, U-Haul, kill in an interview, which eventually devolves into them complimenting each other’s past performances

+ Kate Berlant is going to co-host next year’s Spirit Awards

+ Rapper Young Miko has been dubbed the “Sexiest Lesbian Alive” by Curve magazine

+ Aspyn Ovard exposes fellow ex-Mormon socialites to the …

author: Sara Fayyazi
title: Supreme Court Rejects Trump Administration’s Bid to Restrict Gender Affirming Care for Incarcerated People
content:
On October 21, 2026, the Supreme Court rejected the Trump administration’s request to restrict medical treatment and accommodations for transgender people in federal prisons. The decision allows a lower court order blocking the policy to remain in place while the legal challenge proceeds. The ruling is an important development in the ongoing debate over transgender rights, access to healthcare, and the federal government’s authority over incarcerated people.

The dispute began after President Donald Trump issued an executive order restricting federal funding for certain medical treatments for transgender people in government custody. In response, the Bureau of Prisons introduced a policy that would end hormone therapy and gender-affirming surgeries for incarcerated people with gender dysphoria. The policy also sought to restrict certain accommodations for transgender prisoners.

Gender dysphoria is the distress some people experience when their gender identity does not align with their sex assigned at birth. The administration argued that these gender-affirming treatments were not necessary and that restricting them was justified by security and administrative concerns within federal prisons.

However, the policy faced legal challenges from three transgender people incarcerated in federal prisons, including one transgender woman and two transgender men. Their attorneys argued that the new restrictions would force the end of treatments that the Bureau of Prisons had provided to people with gender dysphoria since 1992.

The policy could affect nearly 1,000 incarcerated people in federal custody. The lawsuit raises questions about whether the government can discontinue established medical treatments for incarcerated people and what constitutional protections apply to people in its custody.

A lower federal court blocked the administration from enforcing the policy. The Justice Department then appealed to the Supreme Court, asking the justices to pause that ruling and allow the restrictions to take effect while the case continued. On October 21, the Supreme Court rejected the emergency request in an unsigned order. Justices Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas stated that they would have granted the request. The decision leaves the lower court’s order in place, preventing the administration from immediately enforcing the restrictions.

However, the Supreme Court’s decision does not resolve the underlying lawsuit or determine whether the administration’s policy is constitutional. The legal challenge will continue in the lower courts.

The case highlights the challenges transgender people face when seeking health care in settings where the government controls their medical decisions. Incarcerated people depend on prison authorities for access to doctors, medication, and other necessary services so when a policy restricts particular treatment, people in custody may have limited options for obtaining care independently.

Although the ruling does not end the case, it prevents the Trump administration from immediately implementing the restrictions while the legal proceedings continue. The outcome of the lawsuit will have important consequences for transgender people in federal prisons if the restrictions are placed and as the case moves forward, it shows the importance of questioning how government policies affect vulnerable populations and how government decisions apply to people whose freedom and access to healthcare are already limited.

author: David S. D'Amato
title: La Via Libertaria all’egalitarismo
content:
Di

David S. D’amato

. Originale:

The Libertarian Road to Egalitarianism

, del 14 novembre 2014. Tradotto da

Enrico Sanna

.


Secondo uno

studio recente di Emmanuel Saez e Gabriel Zucman per l’Ufficio nazionale per la ricerca economica

, “

lo 0,1% delle famiglie [americane] possiede tanta ricchezza quanto il 90% meno ricco

”. Sempre secondo lo studio, la tanto declamata “ripresa” non ha raggiunto la classe media; i benefici sono andati alla cima della piramide.


Mentre una piccola frazione della popolazione ammassa gran parte della ricchezza nazionale, esperti e accademici accusano e offrono soluzioni. Com’è facile immaginare, si accusa il libero mercato di causare differenze crescenti di ricchezza e reddito. Fautori delle liberalizzazioni e del libero mercato, i libertari sono spesso accusati di vivere in un mondo di fantasia, di ignorare il problema della disuguaglianza.


Siamo noi stessi a farlo: quando si arriva al dunque, troppi si sentono a disagio, si difendono sostenendo che la disuguaglianza

non è

 un problema, e che bisogna invece vedere lo stile di vita o qualche altro parametro. “Il capitalismo è un bene per i poveri!” Invece i libertari dovrebbero accettare il semplice fatto che la disuguaglianza è un grosso problema.


Non dobbiamo vedere nella disuguaglianza un punto debole del discorso sulla libertà economica, o una questione irrisolvibile. Le attuali relazioni economiche non sono il risultato della libertà di scambio o della legittima proprietà privata. In fatto di disuguaglianza, la ragione sta dalla parte dei libertari. Libertà e eguaglianza sono di fatto complementari, si rafforzano reciprocamente: dalla prima deriva la seconda.


Anarchici individualisti come Lysander Spooner sostenevano che “ricchezza e povertà estreme” sono il risultato del “diritto positivo”, sostituiscono il diritto naturale con un diritto arbitrario, “danno vita a monopoli e privilegi”. Sotto il capitalismo, spiega, chi possiede un certo capitale ha un particolare potere economico che non ha niente a che vedere con la libertà di produrre, scambiare e competere. In un’ottica generale, l’intervento dello stato beneficia chi è ricco e ha appoggi politici, oltre alle élite che possono influire su chi scrive e applica le regole che tutti dobbiamo rispettare.


Il meccanismo non è perfetto, e per questo sopra il capitalismo monopolistico troviamo tutto uno strato di misure chiaramente intese a proteggere i lavoratori, i consumatori e i poveri. Ma nessuna di queste misure riesce a intaccare l’obiettivo di fondo dell’intervento statale, il quale espropria i legittimi proprietari e mette le masse al servizio dei datori di lavoro. L’obiettivo storico dello stato, in breve, è la lotta di classe permanente, l’uso del proprio potere per tenere al sicuro un’aristocrazia socioeconomica.


La sinistra istituzionale ha certamente ragione sull’uguaglianza, ma tende a sbagliare in fatto di libertà, diritti individuali e mercato. L’anarchismo di mercato è per la libertà

ma anche

 per l’uguaglianza, e vuole una società senza stato in cui la legge ultima sia la parità di libertà e autorità.


La vera competizione aperta è una forza che ha il potere di dissolvere e disperdere. I libertari dovrebbero smettere di giustificare le attuali sconcertanti disuguaglianze come se fossero il risultato del

laissez-faire

 e della sovranità individuale.


Le nostre traduzioni sono finanziate interamente da donazioni. Se vi piace quello che scriviamo, siete invitati a contribuire. Trovate le istruzioni su come fare nella pagina

Sostieni C4SS

:

https://c4ss.org/sostieni-c4ss

.

author: Slingshot robot #1
title: a14 – What’s fermenting underground – Jazz Dance with today’s zine scene
content:
Our collective can barely process all the correspondence coming our way. The least of which comes with scrappy limited edition zines. We endeavor to highlight them here when we can. Thankfully we have found a bright and wise ally who, when not tending to the garden warmly sits and reads deeply and widely freaky shit on paper. Maybe you will find a new life of reading zines, reviewing or even making them to thicken the plot we’re in.

Ear of Corn #66 24 pages – $2 foodfortunata@hotmail.com

It’s really endearing that even after 18 years, Ear of Corn still uses pasteup for the design, even as it’s moved to glossy paper. You can see on every page that Ear of Corn is still assembled old school and copied like we all used to do at Kinkos with glue sticks. The glue had a mild starchy taste, slightly sweet with a bitter finish; not unlike bad cheese pizza.

I have this conspiracy theory about this zine. I usually write reviews in batches, and I’ll often have multiple issues of Ear of Corn on my desk at a time. But I’ve never had any sequentially numbered issues. I’ve begun to suspect issues are not numbered non-sequentially or perhaps they are sequential, but aren’t printed in that order. Their practice of reviewing old and new releases side by side makes it impossible to know for sure; but they’re definitely up to something other than eating the glue.

Out From The Void #8 $5 – 70 pages outfromthevoid@yahoo.com

This issue goes places Out From The Void hasn’t gone before. The new topics are mostly adjacent to the core topic: the missing. So it’s the CAHOOTS program, police records requests, suicide, and police killings. But on page 51 begins a 6 page essay about Israel’s genocide in Gaza. It’s sober, historical and philosophical without trumpeting statistics.

In the middle of Issue #8 is a photo essay reprinted from the zine Here’s What I’ve Hidden Under My Tongue. Writer DJT was visiting an abandoned and mostly collapsed mental institution. In the introduction Brenton Gicker comments that he didn’t write any of the stories in this issue. I appreciate that Gicker puts his mission ahead of his ego to spread awareness of these topics but I do miss his voice as a writer. But until next time, we get more tales of the missing, the lost and the found.

The story of James B. Hunt and Fluke goes back to issue #16 of the infamous Fluke fanzine in 2018. Kudos if you kept that issue, it’s now a fine collectible. Even Maximum RockNRoll said so. They saw the future, perhaps even more clearly than I did. Gina Murrell always had a sixth sense for such things. But if you wake up feeling a bit goth, have a soft spot for monsters, or just like dead stuff, NXOEED might be for you.

If you don’t recognize his art that tells me you don’t skate bruh. His art appears on show flyers, album covers, websites, rad stickers and other greasy places. But among all that ephemera this issue is special. Usually Mr. Hunt lets the ink speak for him, but this time we actually get a few precious pages of text; our first sense of the man himself. He’s a geezer, like me, trying to do punk rock things, but to also go to bed on time. I feel that in my soul.

$20 – 192 pages inequitypress@hotmail.com

It’s hard to say that many poets are famous today. But as poets go, some of those published in Big Hammer are highfalutin people now like David Cope, Donald Lev, Chris Stroffolino, Ken Greenley, and Enid Dame (RIP). Others, like Michael Pingarron, are still writing for Big Hammer. They’ve found their layer of strata, and one would hope some sense of belonging.

The first issue of Big Hammer rolled off the press in 1988. That was 38 years ago, kids. Statistically most of you reading this weren’t even born yet. That zine was way underground, like the Lincoln Tunnel; like the FDR Train Car in the pitch blackness of Track 61 marooned below Grand Central since 1945. But Dave Roskos is still out there in the tunnels, in the darkness, still editing and publishing Big Hammer. He’s doing it his own way, and accountable to no one. Doesn’t it sound grand?

Zine content from the eighties makes more sense in the context of its contemporary punk 7-inches” like “Too scared to be queer,” “Be a Fag,” and “Forbidden Love.” So I queued up the Homocore Hit parade cassette, and pondered its place in history. Homocore ran for just 7 issues between 1988 and 1991. If you didn’t catch my drift, it tapped into two communities which still remain the core of the underground today: queers and …

author: Unknown
title: “How Has Serving Impacted You?” : Veterans of the US Military in Their Own Words
content:
What is it like to serve in the United States military? If only it were possible for those who are considering enlisting to learn the unvarnished truth. In 2019, a viral

tweet

 from the official US Army twitter account unexpectedly drew over 11,000 candid replies in the course of 48 hours. These responses offer a rare window into the real experiences of servicemembers and veterans. We present a selection of them here for the benefit of anyone who is thinking about joining the military.


This is a document of an

earlier era

 of social media, captured here before it

vanishes

. You can obtain a book collecting the first twenty-four hours of responses

here

.


Just before Memorial Day in 2019, the United States Army made a strategic blunder almost on par with invading Vietnam. They posted this inquiry on their official Twitter account:


In response, veterans and their family and friends posted thousands upon thousands of tweets recounting broken promises and broken people. They described cancer, PTSD, domestic abuse, unpaid college and housing loans, Gulf War syndrome, insomnia, sexual abuse, poverty, Agent Orange, racism, nightmare disorder, unemployment, burying loved ones, misogyny, orphaned children, burn pit syndrome, homelessness, debilitating injuries, divorce, alcoholism, disappearances, a Veterans Affairs department that was unwilling or unable to help, and suicide, suicide, suicide.


The United States military is one of the largest concentrations of power in the world. With

tens of thousands

 of missiles,

millions

 of firearms, and over

5000

 nuclear weapons—about 40% of all the nuclear weapons in the world—the US military can hold the entire world hostage.


The US military is also the largest employer in the United States,

employing

 almost 2,900,000 workers—roughly 17 out of every 2000 people. If we add private military contractors like Blackwater (250,000 workers), the employees of non-combat support companies like Halliburton who build military infrastructure, provide food, and the like (150,000-250,000), US-based war manufacturers like Lockheed Martin and Boeing (1,500,000), and

veterans

 who receive disability or pension payments (2,000,000), we find that roughly 1 out of every 50 Americans is economically dependent on US militarism.


As in all industries, without this workforce, the military would grind to a halt. It especially depends on regular transfusions of young blood—young people sold stories about adventure, duty, and upward mobility.


If we were to ask new recruits why they joined, we’d

likely

 hear a mix of narratives about gaining strength, seeing the world, paying for college, serving God and country, learning life skills, continuing a family tradition, escaping poverty or an unsafe home, obtaining housing, having fun, and protecting loved ones. Most people join the military because they think it will benefit them or because they believe they are serving a higher calling.


Some recruits get to live out their dreams. Some leave instability, danger, or deprivation for a more structured and economically stable life; some even gain a sense of belonging. If they’re lucky, they serve their time without incident, then move on to free college tuition, a no-down-payment housing loan, health insurance, and a free meal at Golden Corral once a year.


But thousands of veterans’ dreams become nightmares. The promises of recruiters, family members, and Hollywood movies offer a gamble at best—a roll of the dice that

frequently

 ends with being harmed physically, psychologically, and sexually. Military service can lead to

substance abuse

,

homelessness

, and

suicide

. It can also end in unspeakable acts of violence against others, whether those be the declared enemies of the United States, noncombatants, or veterans’ own loved ones.


It is striking how many of these responses speak of being hoodwinked out of college, housing loans, and medical care—how many describe the pain of family members lost to PTSD, alcoholism, or suicide after witnessing or committing atrocities.


American media bombards us with war propaganda. Almost every video game spreads the myth that combat makes us stronger: more powerful weapons, tougher armor, a bigger health bar, greater fortunes. Hollywood promises that the hero can weather any fight—or, if he can’t, his death will be meaningful and glorious.


Statistically speaking, the more we are exposed to combat, the more likely we are to be …

author: Daniel Avalos
title: Residentes en movilización por el descuido de quienes nos cuidan
content:
Residentes de hospitales de Nación, Provincia de Buenos Aires y CABA realizaron este miércoles un paro y una movilización conjunta. Reclaman una recomposición salarial y mejores condiciones laborales, pero también advierten sobre el deterioro de la calidad de atención y la falta de recursos en el sistema público de salud.


Fotos y texto Daniel Ávalos para ANRed.


No era solamente una discusión por el sueldo. En las caras y en las palabras de quienes marcharon este miércoles había una preocupación que iba más allá de los números: sentir que todo el esfuerzo puesto en formarse, estudiar y sostener guardias interminables no tiene reconocimiento. Son profesionales que eligieron la salud, se esforzaron durante años de formación, y hoy trabajan en hospitales públicos. Atienden pacientes, forman parte de los equipos de atención y sostienen buena parte de la actividad cotidiana de los servicios. Sin embargo, sienten que ese trabajo pierde valor frente a salarios insuficientes, falta de recursos y decisiones de los distintos gobiernos que afectan directamente sus tareas.


 


Con un paro y una movilización conjunta, residentes de Nación, Provincia de Buenos Aires y Ciudad Autónoma de Buenos Aires llevaron sus reclamos a las calles. La jornada comenzó en la Casa de la Provincia de Buenos Aires. Desde allí marcharon hacia el Ministerio de Salud de la Nación y luego al Ministerio de Salud porteño. Tres jurisdicciones, distintos gobiernos y una preocupación compartida.


En la provincia de Buenos Aires, un residente de primer año cobra alrededor de $1.300.000. El reclamo es llevar ese ingreso a un piso de $2.600.000. La diferencia entre ambas cifras no es un detalle . Es la distancia entre el trabajo que realizan y las condiciones materiales en las que pueden sostener su vida. Porque la vocación no paga el alquiler ni llena la heladera. Tampoco debería ser una excusa para naturalizar jornadas extensas, salarios bajos o pérdida de derechos laborales.


Pero hay otra preocupación que apareció con fuerza durante la jornada: la calidad de la atención.


Los residentes advierten que cada vez cuentan con menos herramientas para hacer su trabajo. Faltan medicamentos, insumos y personal. Los equipos se reducen y la demanda de atención sigue estando ahí, del otro lado de la puerta del consultorio o de la guardia. Cuando un profesional no dispone de los recursos necesarios y debe multiplicar esfuerzos para cubrir las necesidades de un servicio, el problema no queda dentro del hospital. También lo padecen quienes llegan buscando atención.


El ajuste también tiene responsables, el deterioro que denuncian los residentes no puede separarse de la política presupuestaria del Gobierno nacional. El ajuste sobre el sistema sanitario tiene números concretos. En mayo, el Ejecutivo recortó más de $63.000 millones de distintas partidas del Ministerio de Salud. Entre ellas, $25.000 millones fueron destinados al fortalecimiento de los sistemas provinciales, y otros $20.000 millones para medicamentos, insumos y tecnología médica. No es una discusión contable. Son recursos que deberían traducirse en hospitales funcionando, medicamentos disponibles y mejores condiciones para atender a la población.


El ministro Mario Lugones está al frente de ese Ministerio y tiene responsabilidad política sobre las decisiones que se toman desde allí. No alcanza con administrar el ajuste ni la precariedad que promueve su gestión, y hablar de eficiencia cuando son los trabajadores y los pacientes quienes terminan enfrentando sus consecuencias. En ese contexto, la situación de las residencias nacionales suma otro problema. El nuevo régimen de becas, establecido por una resolución firmada por el propio Lugones, elimina derechos como el aguinaldo y los aportes jubilatorios.


Los trabajadores también denuncian recortes de cupos y cierres de espacios de formación. La preocupación alcanza al futuro de las residencias y a la posibilidad de seguir formando profesionales dentro del sistema público.


En el documento conjunto, los residentes también alertan sobre el desfinanciamiento de las áreas de salud mental y discapacidad, la falta de recursos para garantizar tratamientos y medicamentos, y el incumplimiento de políticas previstas en la Ley Nacional de Salud Mental.


En CABA, además, denunciaron amenazas y medidas de amedrentamiento contra quienes participan de las protestas.


Esta movilización excede el reclamo salarial. Hay profesionales que identifican que el esfuerzo …

author: Darío Aranda
title: Un molino agroecológico en plena Pampa Húmeda y el cooperativismo que produce alimentos sanos
content:
Por Mauricio Amaya


Existe un molino que genera entusiasmo en el partido bonaerense de Lincoln. No es un molino cualquiera: es de producción agroecológica y uno de los últimos logros de un grupo de productores y vecinos que, inspirados en otras experiencias, se aventuró a conformar la Cooperativa Newen Pampeana. Tienen un triple objetivo: respetar los ciclos naturales, generar un alimento sano para la comunidad y demostrar que la producción agroecológica es rentable. La historia de un proyecto contrahegemónico y solidario.


Pablo Argilla es ingeniero en sistemas y uno de los referentes de la

Cooperativa Newen Pampeana

, que se conformó hace seis años pero que tiene todo un recorrido previo en la zona del noroeste bonaerense con el objetivo de

retornar a sistemas de producción de alimentos sanos y diversos

.


Todo inició en 2016: “Viajamos junto a mi familia a un encuentro de agroecología en Rojas, organizado por la

Red Nacional de Municipios Agroecológicos (Renama)

, que recién surgía como institución. Nos hicimos más conscientes de la problemática de los agroquímicos en la salud y sobre todo el ambiente, que es lo que más nos sensibilizó. Volvimos a Lincoln con la intención de difundir la agroecología en nuestro territorio, organizamos una reunión en mi casa y se dio una gran convocatoria”.


Entonces conformaron el grupo ConCiencia Agroecológica, que llegó a reunir a casi 100 personas entre

productores, docentes, ingenieros, jubilados, dueños de campo, abogados, veterinarios y comerciantes

. “Empezamos a recorrer establecimientos y experiencias agroecológicas, aprendiendo y conociendo”, añade Argilla sobre las visitas a la

chacra La Aurora

 de Benito Juárez (en el sur bonaerense, distinguido por la FAO),

Guaminí

 y Coronel Suárez, entre otros.


Entonces se inició una transición hacia la agroecología, que antes estaba ligada localmente a espacios de huerta familiar. De forma colectiva, el grupo ConCiencia Agroecológica encaró el proyecto hacia dimensiones mayores y con escala de hectáreas en una zona donde el núcleo es la soja o el monocultivo.


Foto: Cooperativa Newen Pampeana


Una red de iniciativas agroecológicas


Con el proyecto de ConCiencia Agroecológica en marcha se creó un grupo de compras llamado Amaranto, para contactar proveedores de productos agroecológicos de todo el país. Y en conjunto con ingenieros agrónomos, empezaron a formar un equipo de trabajo que para 2019 integraba a 40 productores.


“Nos dimos cuenta que empujábamos por una alimentación sana en la producción pero nuestras alacenas no tenían esos productos. Entonces emprendimos esto en contacto con proveedores de todo el país”, cuenta Magalí Roncoli Arana, productora ganadera.


Forma parte de Horizonte Agroecológico, otro espacio que se desprende de ConCiencia Agroecológica: “Nos dimos cuenta de que varios éramos ganaderos y vimos que la agroecología es muy amplia. Entonces nos agrupamos para intensificar en conocimiento y trabajo en esa área”, añade. Con el apoyo del

Programa Cambio Rural del INTA

, este espacio empezó a funcionar en 2023.


El molino agroecológico en funcionamiento


“Recibimos el cereal, lo mantenemos libre de posibles ataque de insectos a través de un gas que es agroecológico y lo trabajamos en el molino. Es un molino de mecanismo muy simple. Estamos haciendo

harina envasada en un kilo, cuatro kilos y diez kilos

”, cuenta Santiago Antonio Paolucci, de 82 años, sobre el funcionamiento de la molienda.


Paolucci tiene mucha experiencia para brindarle a la cooperativa Newen Pampeana. “Nuestro objetivo es transformar la materia prima en producto de oferta. Hay un mercado que lo estamos haciendo nosotros”, comenta sobre el estímulo de ser parte del proyecto que avanza de forma incipiente. “Viene el trigo, se pasa por la clasificadora de granos, se procesa, se sacan las impurezas o tierra y va al molino. La moledora tiene sus aspiradores, se le saca el polvo y la harina sale con los microgranos justos, mantiene el color original y es una harina sin agregados de ningún tipo”, relata.


Se trata de un molino de "motor martillo" (como se lo conoce en el sector), que funciona mediante el impacto a alta velocidad de una serie de martillos metálicos contra el material para reducirlo a partículas más pequeñas. Lo trabajan dos personas por jornada. En ocho horas, puede producir alrededor de 2.000 kilos de harina.


Luego se hace la molienda y se envasa de forma directa; no se le agrega nada. El salvado va junto …

author: Sofia Amaral
title: COP e Amazônia: o futuro emergente e a emergência do presente
content:
Lula passou em grande estilo pela Cúpula dos Líderes na

COP31

. Servindo carisma, apesar da voz rouca, o presidente foi ovacionado e reafirmou o compromisso do Brasil com o clima, chegando a prometer a realização de uma conferência sobre a transição para longe dos combustíveis fósseis no Brasil. De um lado, protagonismo; de outro, contradição; já que o mesmo presidente é entusiasta da exploração de petróleo na foz do rio Amazonas e tem o desafio de manter o apoio dos movimentos sociais.


Enquanto isso, aqui no Brasil, a Amazônia está em chamas, graças — mas não apenas — ao efeito do

El Niño

. No episódio dessa semana, Isabel Seta, Marina Amaral e Ricardo Terto analisam os trunfos e contradições do presidente Lula na construção de seu legado na área climática. Ouça agora.


E MAIS:


Na Trombeta, as dicas de beleza da machosfera. E no quadro “Se é pra falar de economia…”, Clara Marinho analisa os efeitos do El Niño na economia.

author: Rizomatica
title: Juana Paillalef denuncia discriminación racial hacia su familia y la infancia Mapuche en Lavkenmapu
content:
Luego de que la machi Millaray Garrido Paillalef, del territorio Lawen Mapu, Lanalhue, realizara un video denunciando violencia institucional y discriminación en el hospital de Arauco, su madre, Juana Paillalef, quien fue directora del Museo Mapuche de Cañete durante 20 años, junto a Mario Cayupi hacen una reflexión sobre diversas situaciones de discriminación racial hacia su familia.


Juana Paillalef a través de su relato explica cómo han vivido vulneraciones, violencia institucional y discriminación, a través de todas las generaciones de su familia. Ella, su hija y ahora su nieta, ven como se vulneran los derechos de niños, no solo mapuches. Comenta cómo han sido vulnerados en su mogen, en su vida como Mapuche, luego de haber levantado a su hija Machi, quien desde estudiante vivió vulneraciones, en el liceo se le discriminó por el uso de sus chaway y su tukuluwün y en la universidad también existieron educadores que la discriminaron por ser Mapuche. En su primer embarazo también vivió vulneraciones en centros de salud, y ahora en la actualidad denuncian haber vivido discriminación y maltratos por un profesional de la salud del hospital de Arauco en contra de su nieta.


“

Se habla de interculturalidad, cambiando por el racismo, ¿pero qué hemos visto de interculturalida hasta este momento? Seguimos en lo mismo. La colonización ha triturado nuestro pensamiento, nuestras formas de vida, nuestras formas de comportamiento, nuestra forma de exigir nuestros derechos, nos han apagado en vez de abrirnos. Llamo a la población a no dormirse, estar atentos y no dejar de caminar al lado de nuestros niños. Hay muchos niños y jóvenes en colegios que se están levantando como machi, y no hay como atender esas situaciones.”

Radio Kurruf

author: Publicación Abierta
title: En el Día de la Militancia Peronista recordamos a John William Cooke
content:
Cada 17 de noviembre se celebra el Día de la Militancia Peronista, una fecha emblemática para el movimiento justicialista que recuerda el regreso de Juan Domingo Perón a la Argentina en 1972, luego de permanecer 17 años en el exilio tras el golpe de Estado de 1955. La jornada representa la resistencia, la organización política y la lucha de miles de militantes que sostuvieron la consigna de su vuelta.


El regreso se produjo el 17 de noviembre de 1972, durante la dictadura encabezada por el general Alejandro Agustín Lanusse. Perón llegó al aeropuerto de Ezeiza a bordo de un avión de Alitalia, acompañado por una comitiva integrada por dirigentes políticos, sindicalistas, artistas y representantes de distintos sectores del peronismo. Su retorno se concretó después de años de proscripción y de un primer intento frustrado en 1964.


Hace 107 años, un 14 de noviembre de 1919, en la ciudad La Plata, nacía John William Cooke. A lo largo de su vida ejerció diversos oficios: fue diputado peronista entre 1946 y 1952, jefe de la resistencia peronista y delegado de Juan Domingo Perón a fines de la década de 1950, colaborador estrecho de Ernesto Che Guevara en la década de 1960, referente indiscutido de la generación que asumió los lineamientos generales de un proyecto orientado a la transformación radical de este país. Cooke murió unos meses antes del Cordobazo.


En el Día de la Militancia Peronista recordamos a quien tal vez fuera la figura central dentro del peronismo para generar una transformación interna con una orientación revolucionaria.


En base a extractos de El peronismo que no fue. La (otra) otra historia de Gerardo Bavio (GB) y Mario Hernandez (MH). Editorial Metrópolis, Buenos Aires, 2014.


John William Cooke (1919-1968).


John William Cooke fue la figura central dentro del peronismo para generar una transformación interna


GB:- Con unos amigos decidimos irnos un verano a Carlos Paz, a la noche nos juntamos a conversar con Jorge Vexenat, que acababa de volver de Cuba, nos relató cómo eran las cosas. Ahí yo creo que surgió la idea de que era necesario ir a Cuba, para ponernos en contacto no solo con el Che, sino también con John William Cooke que considerábamos que era la figura central dentro del peronismo para generar una transformación interna. Era transformar ese «gigante invertebrado y miope» en «organización y conciencia», como decía Cooke.


MH:- Cooke había planteado que el gobierno popular había caído en septiembre de 1955 porque la clase trabajadora no participó en la lucha.


GB:- Había una evidente conspiración por parte de los llamados partidos opositores. También hubo un llamado de Perón a la pacificación, que no es escuchado, vienen los discursos de los distintos sectores políticos, todos opinando en contra del gobierno y con una actitud completamente conspirativa, así se desencadena el 16 de septiembre de 1955, con esa escalada de sublevaciones que comienzan en Córdoba, que en realidad se frustran, fueron tres días de movimientos, de actores militares que se sublevan, que son rodeados, parecía que el gobierno había logrado vencer la conspiración antiperonista.


MH: Y que John William Cooke dijera que fueron vencidos porque los trabajadores no fueron movilizados.


GB: Exactamente, ahí falló algo que es fundamental, que fue la burocracia sindical, que tuvo actitudes que podrían calificarse de claudicantes. También el Partido Peronista en cuyo frente estaba el Almirante Teisaire en esa misma actitud. Y la ausencia de los trabajadores, pero también la política de Perón que llamaba a los trabajadores a no armarse.


John William Cooke fue designado por Perón en la última etapa de la conspiración, en el cargo de interventor del partido en la Capital Federal. Cooke tuvo actitudes muy firmes, dijo que debían tomarse las calles, que debían organizarse, las armas que había comprado Eva Perón para los trabajadores habían sido devueltas a la Gendarmería, es decir, se combinaba toda una política destinada a la claudicación por parte de los sectores que se supone que eran peronistas.


La clase trabajadora estaba encerrada por la burocracia sindical, marginada del eje de la resolución, el mismo Perón dijo: «del trabajo a casa y de casa al trabajo, y dejen que este es un asunto entre soldados». Que era una forma de determinar su derrota, porque evidentemente si había algo o alguien que podía ayudar al gobierno de Perón era la clase obrera en la calle, los «milicos» ya estaban en otra, ya habían dado el salto …

author: La Zarzamora
title: Comunicado y llamado Internacional del Frente en Defensa del Guaíba y contra la CMPC
content:
Como Frente en Defensa del Guaíba y contra la CMPC hacemos un llamado de solidaridad para enfrentar a la ofensiva ecocida de la multinacional fascista $hilena Celulosa CMPC, comandada por los Matte, en el territorio ancestral Guaraní M’Byá y lafken Guaíba, Barra do Ribeiro, sur de Bra$il.

El pasado miércoles 11 de noviembre se realizó una manifestación y marcha en el centro de Porto Alegre, donde se reunieron más de 300 personas para exigir la retirada total de dicha empresa y su nefasto «Projeto Natureza».

El «Projeto Natureza» es una planta procesadora de celulosa que pretende instalarse a las orillas del Rio Guaíba, en el fundo Barba Negra y en la Ponta da Formiga, territorio sagrado Guaraní M’byá. Su objetivo es duplicar la capacidad de producción total de celulosa de la CMPC. Hoy, cuentan con 44 plantas de procesamiento de celulosa en el continente, 3 de ellas en territorio $hileno, sumado a la planta que ya está instalada a las orillas del Guaíba en el municipio del mismo nombre. CMPC tiene la capacidad de producir 4,5 millones de toneladas de celulosa al año. Con el Projeto Natureza, su capacidad de producción podría llegar a 7,5 millones de toneladas de celulosa al año. Las consecuencias a largo plazo son difíciles de dimensionar, pero es sabido que el proyecto incluye el dragado del Guaíba, deforestación del bosque nativo, cambios en las leyes de protección ambiental, contaminación del agua y, sin dudas, la expansión masiva de plantaciones de eucalipto en Brasil, Uruguay y Argentina.

Al finalizar la marcha se realizó una acción directa coordinada en contra de la FEPAM, órgano del gobierno que otorga los permisos ambientales y de instalación a la CMPC. Manifestantes hicieron okupación de la institución, rayaron las paredes exigiendo «FUERA CMPC» y denunciando el actuar corrupto de la FEPAM, quienes ignoran por completo decenas de informes y cuestionamientos técnicos de diversas áreas sobre el impacto real de este proyecto en el territorio. Marcaron las paredes pulcras de ese actual antro de mafiosos que solo sirve como pantalla, ya que sin escrúpulos aprueban cualquier proyecto extractivista que se les ponga en frente.

El río Guaíba es parte medular de la vida en la ciudad de Porto Alegre y la región metropolitana. Es el horizonte con el que nos relacionamos cada día y gran parte del agua potable proviene de las aguas tratadas de este rio. Cuando protestamos contra la CMPC necesitamos que se entienda que esta empresa pretende derramar más desechos en el rio que toda la ciudad en su conjunto. Es un proyecto que básicamente contaminará el agua de consumo público de la región.

El actual gobierno de Lula, que basó su propaganda en ser una “alternativa al fascismo”, apoya y fomenta abiertamente el proyecto de la Familia Matte y la CMPC, que además de usurpar sistemáticamente territorio mapuche, apoyaron la dictadura de Pinochet y promovieron la Masacre de Laja en la que 19 trabajadores de la CMPC fueron fusilados por militares chilenos. El presidente Lula concedió a la CMPC una terminal portuaria de exportación en el puerto de Río Grande, en este puerto la empresa está asociada a Ultramar, empresa de la família Von Appen con infame trayectoria nazi.

Esta concesión transforma al rio Guaíba y a la Laguna dos Patos en hidrobia de madera y celulosa, impactando drásticamente la naturaleza y la pesca artesanal. Todo esto sin respetar y seguir los protocolos Guaraní y menos la convención 169 de la OIT que se supone consulta de manera previa, libre e informada a las comunidades indígenas afectadas. Esta maliciosa colaboración entre el gobierno y la CMPC se logra a través de la entrega de millones de pesos a algunas autoridades ancestrales para otorgar el visto bueno al gobierno, dividiendo a las comunidades y generando rupturas entre ellas.

Sobre la familia Matte es importante hacer memoria de que no es solo dueña de la celulosa CMPC, sino que también es dueña de Colbún, responsable por secar el Lago Chapo en la Región de Los Lagos en $hile, y de la Forestal Mininco, vieja empresa forestal conocida robar tierra mapuche, devastar bosque nativo, secar la tierra y por el asesinato de Alex Lemún de 17 años y de Pablo Marchant de 25, ambos asesinados en contexto de recuperación territorial y defensa de la tierra.

También, en 2021 se hizo famoso Fernando Puga Matte, uno de los integrantes de dicha familia, dueño del condominio de lujo Riñimapu donde trabajaban los «jardineros» que asesinaron a Emilia Milen, la Bau …

author: anred
title: Los tres megayates que pretendían anclar en el Parque Nacional Tierra del Fuego arribaron a Ushuaia
content:
Los cruceros Lonian, Hodor y Sherakhan este miercoles 18 por la mañana, captados por la cámara del fotógrafo Juan Odela.


La flota de megayates de super lujo que desató una fuerte controversia ambiental, legal y geopolítica en Tierra del Fuego ya se encuentra en aguas fueguinas, pero lejos de los ecosistemas protegidos de Bahía Lapataia. El lunes 16 de noviembre, los buques Lonian, Hodor y Sherakhan – los dos primeros con bandera británica – arribaron a la capital provincial y permanecen fondeados en la Bahía de Ushuaia, cerrando en los hechos la pulseada administrativa que obligó a dar marcha atrás con la autorización firmada por la Intendencia del Parque Nacional Tierra del Fuego.

Por Agenda Malvinas.


Los registros del sistema de seguimiento marítimo satelital

VesselFinder


confirman que las tres embarcaciones navegan de manera coordinada, operando como una verdadera escuadrilla logística de turismo VIP:


M/Y Lonian:

 Fue el primero en tocar aguas de la bahía local, arribando a las

14:10

. Con 87 metros de eslora y bandera de Islas Caimán, es la nave insignia vinculada al magnate estadounidense Lorenzo Fertitta.


M/Y Hodor:

 Ingresó en segundo lugar, a las

17:08

. Este buque de apoyo de 67 metros —también registrado en el enclave colonial británico de Islas Caimán— funciona como plataforma logística y transporte auxiliar para la expedición.


M/Y Sherakhan:

 Cerró el despliegue de la flota ingresando a las

17:34

, completando el posicionamiento conjunto frente a la costa de Ushuaia.


El desenlace que confirmó la advertencia técnica


La permanencia de los tres buques en la bahía de Ushuaia ratifica, en la práctica, la solución que el propio cuerpo técnico del Parque Nacional Tierra del Fuego había planteado antes de que estallara el escándalo.


En el informe conjunto del 20 de octubre

(IF-2026-102110148-APN-PNTF#APNAC)

, siete profesionales y jefes operativos del área protegida habían dictaminado que resultaba improcedente habilitar el fondeo en Bahía Lapataia y el sobrevuelo de sus dos helicópteros, señalando de forma explícita que estas operaciones podían desarrollarse perfectamente en otros sectores costeros,

«como la bahía de Ushuaia – ubicados afuera del área protegida»

.


Pese a ese dictamen categórico, el

intendente Marcelo Almirón

 había firmado el permiso el 27 de octubre

(NO-2026-104217762-APN-PNTF#APNAC)

 a instancias de la agencia marítima local

USHIP S.R.L..

 Solo tras la difusión pública de los expedientes oficiales y la repercusión periodística a nivel provincial y nacional, la empresa operadora desistió del pedido y la Intendencia debió emitir un comunicado de repliegue para dar por cerrada la autorización.


El saldo institucional y la alerta sobre la intermediación


El fondeo actual de la escuadrilla en la Bahía de Ushuaia evita el arrastre de cadenas y anclas de gran porte sobre los bosques sumergidos de cachiyuyo (

Macrocystis pyrifera

), así como la perturbación acústica de helicópteros sobre los hábitats del huillín y las aves costeras dentro del Parque Nacional.


Sin embargo, el episodio deja abierta una discusión de fondo sobre el funcionamiento de los controles estatales en el extremo sur. La secuencia documental expuso cómo una agencia marítima local puede tramitar permisos a medida por encima de las leyes nacionales y los informes técnicos, instalando un precedente de excepcionalidad que, como demuestran antecedentes similares en reservas provinciales como

Península Mitre

 e

Isla de los Estados

, exige un escrutinio público permanente sobre el manejo.

author: Kodao Productions
title: Muntinlupa refuses to free 15 Indigenous children despite release order
content:
Fifteen minors arrested by the police last Sunday remain in custody even as 216 adults and five fellow children already walked free from detention on Wednesday.


The Office of the City Prosecutor of Muntinlupa City ordered the release of the Indigenous children from Mindoro Island’s Mangyan community at approximately 9:00 PM on Tuesday. Muntinlupa Mayor Ruffy Biazon also announced on Tuesday the processing of the children’s release.


The city’s Bahay Pag-asa, however, refuses to release the remaining children in their custody, earning condemnation from the group Salinlahi Alliance for Children’s Concerns.


“Bahay Pag-asa [of] Muntinlupa must stop delaying their release and immediately, unconditionally, turn the children over to their families or legal guardians,” Salinlahi said.


Salinlahi revealed that Muntinlupa City’s Social Welfare and Development Office have instructed the children’s parents “to mislead paralegals” by claiming that the children must undergo another week of quarantine.


“If true, this is a deliberate obstruction of the children’s release and an additional form of harassment against already traumatized children and their families,” the group said.


The children’s rights advocates group pointed out that the children’s continued detention constitutes arbitrary deprivation of liberty.


“Bahay Pag-asa is mandated to protect and rehabilitate children—not become an instrument for prolonging their detention and suppressing their rights,” Salinlahi added.


Aged 11 to 14 and arrested with more than 200 other participants of the Lakbayan ng Timog Katagalugan by the police on Sunday, the 15 have been under custody for more than 90 hours as of Thursday morning.


Nine more protesters arrested in Manila on Sunday also remain in custody.


Meanwhile, rights group Karapatan announced a grand welcome for the hundreds of released activists on Thursday at the University of the Philippines campus in Quezon City.


The arrested protesters were supposed to join this week’s massive protests against US President Donald Trump and the US-led Pax Silica microchip supply chain control project.


Trump left the country on Wednesday, failing to sign an agreement with President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. Bagong Alyansang Makabayan hailed the postponement of the signing as a “temporary victory,” crediting the protests as one of the reasons for the failure. #

(Raymund B. Villanueva)

author: Dae-Oup Chang
title: International Labour Solidarity from Below: Reflections on Inter-Asian Solidarity Building of Asia Monitor Resource Centre
content:
Since its establishment in 1976, the Asia Monitor Resource Centre (AMRC) has served as a regional hub for labour solidarity in Asia. This article reflects on the AMRC’s half-century journey towards building inter-Asian labour solidarity. It discusses not only what AMRC has achieved, but also what it has failed to achieve, why it has failed, and what these experiences might tell us about the future of inter-Asian labour solidarity. This is a personal reflection, drawing on my 23 years of involvement with the AMRC in various capacities: as a full-time activist, a member of the Board of Directors, a member of the Regional Council, and Chair of the Board of Directors.


International labour solidarity has long occupied a prominent place in the political imagination of labour movements. Almost every major trade union has declared its commitment to internationalism. However, there is a considerable distance between internationalism as a declared principle and internationalism as an actual process of movement building. Affiliation to international trade unions, participation in international conferences, and occasional solidarity campaigns do not necessarily generate lasting solidarity among workers across national borders.


This distinction between international solidarity as a dead principle and as a living practice was central to an experiment in building bottom-up inter-Asian labour solidarity in which I participated during the 2000s as an AMRC activist coordinating the Asian Transnational Corporation Monitoring Network (ATNC Network). As  one of the regional labour networks AMRC initiated, the ATNC network sought to connect grassroots workers’ organisations across Asia. Its broader ambition was to build an alternative foundation for international labour solidarity in Asia. 


Building a Network from Below


When I joined AMRC in 2003, the ATNC Network already existed as a pilot initiative, with a substantial emphasis on

corporate codes of conduct

. Such an approach was becoming increasingly popular in international labour advocacy, particularly following the emergence of consumer campaigns targeting major international brands during the late 1990s and early 2000s.

1


We were sceptical of the political consequences of this prevailing model of north–south labour solidarity. Our scepticism concerned the underlying structure of solidarity that this approach

reproduced

. Northern organisations possessed the resources, connections, and influence required to pressure major brands, while workers and their organisations in Asian production sites were primarily positioned as

recipients of assistance

. The political focus often shifted from workers’ collective struggles to consumer organisations’strategies and their relationships with corporations.


Such campaigns sometimes achieved meaningful results. They can generate international attention, provide protection to workers, and force employers to negotiate. We did not deny their practical value. However, they had little to do with building the larger collective power of workers. For us, workers’ power was something to be built collectively by workers in and beyond workplaces rather than granted by individual employers’ moral behaviour. 


Therefore, we sought to reverse the direction of the network’s activities. Instead of beginning with corporations and their codes of conduct, we wanted to begin with workers’ struggles, their own organisations emerging from such struggles, and solidarity-based relationships built  between such organisations. 


These relationships developed through practical engagement. A group of workers or worker organisations might initiate a strike or an organising campaign. AMRC and its local partners could support the struggles on the ground. Over time, this process allowed us to include more organisations, whether unions or NGOs. Through such activities, new relationships emerged between organisations participating in the same struggles. 


Our criteria for partnership were therefore not primarily based on size, institutional recognition, or formal representativeness. We were interested in organisations with real connections to workers’ struggles. This frequently meant working with small but independent unions and grassroots NGOs rather than established national trade union centres.


While building a network of such organisations, the network operated through collaborative research, education, organising, and advocacy. Activities involved …

title: Trump Out, dumagundong sa Maynila sa kulminasyon ng protesta
content:
Sinalubong ng military honors ni Ferdinand Marcos Jr. si US President Donald Trump sa Malacañang kaninang umaga, Nobyemre 18, para sa kanilang bilateral meeting.

​Sa kabilang banda, kilometro lang ang layo mula sa palasyo, dumagundong ang panawagan ng sambayanan sa kulminasyon ng apat na araw na protesta kontra sa Pax Silica at sa imperyalistang Estados Unidos.

​Taliwas sa mainit na pagtanggap sa loob ng Malacañang, dahas at harang ang sumalubong sa mga nagpoprotesta sa lansangan.

Sa kahabaan pa lang ng Recto Avenue, hinarang na ang hanay ng mga raliyista at hindi pinayagang makapagmartsa patungong Mendiola. Hinarang din ng mga pulis ang mga delegasyon ng Gitnang Luson at Timong Katagalugan na nagmantini sa kampuhan sa Liwasang Bonifacio.

Hindi na napigilan ng galit na bulto ang magbulalas ng “Pax you, Trump” kasabay ng panawagang itigil ang Pax Silica at Trump Out.

Noong Nobyembre 17, pinuri ni Trump si Marcos Jr. sa pagsasabing mayroon itong “very good genetics” sa kanyang talumpati sa hapunan para sa mga lider ng ASEAN at Estados Unidos sa Maynila. Inalala rin ni Trump ang matagal na niyang pagkakakilala sa mga magulang ni Marcos Jr. bago pa siya naging pangulo ng Estados Unidos.

Para sa mga progresibong grupo, tumatagos sa katotohanan ang papuring ito, ngunit hindi bilang karangalan, kundi bilang patunay na manang-mana si Marcos Jr. sa kanyang ama at ina bilang masugid na papet ng Estados Unidos.

Hindi lingid sa kaalaman ng nakararami ang pagpapatayo ni Imelda Marcos ng mga pader upang itago ang kahirapan ng mga maralita noong idinaos ang Miss Universe sa bansa noong 1974. Sa kasalukuyan, gumastos ng humigit-kumulang ₱22.9 bilyon ang administrasyong Marcos Jr. kaugnay sa 49th ASEAN Summit. Ayon sa Defend Jobs Philippines, libo-libong maliliit na manininda at manggagawa ang pinatigil sa paghahanapbuhay sa tabing ng paglilinis sa daraanan ng mga dayuhang lider.

Sa isinagawang program sa Recto Ave., binatikos ni Bayan Secretary-General Raymond Palatino ang pag-host ni Marcos Jr. ng kauna-unahang leader-level QUAD meeting sa Pilipinas kahit hindi naman miyembro ng nasabing alyansang militar ang bansa.

Aniya, manang-mana rin si Marcos Jr. sa diktadurya ng kanyang ama sa paggamit ng makinarya ng estado at kapulisan upang supilin ang lehitimong pagkilos ng taumbayan.

Bago pa man buksan ang ASEAN summit, tatlong kabataang estudyante na ang inaresto sa University of Makati na lumahok sa ikinasang kilos-proteta laban sa Pax Silica noong Nobyembre 13. Habang may higit 200 indibidwal ang marahas na dinampot sa malawakang pag-aresto sa Muntinlupa at Kamaynilaan noong Nobyemre 15. Dagdag pa rito ang sa marahas na pagharang, panggigipit, paniniktik at iba pang porma ng brutalidad na ipinatupad ng Philippine National Police.

Inihalintulad naman ng National Union of Peoples’ Lawyers (NUPL) sa kalagayan noong Martial Law at pagkakaroon ng concentration camps noong World War II ang pagtrato sa mahigit 200 indibidwal na inaresto sa kasagsagan ng mga protesta kaugnay ng 49th ASEAN Summit.

“Ang pagtrato sa kanila bilang mga detinido ay hindi nalalayo sa pagtrato ni Marcos Sr. sa mga protesters noong Martial Law at pagtrato ni Hitler sa mga Hudyo noong World War II,” ani Atty. Arman Hernando ng Pro-Labor Legal Assistance Center (PLACE), isa sa mga abogadong tumayong legal counsel ng mga inaresto sa Muntinlupa.

Nanawagan ang NUPL sa agarang pagpapalaya sa lahat ng inaresto at pagpapanagot sa Philippine National Police (PNP), Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG), at administrasyong Marcos Jr. sa paghahasik ng dahas at brutalidad laban sa mga aktibista.

​Wala mang 24 oras ang itinagal ng pagbisita ni Trump sa bansa, babala ng mga grupo na habambuhay namang pasanin ng sambayanang Pilipino ang epekto ng anumang hindi pantay na kasunduan o lihim na napag-usapan sa bilateral meeting nina Marcos Jr. at Trump.

Sa kabila ng maagang pahayag nina Marcos Jr. at Trump sa harap ng media na hindi muna pipirmahan ang Pax Silica sa biyaheng ito, bigla namang ibinida ni Trump sa state luncheon sa Malacañang na nakapagkasundo na sila sa tinawag niyang “very big trade deal—the biggest trade deal we’ve ever made by far.”

Nagsara naman ang programa sa Mendiola sa pamamagitan ng simbolikong pagsunog sa watawat ng Estados Unidos habang dumadagundong sa mga sound system ang kantang “Trump Out” ng Switchbitch na sinabayan ng sigaw at indak ng bulto.

Sa kulminasyon ng apat na araw na kilos-protesta, iginiit ng mga progresibong …

author: rti_admin
title: Building Safe Spaces: Women’s Safety Must Mean More Than Protection
content:
A safe workplace is not defined only by the absence of harassment. It is also a place where women can speak, disagree, seek support, and participate in decisions without fear.

We often assume that organizations are safe places because they have rules, policies, and systems in place. But is that enough? A workplace may have a policy against sexual harassment and a committee to receive complaints, yet a woman may still hesitate to speak because she fears being judged, ignored, or facing consequences. This makes me ask a simple question: what does it really mean for a woman to feel safe at work?

Safety is usually understood as protection from harm, injury, or danger. In a workplace, that includes physical safety and freedom from sexual harassment. But it also includes something less visible: the freedom to express an opinion, raise concern, disagree with a colleague, or ask for help without fear of humiliation or retaliation. A woman may be physically safe in an office and still feel unsafe if she cannot speak openly. For me, women’s safety is connected to dignity. It is about being able to work without fear, but also about being treated as a human being whose experiences, feelings, and responsibilities matter.

Physical safety means being protected from violence, injury, threats and other forms of bodily harm. It also includes a safe working environment, appropriate security arrangements, transport where required and access to help in an emergency. Sexual safety means being free from unwanted sexual comments, gestures, messages, touching, harassment and violence. Everyone should be able to decide what happens to their body and should not have to tolerate unwanted behaviour as part of working life. Economic safety includes fair wages, equal opportunities and the ability to earn a livelihood without exploitation or threats. Social and organizational safety means being treated fairly and respectfully, without discrimination, bullying or harassment based on gender, caste, colour or social background.

Psychological safety is equally important. It means being able to express thoughts, ask questions, raise concerns, share ideas and admit mistakes without fear of humiliation or punishment. Amy Edmondson has described it as a shared belief that a team is safe for interpersonal risk-taking. Earlier work by Edgar Schein and Warren Bennis in 1965 also discussed psychological safety in relation to organisational learning and change. The central idea is straightforward: people should be able to speak honestly, ask for help and participate without worrying that they will be mocked, ignored or penalised. Psychological safety does not mean avoiding disagreement or accountability. It means that people can engage in difficult conversations without being degraded or threatened.

Safety should be a basic right, not a privilege available only in certain places or under certain conditions. Article 21 of the Constitution of India protects the right to life and personal liberty, and the right to live with dignity has been recognised as part of this constitutional protection. Yet many women continue to experience harassment, discrimination and fear in daily life. When women do not feel safe, the effects go beyond the immediate risk of harm. They may limit their movements, avoid certain jobs, turn down opportunities involving travel or give up professional goals. Insecurity can affect confidence, mental well-being, economic independence and participation in society. It becomes a barrier to equality and empowerment.

For many women, fear begins long before they reach the office. Roads, bus stops, railway stations, public transport, markets and the route home are all part of the working day. Some think twice before travelling alone, returning late or visiting an unfamiliar place. Some ask a father, brother, male relative or friend to accompany them because they believe another person’s presence may protect them from unwanted attention. Instead of feeling free to move independently, they make arrangements simply to feel secure.

A baseline household survey conducted in Delhi in October and November 2012 offers a stark illustration of this fear. The study, carried out by the International Center for Research on Women (ICRW) as part of the Safe Cities programme with UN Women and local partners, found that only 5% of women and girls surveyed ranked public spaces in Delhi as safe from sexual violence. This is sometimes summarized as 95% feeling …
