author: Bulatlat Staff
title: Int’l groups condemn police brutality
content:
Police officers forcibly grab human rights activists and multisectoral leaders during a protest in Cebu City on November 16, 2026. Screengrab from Bulatlat's video

By Dominic Gutoman and Anne Marxze Umil

International groups denounced the police brutality on November 15, the first day of the 49th ASEAN Summit.

In a statement, the International Association of Democratic Lawyers (IADL) expressed strong condemnation over the violent dispersal and mass arrests of the activists.

They said that instead of arresting international offenders like Sen. Ronald “Bato” Dela Rosa who has an outstanding International Criminal Court warrant, “the Philippine police and military are using their superior force to harass and arrest peaceful demonstrators and protestors and to stifle dissent and lawful redress of grievances.”

The group stressed that the police brutality and mass arrests are overkill, violating the Philippine Constitution and the country’s laws in the presence of ASEAN member-states, other heads of state, and the United Nations Secretary General.

“The IADL in particular is holding the police Chief PGen Jose Melencio Nartatez, Jr., Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla, and President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. himself as well as identified individual members of security forces responsible,” the group said in a statement.

The events of the 49th ASEAN Summit happen at the Philippine International Convention Center in Pasay City until November 18, bringing leaders from 11 member-states and representatives of nine dialogue partner-countries.

The Asia Pacific Forum on Women Law and Development (APWLD) stressed that police brutality and state-sanctioned harassment are blatant attacks on fundamental rights to freedom of expression and peaceful assembly which violates Articles 19 and 21 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR).

“The Philippine government’s actions also violate their international obligations under the UN Declaration on Human Rights Defenders and the UN General Assembly resolution which calls upon all States to take concrete measures to protect human rights defenders and recognise the vital work they do,” APWLD said in a statement. “We call on the international community, civil society organisations and feminist movements across Asia and the Pacific to amplify their demands, release statements of solidarity and support ongoing legal and humanitarian aid for those detained.”

In a press conference on November 16, Jheri Lising, representative of International League of Peoples’ Struggles (ILPS)-US, said that these arrests are part of a broader pattern of repression against people who stand up to US imperialism and its wars of aggression. “The Philippine government is once again demonstrating its willingness to trample on people’s democratic rights to protect US interests. We stand with the Filipino people in opposing Pax Silica, Trump’s visit, and the continuing US intervention in the Philippines.”

June Colcol of Bagong Alyansang Makabayan-US said that “the Filipino people, including our diaspora, have every reason to oppose Trump’s visit and the US economic and military agenda behind it.”

Colcol said that Pax Silica serves US strategic interests, deepens the Philippines’ dependence on foreign capital and technology, and offers no real path to national development. “The Marcos government will not silence us for exposing this agenda. We will not allow these mass arrests to set the tone for the international week of action. We remain indignant and determined to push through with our planned actions and mobilizations, in the Philippines and around the world.”

Arnold Padilla, secretary general of ILPS-Philippines said that the Marcos government will not succeed in silencing them.

“We will not allow yesterday’s arrests to dictate the course of this international week of action. We remain indignant, and we will push through with our plans to expose and oppose the agenda of Trump and Marcos. The demand for accountability will continue to be heard in the streets of the Philippines and across the world,” Padilla said. (DAA)

author: Brett Wilkins
title: Israel extends imprisonment of Gaza doctor Hussam Abu Safiya for 6 more months
content:
Israeli authorities on November 18 extended the detention without charge of Dr Hussam Abu Safiya, the former director of northern Gaza’s Kamal Adwan Hospital, for another six months, prompting outrage from human rights defenders and renewed calls for the release of the pediatrician and scores of other imprisoned Palestinian medical professionals.

According to Abu Safiya’s lawyer, Nasser Odeh, an Israeli court in Beersheba extended the 53-year-old’s indefinite imprisonment through May 2027.

“Why must I spend another six months away from my family?” Dr Abu Safiya reportedly asked the court, claiming he is being punished for doing his job.

According to Al Jazeera, the court justified the continued detention by declaring that Abu Safiya “poses a threat to the state of Israel.”

Israel claims Abu Safiya is a colonel in Hamas’ Military Medical Services and has shown a photo of the doctor wearing a uniform that Al Jazeera said belongs to the Palestinian Directorate of General Military Medical Services, an organization providing healthcare to Gaza security personnel and civilians. The Qatar-based news network said that wearing the agency’s uniform does not establish Hamas membership.

There is also a dispute over the word “colonel”. Critics of Israel’s allegation say this is a professional or honorary designation within the medical services, not proof of a Hamas military command position, much like the United States surgeon-general is not an actual general.

The court’s decision came despite mounting international concern over Abu Safiya’s health and treatment in Israeli custody.

“The information that we are receiving about the health conditions of my father and how he’s being treated is very concerning,” Elias Abu Safiya, the imprisoned doctor’s son, told Al Jazeera on November 12. “My father weighs only 53 kilograms now, and he’s been suffering from very harsh conditions, three floors underground. He is in a solitary room, deprived of food, water, and medicine.”

Elias Abu Safiya continued: “We know he’s been subject to torture and bad treatment. My father still has some shrapnel stuck in his body, and he’s not seen a surgeon. This is inhumane, very harsh conditions that not even animals should be living in inside Israeli prisons. To add to this, he’s not been charged with anything. I don’t know why he’s being tortured this way. He’s a doctor, not a criminal or a murderer. He doesn’t deserve to be treated this way. The court denied the appeal to release him and 14 other doctors.”

Last week, Israel’s Supreme Court rejected a petition seeking the release of Abu Safiya and those 14 doctors, who are also imprisoned without charge or trial.

In July, the United Nations Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights urged Israel to release the doctor immediately, or charge him and hold a fair trial. OHCHR said there were indications that Abu Safiya had been tortured and subjected to other abuse, including prolonged solitary confinement, repeated severe assaults resulting in serious injuries, and denial of medical care.

Abu Safiya’s 15-year-old son, Ibrahim Abu Safiya, was killed in an Israeli drone strike at the entrance to Kamal Adwan Hospital, where he was sheltering with his family, in October 2024. The following month, Abu Safiya suffered severe shrapnel wounds during yet another Israeli drone strike on the facility.

Israeli troops detained Abu Safiya on December 28, 2024 amid a prolonged siege and assault of the hospital after the director defied a forced displacement order and refused to evacuate the facility as long as patients were still being treated.

Former detainees released from Sde Teiman, the notorious torture prison in southern Israel, said they saw and met Abu Safiya there. According to testimonies collected by the Geneva-based Euro-Mediterranean Human Rights Monitor, Abu Safiya was tortured prior to his arrival at Sde Teiman, and also while imprisoned there.

A United Nations commission concluded in 2024 that “Israel has perpetrated a concerted policy to destroy Gaza’s healthcare system as part of a broader assault on Gaza” that has left more than 250,000 Palestinians dead, maimed, or missing. The commission — which separately found that Israel is committing genocide in Gaza — further accused Israeli forces of “committing war crimes and the crime against humanity of extermination with relentless and deliberate attacks on medical personnel and facilities.”

author: Jack Munafo
title: City of Newcastle chooses business bottom line over the climate
content:
The Newcastle City Council has voted to ban Rising Tide, Australia’s largest climate activist group, from hosting events on council-owned land. The motion, put by right-wing independent mayor and former weather reporter Gavin Morris, has sought to rid Newcastle of climate protests.

For many years, Rising Tide has forced the Newcastle City Council to confront the reality of hosting the world’s largest coal port. One hundred and fifty million tonnes of coal left the port in 2025, over 95 percent of which was sold to various Southeast Asian countries. Emissions from its usage, which are approximately 1 percent of Earth’s total CO2 emissions each year, are not counted towards Australia’s CO2 emissions.

The council motion passed 7-6. Voting against were three Greens and three Labor councillors. One Labor councillor, failed mayoral candidate Declan Clausen, voted for the bill. He attended the council meeting over Zoom from the COP31 climate conference in Türkiye. 

The council’s ban is not restricted to Rising Tide. It also applies to “its associates, subsidiaries, affiliated Issue Motivated Groups; and individuals”. Who counts as an “issue motivated group or individual” is at the discretion of the council. When interviewed by ABC Radio the morning after the vote, Morris said he “would be comfortable with” the wide-reaching powers of prohibition granted to the council targeting other groups. He specifically mentioned Palestine-related groups as being potentially affected by this motion.

Morris’ principal bugbear is Rising Tide’s annual People’s Blockade, where protesters take to Newcastle Harbour to prevent coal ships from moving into the port. Morris couched his motion in terms of community safety, but Business Hunter CEO Bob Hawes, in his letter of support for the motion, was willing to say the quiet part out loud:

“[Rising Tide] continues to have adverse impacts on regional businesses and the local visitor economy ... Rising Tide supporters might not like what some of these operators do but they are undertaking legal business activities ... and they have a right to undertake them without disruption.”

The operation of the port alone generated about $107 million in 2025, let alone the profits that come from actually selling the goods that move through it. 

Morris also received letters of support from NSW Premier Chris Minns and police minister Yasmin Catley. Their support tells you everything you need to know about Labor’s stance on climate change. These letters came only weeks after Minns’ approval of the largest coal expansion in NSW history, and months after his announcement that the Great Koala National Park will be funded by pay-to-pollute carbon credits.

Morris was elected in February this year. He has taken his election as a mandate from “the community” to clamp down on Rising Tide. We must show him that the Newcastle community stands with Rising Tide and for real action on climate change, not the profits of the coal industry.

title: Yeah Nah Pasaran #306 w James Hogg on inter-war fascism and radical Melbourne history : November 19, 2026
content:
This week on Yeah Nah Pasaran! we talk to James Hogg. James is an historian and one of the organisers of ‘Radical Melbourne! A People’s History Festival’, which takes place this Saturday at balam balam place in Brunswick:

Radical Melbourne! is a full-day festival celebrating Melbourne’s incredible history of ordinary people fighting collectively for a better life and a better world – from migrant strikes, to fighting the far-right, to Aboriginal resistance to colonisation.

For tickets, see here and see/hear also : People’s History of Australia.

We last spoke to James in September 2024 about Greek & Yugoslavian Anti-Fascism in Melbourne’s “Long 1960s”. On this occasion, we talked to James a little about the conference (where he’ll be presenting on ‘Fighting Imperial Fascism in Melbourne: the British Fascisti and the Australian Labour Movement, 1921-26′), and his research into inter-war anti-fascism in (‘so-called!’) Australia.

author: Chris Lang
title: The Antalya AI pledge: Voluntary commitments to greenwash a destructive industry
content:
The COP31 Presidency and the International Telecommunication Union, the United Nations agency for digital technologies launched the Antalya AI Pledge at COP31 in Türkiye, on November 16.

The Pledge is yet another voluntary pledge produced over more than three decades of COP meetings that will do less than nothing to address the climate crisis. Worse, the governments endorsing the Pledge are actively supporting a massively polluting industry that is accelerating the climate crisis.

The Antalya AI Pledge was launched at a “High-level Green Digital Action Roundtable on AI”. The Roundtable discussion is available here.

Tomas Lamanauskas, the deputy secretary-general of the International Telecommunication Union told the meeting that, “AI is really the technology that’s transforming our lives and mostly for good, I should say. From our daily ability to write speeches ... to much more high level aspects from medicine to agriculture, to education, as well as industries.”

Obviously, Lamanauskas didn’t give any concrete examples of any of this. Neither did he mention that the AI bubble is threatening another global financial crisis. Or that the main use of AI is to extract ever more fossil fuels. And he made no mention of the military AI industry.

“It has a really transformative potential to make everyone’s lives much better,” Lamanauskas said. Presumably Lamanauskas is oblivious to the recent United States elections in which voters made their feelings crystal clear about the data centres that have devastated so many communities.

Lamanauskas talked about AI’s energy use as a “challenge that we need to rein in if we want AI to sustainable power the world and to make sure that AI is a solution not the problem”.

Simon Stiell, executive secretary of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change, told the meeting that, “AI and other frontier technologies are a double edged sword. The task ahead is to blunt their dangerous edges, sharpen their catalytic ones, and put these technologies responsibly to work.”

Stiell noted that communities are “pushing back against data centres, concerned about their water, their energy bills, and their environment. So public support is already sinking deeper under water.”

Companies should, according to Stiell, “power data centres with renewable energy”.

But the Pledge makes no mention of fossil fuels. Instead it consists of vague statements about powering and building AI “sustainably”, managing AI “responsibly”, reporting the environmental impacts, and strengthening “financial support and technical infrastructure for AI for climate action”.

There is no mechanism to hold any of the companies or governments that sign the Pledge to account if they breach the terms of the Pledge.

The reality is that the Antalya AI Pledge is greenwashing a massively destructive, extractive, unethical, thieving industry. “AI companies’ license to operate is already on thin ice, right across political spectrums in many countries. And under that thin ice lie some potentially very deep regulatory waters, as political landscapes shift,” Stiell said in his speech at the launch.

“Very deep regulatory waters” is exactly what the world needs to prevent the damage that AI is already causing — damage that is accelerating every day.

“CEOs and boards need to step-up, and align business and investment plans with the world’s agreed climate goals,” Stiell said. The voluntary Antalya AI Pledge exists to allow the AI industry to continue its destructive business as usual.

Justine Calma, writing in The Verge, describes the Pledge as a “cruel joke”.

She points out that the Pledge even states that, “these objectives of the pledge are voluntary and non-prescriptive, create no new obligations, and are to be implemented in accordance with national circumstances”.

“In other words,” Calma writes, “these are voluntary commitments that countries can choose to follow or not follow based on their whims”.

On the same day as the launch of the Antalya AI Pledge, an assessment of the carbon emissions and energy consumption of US hyperscale data centres was published in Nature Sustainability. This is the first peer-reviewed estimate of the climate impact of data centres in the US.

The study estimates that hyperscale data centres in the US emitted between 21-31 million metric tonnes of CO₂ from May 2024 to April 2025 and used about 2% of US electricity. As Emily Atkin writes in Heated, these are big numbers, but “they’re also …

author: Shirley Killen
title: Building the socialist movement in regional Victoria
content:
Victorians from Mildura to Mallacoota will have the chance to vote socialist for the first time in generations at this month’s state election. In a campaign that’s been full of milestones for the Victorian Socialists, one of the biggest is that the party is standing candidates in all 88 lower house seats for the first time. 

Networks of socialist activists have sprung up across the state with the goal of getting these candidates elected, putting on meetings, organising local rallies, door knocking and letterboxing. In some places, like Bendigo and Ballarat, local branches already existed, while in others, coordinators are starting from scratch.

David Suter is one of the local coordinators starting from scratch. He describes turning up to a polling booth after moving to Garfield, in eastern Victoria and part of the electorate of Narracan, looking at his options and thinking “this is bullshit”. The dearth of organised radical politics in regional areas could easily make a person feel disheartened. But David was encouraged by the result the Victorian Socialists achieved in last year’s federal election, so he signed up to attend the party’s state conference later that year. He left with a list of phone numbers and a plan to activate socialists in his region, and established a crew of seven who began sketching out a state election campaign. Now, the party has candidates contesting all eleven lower house seats, and the beginnings of local branches in Narracan, Shepparton, Bairnsdale and the Mornington Peninsula—to name just a few. 

These are “baby steps”, according to David. It’s a big task to rebuild (or just build, sometimes) a socialist tradition in regional Victoria. But the Victorian Socialists’ state election campaign so far has proved it is not impossible, and that with a common goal and some organisational infrastructure, socialists who previously felt isolated in the regions can make a difference.

Renee Nayef, the Victorian Socialists candidate for Mildura in Victoria’s north-west, described a “meet the candidate” event she put on recently. Two men drove into Mildura separately from a nearby town of 97 people, both assuming they were the only socialists for kilometres. They met for the first time at Renee’s event. Without the scaffolding of a statewide socialist campaign, they might have gone on for years not knowing there was another radical a couple of streets over. 

Sometimes these connections are made in unorthodox ways. For socialist campaigners in metropolitan Melbourne, the movement is built by knocking on other people’s doors and starting up conversations about socialism. Socialists in the regions report the opposite experience—locals are instead knocking on 

their 

doors because they’ve seen a yard sign and are thrilled to know there’s another socialist in town. 

In some parts of the state, the campaign is reviving largely forgotten radical traditions. Bass candidate for Victorian Socialists Chris Jobe had to correct the record when the local paper announced his candidacy with the headline “Red flag planted in Bass for the first time”. In fact, the seat of Bass takes in the old mining town Wonthaggi, known for much of the twentieth century as “Red Wonthaggi” because of the militancy of the local communist-led miners’ union. A more accurate headline would have been “Red flag planted in Bass 

again

”. 

The picture in regional Victoria today is clearly very different from the days when the Wonthaggi miners fought bitter industrial battles with coal bosses and the state. With few exceptions, these seats are the preserve of the Liberals and Nationals, with One Nation now poised to make serious gains. Socialists campaigning outside Melbourne don’t sugarcoat the challenges they are facing.

But socialist politics haven’t been seriously tested outside the state’s biggest cities in decades. It’s not surprising that conservative politics dominate when there’s nothing much else on offer. 

And working-class people in rural Victoria face the same stresses as their counterparts in Melbourne. The rising cost of living, the health system stretched to breaking point, the failure of successive governments to invest in transport and education—these issues are coming up all across the state. 

For Hera Sheppard, Victorian Socialists candidate for the South-West Coast, it was growing up in Warrnambool’s public housing that made her a socialist. She witnessed the way Labor neglected its housing stock and failed to …

author: @ndy
title: The struggle is real with Jillian Segal.
content:
See also : Jillian Segal and husband funding far-right group “Advance”, Anthony Klan, The Klaxon, July 12, 2025.

Jillian Segal — the South African–born Australian lawyer, business executive, and Australia’s Special Envoy to Combat Antisemitism — recently dropped another Report, ASECA Priorities. According to the Special Envoy, a newly-hatched “modern progressive antisemitism” … is taking “the hostility of Islamic extremism and far-left antisemitism, together with traditional antisemitic tropes”.

My first reaction on reading this passage was to recall the unforgettable 2014 framing by the Australian Defence League of the alleged “evil anarcho-pinko-anarchist-islamic cabal of dirt”; the wicked coalition then allegedly intent on turning Penrith into a no-go zone for patriots.

In any case, inre the Report, Jeffrey Loewenstein doesn’t hold back in It’s time to sack Jillian Segal (Deepcut News, November 2, 2026), the Jewish Council of Australia (October 30, 2026) has slammed it, and Jeff Sparrow has characterised it, not unfairly, as a Trumpian plan to curtail free speech (Crikey, November 2, 2026). The Report is also subject to critical scrutiny by Robert Manne, who examines it in On the Rise of Antisemitism in Australia (November 8, 2026), along with the thoughts of Lord Andrew Roberts and Sir Simon Schama on the subject of ‘antisemitism’. Manne concludes that:

Schama believes he can help combat the rise of antisemitism in the Diaspora by defending the indefensible, the war crimes of the IDF under Benjamin Netanyahu. I believe a more likely remedy would be for leading Diaspora thinkers, like Schama, and influential publishers, like Morry Schwartz, and the leaders in Australia of the principal Israel and Jewish lobbies, like Jillian Segal, to speak the truth about what, under Netanyahu and the two Kahanist-fascist members of his Government, Israel has become, and the moral revolution that has to happen in Israel if Jews in the Diaspora are to be spared from the dreadful rise of antisemitism that is spreading around the Western world.

FWIW, for over 20 years I’ve been attempting, inter alia, to monitor and document organised, public expressions of antisemitism and other racisms in Australia — the better to disrupt it. I’m also an anarchist, and one of many people to hold the view that the Israeli state has engaged in a genocidal assault upon Palestine in the three years since October 7 (the latest chapter in a much longer history of deadly state violence). On that basis, I assume that Segal et. al. would categorise myself as an exponent of ‘far-left antisemitism’, the meaning of which is elaborated upon in this passage:

Far-left antisemitism or issue-motivated antisemitism

Far-left ideology and associated activism feature a worldview that casts the world in terms of ‘oppressors’ and ‘oppressed’. Within this binary framework, Israel is portrayed as a colonial project that is inherently racist and Jews who support Israel’s existence are portrayed as representatives of ‘whiteness’ (regardless of their ethnicity), privilege (regardless of their means), imperialism (notwithstanding the absence of an empire), greedy capitalism and the projection of Western power.

This framing allows longstanding antisemitic motifs to be repackaged in the academic language of anti-racism, decolonisation, human rights, social justice and intersectionality, often in service of a traditional Marxist revolutionary agenda.

When a cause is believed – with ideological fervour – to be absolutely just, its ends can come to justify any means and its adherents can feel free to vilify, harass and seek to destroy those who associate with what is framed as evil.

Over time, the language of human rights and its greatest crimes – apartheid, ethnic cleansing, genocide, etc. – has increasingly been appropriated to portray Israel (and, relevantly, members of the Jewish community who support it) as morally evil, often to the point of being equated to Nazis.

In contemporary Australia, elements of Australia’s historically fringe radical left have sought to appeal to well-meaning mainstream progressive Australians who may perceive the Palestinian cause as a matter of social justice. This ‘gateway’ issue, of sorts, has been used by far-left activists to magnify their appeal and prominence and to attempt to introduce traditionally moderate Australians to radical and anti-Jewish propaganda that would previously have been of little interest.

author: Önder Algedik
title: COP31 week one: A summit without discussion of fossil fuels
content:
If you followed the first week of COP31 from Australia, you probably heard about the $32,000 coffee cart at the Australian pavilion and the hot mic that caught Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and energy minister Chris Bowen joking about where to keep their phones.

Much less was said about what happened in Türkiye on the opening day.

On November 9, while the summit opened with a lavish ceremony in Antalya, President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan came out of a cabinet meeting in Ankara with good news: 135 million barrels of new oil potential had been found at Gabar, in Türkiye’s south-east.

The same day, at the HABAŞ steel plant in Aliağa, near İzmir, an overhead crane fell and ruptured a gas line. The explosion that followed killed 19 workers.

This workplace disaster did not make the agenda of the climate summit. HABAŞ runs its arc furnace on electricity from coal and gas, and supplies steel to the construction and car industries.

But COP31 does not talk about fossil fuels as a material order made of steel, cement and workers. It talks about an abstract “emission” to be managed from a distance. A worker killed in a fossil plant falls, by definition, is outside the frame.

Three days later, union confederations met inside the COP31 venue to discuss “just transition”. Nineteen workers were killed and Türkiye is speeding up its transition to fossil fuels but neither was on their agenda.

Türkiye, which holds the COP31 presidency, prepared well for a climate-changing summit. Since it was named host, it has signed 19 fossil fuel supply and exploration agreements, plus six nuclear and mining deals. It kept signing during the summit.

Australia, which presides over the negotiations, is no different. Labor had already approved 37 new or expanded fossil fuel projects. Weeks before the summit it made it 38, clearing the Boggabri coal mine to dig another 30 million tonnes.

In Antalya, Albanese put the Pacific Island nations at the centre of his speech and then spent more time on home batteries than on coal and gas.

Bowen told the ABC that coal and gas exports have not damaged Australia's standing in the talks, and that his job is to land “the most ambitious outcome that consensus will allow”.

Tuvalu’s Prime Minister Feleti Teo described new fossil fuel projects “a death sentence for us”.

The Pacific Resilience Facility, Australia’s showpiece, reached US$200 million in Antalya. By Albanese’s own account, 46% of the money, so far, has come from Pacific countries themselves.

Meanwhile, according to Climate Action Network, Australia has joined the European Union, Japan and Norway in opposing a commitment to triple adaptation finance, in the very text it is supposed to be steering.

This is what I call climate-changing policy. Once you know it, you can see the climate-changing summit behind the “climate summit” and the transition to fossil fuels behind the “just transition” slogan.

COP31 President Murat Kurum, Türkiye’s environment minister, did not say the word “fossil” once in his opening speech. Bowen said it twice. At the leaders’ summit, Erdoğan and Albanese barely touched it.

In the first week, 56 negotiating documents were published; draft texts, informal notes, draft conclusions and decisions. They run to 268 pages. Coal and oil do not appear in them. “Fossil” turns up, at most, in a heading.

The only text that plainly mentions transitioning away from fossil fuels is a non-binding summary of views from the presidency. It repeats the 2023 Dubai sentence, limited to “energy systems”, so asphalt, cement and plastics are out from the start.

Brazil’s road map is voluntary. Even so, the Arab Group reportedly objected from day one to any reference to the road map in decision texts.

The words are missing because of how COP31 works. Decisions are taken by consensus, so a single bloc can strike it. The hosts are sitting on their own fossil expansion and have no wish to force it. The silence suits everyone.

Instead, Türkiye and Australia are selling another target: Lifting electricity’s share of final energy use to 35% by 2035. Whether that electricity comes from renewables or from fossil fuels is not the question. Bowen says tying it to renewables would be too hard for many countries.

Türkiye generates much of its own electricity by burning coal and gas, and Australia is among its top five coal suppliers.

The other big topic is finance: Extra money for climate projects, while the public keeps paying for the fossil order. Free …

author: Sarah Garnham
title: One Nation is waging war on progress. Why won't progressives fight back?
content:
In 2018, One Nation struggled to get registered as a political party in Victoria, and progressives across the state took pride in it. Labor won the state election that year with a whopping 43 percent primary vote. Twenty years earlier, One Nation leader Pauline Hanson had been prevented from organising in Melbourne by protests, blockades and community events.

Today, the snarling menace and enemy of workers and the left that is One Nation is a major force in Victoria; it enjoys mass support, is vying for lower house seats, and setting the agenda in the state election campaign. The party and its policies have been legitimised by the capitalist press, the Liberal Party and, to a lesser extent, Labor. One Nation’s Victorian leader, Warren Pickering, has been invited to appear at the leaders’ debate.  

Progressive Victoria should be in uproar. This is the state of Trades Hall, Treaty and Pride. But aside from a few important exceptions—most notably high school students—the response to One Nation’s rise has been decidedly muted. Progressive NGOs and organisations have mostly stayed silent or offered tepid statements focusing on the fears of their constituents rather than forthright denunciation of One Nation and all it represents. The mood is closer to stunned awe than anger, almost as if the capacity to generate the ever-more-elusive commodity of popularity makes a party worthy of respect, however the popularity might be gained. 

Worse still, a layer of trade union organisers, Greens members and other progressives is arguing that the left must sympathise with the concerns of One Nation voters, or at least avoid antagonising them through political argument. In practice, this means sidestepping the signature issues that One Nation is pushing and building a base around. 

GetUp and Victorian Trades Hall Council (VTHC) are 

directing

 campaigners not to “play the racism card” or explicitly attack Pauline Hanson. After its costly and high-profile intervention in the Farrer by-election, GetUp concluded that criticising Hanson, her wealthy backer Gina Rinehart, celebrity defector Barnaby Joyce or the party’s links to Trump is not electorally expedient. Campaigners should instead seek to establish common ground with potential One Nation voters based on economic grievances. 

Senior VTHC researcher Oscar Kaspi-Crutchett 

argues

 to ignore the politics: “Don’t listen to the lyrics, listen to the beat of what they are saying”. The beat, he says, is dissatisfaction with the status quo, so supporters should be helped to “tease out” what that looks like and how it makes them feel. 

Federal Greens leader David Shoebridge 

says

 he has “understood the anger” driving One Nation support. Former Queensland Greens MP Max Chandler-Mathers 

goes further

, arguing that One Nation voters, especially the workers among them, are expressing legitimate protest against the system. He says they are driven by an “almost political nihilism”, and a desire to “blow it up” that makes them open to left-wing arguments and solutions. 

The same basic approach is being taken by more establishment political forces. Teal consultant Sue Barret gives the 

same advice

in four steps: validate the feeling, not the target; ask a genuine question and then be quiet; acknowledge the ground you share; offer a different path, not a different diagnosis.

Labor’s federal treasurer likewise 

warns

 progressives not to “scold” One Nation supporters, and to approach them “from a place of genuine respect and understanding”. The same advice is given by the media, from the establishment right through to liberal outlets. And all of this helps to reinforce One Nation’s 

spin

 about itself: that it is the party of “everyday Australians” who are “sick and tired of being ignored”. 

This appeasement goes further than merely tempering criticisms of One Nation for fear of alienating the party’s voters; it leads to actively opposing efforts to build resistance. 

The Labor-controlled National Union of Students, for example, pulled out of supporting the second student walkout against One Nation, and attacked office bearers for promoting it. Some Greens MPs have endorsed and spoken at the rallies, but others refused to speak on the grounds that it is not strategic and would alienate bigots. When a socialist promoted an anti-One Nation rally in a union activist online forum, the Victorian secretary of the CPSU and long-time leftist Jiselle Hanna replied that it is “more …

author: Maharnav Bhuyan
title: Labor and One Nation compete to arrest their way out of a mental health crisis
content:
Labor and One Nation agree on almost nothing, with the exception being on crime, where they read from the same script.

Premier Ben Carroll wants 1500 more police. One Nation wants more police, harsher treatment of repeat offenders and a 24/7 bail court. Its campaign launch promised to make Victoria the toughest state on crime. The Coalition has simply raised the bid to 3000. Labor's Attorney-General insists “tough bail is working”.

Victoria has run this experiment before. Labor funded 3135 more police between 2016 and 2021. Over 2024-25, the number of criminal incidents hit its highest level since records began.

Ask Victoria Police what drives crime and the answer reads like a social policy brief.

In June, it named the cost of living, recidivism, organised crime and drugs. In September, it listed organised crime, recidivism, mental health and illicit drugs.

Who ends up on the inside? In the latest national survey of people entering prison, from last year, 51% had been diagnosed with a mental health condition and 73% had used illicit drugs in the past year. In the month before prison, 43% were homeless and 46% were unemployed.

These statistics show that rather than being hardened criminals, prisoners are people who have been failed by a squeezed economy, a broken health system and by communities with nowhere to turn.

When people do reach out, the door is often shut.

About 4550 Victorians were waiting for drug and alcohol treatment on any given day last year. In June 2025, 14 men sat in custody waiting for a bed at Thomas Embling, the state’s secure psychiatric hospital. Victoria’s own royal commission found the mental health system had “catastrophically failed”.

On November 6, HungryPanda rider Feng Jianming was stabbed to death near the Queen Victoria Market. He was 47, a father of two, and had spent nine years working here to support his family. A second rider was seriously injured.

Roberto Urbano, 51, has been charged with the murder. He is presumed innocent, but the court has already seen something every politician promising more police should think about. Urbano’s lawyer told the court that he experiences schizophrenia.

Appearing by video link from a police cell, in front of a magistrate, Urbano stood on a stool and exposed himself to the courtroom. Police custody, a camera and a magistrate; there is no more heavily-policed place. If the law cannot reach a person in that state, another 1500 police officers on the street certainly will not.

People in a mental health crisis need care; they need treatment before things fall apart. Was Urbano seeing a doctor? Did he have somewhere safe to live? Those are the questions this case should prompt every party running in the election to answer.

None of this means people with mental illness are dangerous; they are several times more likely than others to be assaulted.

The lesson is simple: A society where vulnerable people can ask for help and get it is a safer society.

Instead, the money flows to prison cells. Since Labor’s “toughest bail laws in Australia” began in March last year, the prison population has grown by about 19%.

This year’s state budget found $229 million for new prison beds and $43 million for programs that keep people out of them.

Each prisoner costs the public purse almost $600 a day and more than a third of those released are back inside within two years.

One Nation’s other big idea — tougher sentences — is weaker still.

The Coalition offers more of the same. Opposition Leader Jess Wilson’s 3000 extra police would include recruits from Britain, Ireland and New Zealand.

The Coalition also promises a “one-strike” bail rule for serious offences and has promised to expand Adult Time for Violent Crime from eight offences to 20. Youth diversion gets a mention after the police, bail and sentencing pledges.

The Victorian Sentencing Advisory Council found that longer prison terms do not produce a matching increase in deterrence. A longer stretch inside does not treat what it was that put the person there.

You cannot handcuff the cost of living. You cannot arrest a mental illness.

This is not a call on parties to be “soft” on crime. It is about being more serious about crime prevention. That means funding mental health and drug treatment until the queues disappear. It means building the forensic beds, called for by the royal commission. People leaving prison need secure homes to go to. Nationally, a third expect to be homeless on release …

author: Nick Everett
title: Remembering the Santa Cruz massacre
content:
Thirty-five years ago, Indonesian elite Kopassus troops opened fire on a peaceful procession in Dili, the capital of then Indonesian-occupied East Timor (today known as Timor Leste), killing hundreds. The Indonesian generals responsible have never faced justice, protected by the Western governments who armed them and abetted their crimes. 

The procession, on the morning of 12 November 1991, followed a memorial mass at Motael Church for Sebastião Gomes Rangel, a young Timorese man killed by Indonesian security forces two weeks earlier. As the procession of 3,000 mourners made its way to Santa Cruz cemetery, pro-independence banners and flags were unfurled. Minutes after the crowd arrived at the cemetery, troops opened fire without warning.

Shooting continued as people tried to scale the cemetery’s high walls. Some were shot in the back while running away. Others while seeking shelter behind tombstones or in the cemetery’s chapel. More were stabbed and shot as they lay on the ground in pools of blood. According to survivor testimonies, dozens more were executed or disappeared after being taken to the Wira Husada Military Hospital. 

At least 271 East Timorese were killed that day, and an equal number disappeared, believed dead, according to the East Timor Action Network.

Australian foreign minister Gareth Evans was quick to defend Indonesia’s military, which had invaded East Timor in December 1975 and maintained a brutal occupation of the former Portuguese colony. A month after the massacre, Evans

told

 parliament that while the incident was “‘deplorable”, it “was not ... a calculated or deliberate act of the [Indonesian] government as such”. Rather, it was “the product of aberrant behaviour by a subgroup within the country”. 

Two years earlier, Evans had joined his Indonesian counterpart, Ali Alatas, to toast the signing of the Timor Gap Treaty in a plane above the Timor Sea. With a glass of champagne in his hand, Evans declared: “This is a uniquely historical moment that is truly, uniquely historical”.

The treaty, several years in the making, carved up the rich oil and gas resources beneath the Timor Sea and opened the way for their exploitation by Australian resource companies. 

The Santa Cruz massacre was not unique. Many had preceded it, including the Kraras massacres, in the southern municipality of Viqueque in 1983. Prabowo Subianto, a rising star in the army and the son-in-law of Indonesian dictator, General Suharto, commanded the Kopassus special forces unit responsible. 

The Kraras massacres have been

compared

 with the US army’s massacre of Vietnamese civilians in the village of Mai Lai in 1968. Much like the strategy pursued by Israel in Gaza and Lebanon, such attacks sought to isolate combatants via major military operations that killed and displaced large numbers of civilians.

In 2005, East Timor’s Truth and Reconciliation Commission (CAVR)

concluded

 that Indonesia’s 24-year-long occupation resulted in between 102,800 and 183,000 conflict-related deaths, alongside widespread systematic torture, unlawful killings, enforced disappearances, forced displacement, and sexual violence. Many human rights organisations, including

Genocide Watch

, argue that Indonesia committed a genocide in East Timor.

What made the 1991 Santa Cruz massacre different from those that preceded it was that it was caught on

film

. When British cameraman Max Stahl’s footage was subsequently broadcast, it shone a light on Indonesia’s crimes and revived a global solidarity movement.

In Australia in the 1990s, socialists led a campaign group called Action in Solidarity with Indonesia and East Timor (ASIET), which coordinated demonstrations in conjunction with other East Timor solidarity groups across the country to commemorate the Santa Cruz massacre on 12 November each year.

We argued that the overthrow of Indonesia’s military dictatorship would open the road to Timorese independence, and that we therefore needed to support not only the resistance to the occupation, but also the growing student and worker movements in Indonesia that were calling for an end to Suharto’s military rule. We demanded that our own government break military ties with Indonesia.

Military and diplomatic ties between the two countries were extensive and growing, and by 1996 included a military pact. At the time, Australia was training Kopassus forces at the Kokoda Barracks on the Gold Coast. The Keating government also shamefully (and …

author: Jesse Hagopian
title: Students Around the World Are Skipping Class to Enter Class Struggle
content:
High school students’ revolts are shaking governments and transforming struggles over education into struggles over society itself.

High school students’ revolts are shaking governments and transforming struggles over education into struggles over society itself.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

“They never listen to us. They never listen to high schoolers. And if we don’t fight, nobody is going to fight for us,” one French high school student emphatically told the BBC at a recent mass youth protest.

Her frustration reflects a familiar political reality: Politicians routinely dismiss young people’s grievances rather than confront the conditions driving their anger. In 2024, the French newspaper Le Monde described a recurring caricature of French youth as “lazy, resistant to authority and even selfish.” In the United States, Fox News host Jesse Watters dismissed complaints about rising costs from “kids” who, he claimed, had “never had real jobs.” White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt agreed, declaring, “It’s laziness,” and accusing Gen Z of having grown up with “everything handed to them.”

Writing off young people as entitled and incapable of serious political thought is an old political reflex. Yet while those in power accuse young people of laziness and debate what is wrong with them, youth around the globe are hard at work challenging what is wrong with society and changing the world.

On November 20, students and young people in more than 25 European countries will join a coordinated International Youth and Student Strike under the banner “Fight for Our Future, Not Their Wars,” an action emerging from a much wider wave of youth revolt stretching from Mayotte to Morocco, Chile, Argentina, Brazil, and beyond. The strike call links education and housing to austerity, climate breakdown, and militarization.

These revolts led by high school students show how struggles over schools can become struggles over society — and over who has the power to shape it.

While the mass protests in Paris have drawn international attention, the high school revolt began weeks earlier in France’s overseas territories. Students and teachers started mobilizing on August 31 at Lycée de la Cité du Nord in Mayotte — an island off East Africa that remains under French rule despite decades of UN resolutions recognizing it as part of the independent nation of Comoros. Thérèse Lebeault, a 10th-grade student at Lycée Younoussa Bamana, described the conditions:

There are too many students in the classrooms … There aren’t enough toilets — there are three when we’re nearly 3,000 students. There are no fans in the classrooms, not enough nurses, not enough buses for transportation. There’s also a shortage of teachers, a shortage of classrooms — everything, really … nothing is right.

On September 7, students at Lycée Félix-Éboué in French Guiana presented 17 demands over deteriorating school conditions. As the revolt spread, students in Martinique, Guadeloupe, and Réunion — all former colonies that remain under French rule — joined the wave, exposing how struggles over education are intertwined with colonial inequality.

In metropolitan France, students were confronting many of the same problems. Mohammed, a 17-year-old student in the Paris suburb of Sevran, described classrooms where “there aren’t enough chairs or desks to go around, so some students have to stand up,” and said some students go “months without teachers when absent staff aren’t replaced.” Fadila, 17, at Lycée Paul Éluard in Saint-Denis, described “cockroaches and rats everywhere in the school,” broken toilets without running water and classrooms reaching 104°F in summer. “We can’t work in those conditions,” she said. In Strasbourg, 17-year-old Raphael described overcrowding, extreme heat, too few toilets, and water leaks: “The building is falling apart.”

These revolts led by high school students show how struggles over schools can become struggles over society — and over who has the power to shape it.

These were not isolated complaints. Across France, students were identifying common grievances and organizing collective demands. The Union Syndicale Lycéenne, France’s main high school student union, pointed to “lack of teachers and staff,” “dilapidated high school buildings,” “overloaded timetables and overcrowded classes,” and “stress caused by …

title: EMEP ve Sol Parti Kayseri'den Sözcü TV kayyımına tepki: Yasaklara teslim olmayacağız
content:
Emek Partisi (EMEP) ve Sol Parti Kayseri il örgütleri, Sözcü TV'ye kayyım atanmasına karşı ortak basın açıklaması yaptı. Açıklamada, Tele1, Halk TV ve Sözcü TV'ye yönelik kayyım uygulamalarına tepki gösterilerek özgür basınla dayanışma çağrısı yapıldı.

Açıklamada, muhalif televizyon kanallarına yönelik baskılara, kayyım uygulamalarına, erişim engellerine ve gazetecilere yönelik cezalar ile tutuklamalara tepki gösterildi. Basın açıklamasını EMEP Kayseri İl Yöneticisi Barış Timur okudu.

Timur, Sözcü TV'ye kayyım atanmasının basın özgürlüğüne yönelik saldırılara yeni bir halka eklediğini belirterek, "Gelişmeler çok açık bizlere gösteriyor ki, Saray iktidarı medyayı; kayyumlarla, karartmalarla, cezalarla susturma çabası içerisindedir" dedi.

Tele1 ve Halk TV'ye yönelik kayyım uygulamalarını hatırlatan Timur, televizyon kanallarının kapatılması, belediyelere yönelik operasyonlar, sosyal medya hesaplarına erişim engelleri ve gazetelere verilen cezaların baskı politikalarının parçası olduğunu söyledi.

Evrensel, BirGün ve Cumhuriyet başta olmak üzere muhalif gazetelere yönelik cezaların sürdüğünü belirten Timur, muhalif gazetecilerin tutuklanması ve baskıların arttığını ifade etti.

"Ülkemiz dün sabah yine bir basın kurumuna polis operasyonu ile uyandı. Sözcü TV'ye kayyum atanarak demokrasiye ve basın özgürlüğüne karşı yapılan saldırılara bir halka daha eklendi. Bundan önce Tele1 ve Halk TV'ye kayyum atanarak ekranları karartılmıştı. Bir sabah kalkıyorsunuz televizyon kanalları kapatılıyor, belediyelere operasyonlar düzenleniyor, onlarca sosyal medya hesabına erişim engeli geliyor, gazetelere cezalar havada uçuşuyor. Muhalif gazetecilere yönelik tutuklama ve baskı katlanarak devam ediyor. Evrensel, BirGün, Cumhuriyet başta olmak üzere muhalif gazetelere cezalar yağdırılıyor. Gelişmeler çok açık bizlere gösteriyor ki, Saray iktidarı medyayı; kayyumlarla, karartmalarla, cezalarla susturma çabası içerisindedir."

Saray rejiminin kendi denetimindeki kanallardan daha fazla izleyiciye sahip televizyon kanallarının varlığına tahammül edemediğini belirten Timur, fon vurgunu iddiaları karşısında gazeteci tutuklamaları, erişim engelleri ve kayyım uygulamalarıyla baskının artırıldığını söyledi. Timur, yaşananların "aynı zamanda bir çaresizliğin dışa vurumu" olduğunu ifade etti.

Basına yönelik baskıların halkın doğru bilgiye ulaşmasını engellediğini belirten Timur, yaklaşık iki aydır kamuoyunun gündeminde olan ve iddialara göre 700 milyar lirayı bulan fon vurgunu iddialarının üzerinin örtülmek istendiğini öne sürdü.

İzmir HABAŞ Demir Çelik'te 19 işçinin yanarak yaşamını yitirmesinin ardından işçilerin eylemlerine ve olaya ilişkin haberlere yayın yasağı getirildiğini hatırlatan Timur, yurttaşların haber alma ve gerçekleri öğrenme hakkının hedef alındığını söyledi.

Timur, "Yoksullukla, açlıkla baş başa bırakılmış yurttaşların haber alma, gerçekleri öğrenme hakkına saldırılar düzenleneceğine, vurguncuların birkaçının değil tamamının hesap vermesi gerekmektedir" dedi.

Basın üzerindeki sansürün, suskun ve teslim olmuş bir toplum yaratma hedefinin parçası olduğunu savunan Timur, işçi ve emekçilerin baskılara teslim olmayacağını belirtti. Timur, "Bu karanlığı hep birlikte aşacağız. Bu saray ve oligarşik düzen ülkeyi bütünüyle bir hapishaneye dönüştürmek istiyor. Bu keyfiliklere, yasaklara ve kayyımlara asla teslim olmayacağız, geri adım atmayacağız" ifadelerini kullandı.

Açıklamada, işçi ve emekçiler ile halka baskı ve zorbalığa karşı dayanışma, mücadele ve direnme çağrısı yapılarak özgür basın için ses yükseltmeleri istendi.

Basın açıklamasının sonunda gazeteci İsmail Arı'nın yarın görülecek davasına dayanışma çağrısı yapıldı. Tutuklu gazetecilerin serbest bırakılması ve gazetecilerin mesleklerini özgürce yapabilmesi talebi yinelendi.

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

author: Unknown
title: İran: 13 petrol işçisinin trafik cinayetinde ölümüne öfke rejim karşıtı gösteriye dönüştü
content:
İran'ın batısındaki İlam eyaletine bağlı, ağırlıkla Kürt nüfusun yaşadığı Abdanan kentinde otobüsle işe giden 13 petrol ve gaz işçisinin ölümüne yol açan trafik cinayeti, yerel yöneticilerin istifasının talebiyle başlayan protestoların ardından İslam Cumhuriyeti yönetimine karşı gösterilere dönüştü.


14 Kasım Cumartesi akşamı Dehloran Petropalaj Şirketi'nin NGL 3100 projesinde çalışan işçi ve mühendisleri taşıyan servis otobüsü, Deşt Abbas–Murmuri yolunda, Segar köyü yakınlarında devrildi. Kazada 13 kişi yaşamını yitirdi.


Yaralıların sayısını Radio Farda 15, Hengaw ve Kürdistan İnsan Hakları Ağı 17 olarak bildirdi. 


Yas töreninden protestoya


17 Kasım Salı günü Abdanan'da kazada ölen işçilerden birinin cenaze töreninin ardından bir araya gelen yüzlerce kişi, yolların güvensizliğini, ulaşım altyapısındaki eksiklikleri ve yetkililerin ihmallerini protestoya girişti.


Rejimin militan kolluk gücü Devrim Muhafızları'na yakın Fars Haber Ajansı, Veli Asr Meydanı'ndaki gösteride başlangıçta 200–300 olan katılımın giderek 1.000'e ulaştığını bildirdi.


Göstericiler  “Bugün yas günü” ve “İstifa, istifa” sloganlarıyla başladıkları gösteriyi cinayetin sorumlularının hesap vermesi talebiyle sürdürdüler. Ancak gösteri ilerledikçe protestolar yerel yöneticileri aşarak ülke yönetimine yöneldi. Sosyal medyada yayımlanan görüntülerde “Diktatöre ölüm” ve “Liyakatsiz yetkililere ölüm” sloganlarının duyulduğu bildirildi.


Euronews Farsça, bazı görüntülerde seslerin sonradan eklenmiş veya değiştirilmiş olabileceğini belirterek sloganları bağımsız kaynaklardan doğrulayamadığını açıkladı. Ancak rejim yanlısı Fars ajansı da gösterilerin ilerleyen saatlerde siyasal nitelik kazandığını kabul etti.


Bazı görüntülerde de istihbarat bakanlığı ve Besic milis örgütünün propaganda afişlerinin indirildiği görüldü.


Güvenlik güçleri gazla müdahale etti


Kürdistan İnsan Hakları Ağı'nın 18 Kasım'daki açıklamasına göre, özel polis birlikleri göstericilere göz yaşartıcı gazla müdahale etti. Kentte özel müdahale birliklerinin ve Besic güçlerinin yoğun olarak konuşlandırıldığı ve internet bağlantısında kesintiler yaşandığı bildirildi.


Iran International'a konuşan görgü tanıkları, motosikletli güvenlik görevlilerinin havaya ateş açtığını ileri sürdü. Kürdpa ise göstericilere havalı silahlarla müdahale edildiğini bildirdi. 


Abdanan Savcısı Amrollah Meysaei, gösterilerden sonra yaptığı açıklamada olaydan yararlanarak kamu düzenini bozmak isteyenlere karşı sert önlemler alınacağını söyledi.


Gözaltına alınanlardan beşinin nerede olduğu bilinmiyor


İnsan hakları örgütü Hengaw, 18 Kasım'da yayımladığı güncellemede en az 7 kişinin gözaltına alındığını açıkladı.


Örgütün belirlediği isimler şöyle: Sina Dervişi (15), Said Abdullahî, İrec Haydari (51), Muhsin Bavir, Asgar Ekberi, Armin Süleymani ve Behnam Muradi. 


Hengaw'a göre 15 yaşındaki Sina Dervişi ile Muhsin Bavir birkaç saat içinde serbest bırakıldı. Diğer 5 kişinin tutulduğu yerler ve durumları hakkında bilgi edinilemedi.


Kürdistan İnsan Hakları Ağı 6 gözaltıyı teyit edebildiğini duyururken, Hana İnsan Hakları Örgütü de gözaltıların sürdüğüne ilişkin bilgiler yayımladı.


Associated Press'in aktardığına göre, bir eyalet milletvekili gözaltı yaşandığını reddetti.


Trafik cinayetnin sorumlusu kim? 


İlam Trafik Polisi, ilk incelemelerinde otobüs sürücüsünü, aracı kiralayan şirketi ve yol bakımından sorumlu kurumu kusurlu bulduğunu açıkladı. Radio Farda'nın aktardığına göre savcılık, Dehloran taşımacılık şirketinin genel müdürü ve eyalet yol bakım müdürü hakkında adli işlem başlattı.


İlam Valiliği eyalet genelinde bir, Abdanan ilçesinde 2 günlük yas ilan etti.


Mehr Haber Ajansı, hayatını kaybedenlerin ailelerinin trafik cinayetinin nedenlerinin açıklığa kavuşturulmasını ve sorumluların belirlenmesini istediğini; ayrıca kendi adlarına gösteri düzenlenmemesi çağrısı yaptığını bildirdi.


Ocak protestoları hafızalarda 


Yaklaşık 24 bin nüfuslu Abdanan, Ocak 2026'da İran genelinde yaşanan protestoların önemli merkezlerinden biriydi: 9 Ocak'ta Tahran'daki gösterilerde güvenlik güçlerince öldürüldüğü bildirilen 16 yaşındaki Alireza Sayyedi, Abdananlıydı. Cenazesinin 11 Ocak'ta memleketine getirilmesi üzerine kalabalık gösteriler düzenlenmişti.


Kürdistan İnsan Hakları Ağı, cenaze törenine katılanlara gerçek mermiyle ateş açıldığını bildirmişti.


Şubat ortasında Sayyedi'nin ölümünün kırkıncı günü dolayısıyla Abdanan'da yeniden protestolar düzenlenmişti.

author: Miriam Lafontaine
title: Canadian North flight attendants could strike Dec. 19
content:
This story was updated on Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026, at 11:34 a.m. ET.


The union that represents about 200 Canadian North flight attendants said its members could strike as early as Dec. 19 if a new contract with the airline isn’t reached.


Hugh Pouliot, a spokesperson for the Canadian Union of Public Employees Local 8111, said the union hopes to reach a deal with the airline before conciliation talks between them and two federally appointed mediators end Nov. 27. Negotiations for a new collective agreement began in March.


Canadian North meanwhile encouraged the public to tell the Canada Industrial Relations Board how a strike might affect their health and safety. The company shared a social media post Monday about providing submissions.


That board will accept input until Friday before it holds hearings to determine which essential services the airline must continue to provide in the event of a strike or lockout.


“We’ve been surprised at the sudden aggressive change in posture by the employer both in its internal and external communications,” Pouliot said in an interview. “That being said, we’re still hopeful for a deal and to avoid any work stoppage.”


In August, following what it called a

lack of meaningful progress

, the union requested that third-party mediators help negotiations.


Salaries, working conditions, scheduling and unpaid hours are the sticking points, the union has said.


In a Nov. 14 memo to employees, which Nunatsiaq News reviewed, the airline disputed its flight attendants work unpaid.


The email said the company employs “no unpaid cabin crew work” and noted that federal law permits its “credit-based compensation” system, where pay is based on flight time but also includes a calculation for other non-flight duties.


But Pouliot said that, under the credit-based system, junior flight attendants are paid slightly above the federal minimum wage of $18.15 per hour when including their time working while a plane is on the ground.


“When the credit system emerged across the industry in Canada, it was standard that the hourly credit was four times the minimum wage. Now, it’s about two times the minimum wage, and that’s why you’re seeing unpaid work becoming such a big issue,” Pouliot said. “Airlines are refusing to increase the hourly wages, and they’re also refusing to change the credit system.”


Canadian North spokesperson Eileen Carter told Nunatsiaq News in a written statement that the airline “values the important work of our cabin crew” and is committed to reaching a “fair, negotiated collective agreement” with its flight attendants.


The company did not respond to questions about unpaid hours of work.


Nunavut MP Lori Idlout said she’s concerned about a potential strike, especially for people who rely on the airline to travel south for medical care. She said she would not be opposed to workers being ordered back to the job, in the event of a work stoppage.


“We all know in Nunavut how important the airline industry is. It’s very much our lifeline,” she said in an interview. “It’s really important for the people in Nunavut to not see a disruption in services. It could potentially be life-threatening.”


Ian Lee, a Carleton University business professor, said if flight attendants were to go on strike, the federal government would likely order them back to work. That’s historically what happens when Canadian transportation workers strike, he said.


Lee’s own analysis of transportation sector strikes between 1950 and 2024 shows that Liberal and Conservative governments have ordered striking workers back to work on 44 occasions.


“Although workers have the legal right to strike in Canada, in fact, they don’t really have the right to strike if they are in the transportation sector,” he said in an interview. “We are completely dependent on transportation, to a much greater degree than any country.”


Update: 

This story has been updated to include comment from Canadian North.

title: Mala Fama y los desaparecidos de Lozadur: los crímenes de la dictadura llegaron al prime time televisivo
content:
El popular cantante contó en el programa de Andy Kusnetzoff que su padre fue un perseguido de la represión por su participación en el sindicato ceramista. Al otro día, la Comisión Provincial por la Memoria dio a conocer que esa persecución está registrada en el archivo de la Dirección de Inteligencia de la Policía de la Provincia de Buenos Aires (DIPPBA). Un relato inesperado que colocó a la lucha por los derechos humanos en el pico del rating. Aquí, toda la historia.


Por Leo Vázquez, para Canal Abierto.


El fin de semana tuvo una insospechada declaración televisiva vinculada a los crímenes de la dictadura. El cantante

Hernán Coronel

, más conocido como

Mala Fama

 por su trayectoria en el grupo de cumbia de ese mismo nombre, contó en el programa

Podemos Hablar

 que conduce

Andy Kusnetzoff


en Telefé

 que su padre fue un perseguido por las patotas del terrorismo de Estado.


Así, una historia de las tantas que componen la lucha del movimiento de derechos humanos llegó sorpresivamente al prime time televisivo, de la mano de un declarante también poco habitual.


El músico, que además está en un altísimo nivel de exposición pública por su participación en el programa

Máster Chef

, recordó que su papá tenía que dormir en una carpa en la azotea de la casa porque era buscado por la represión por ser parte del sindicato de

Lozadur

, la fábrica de platos y tazas de loza y cerámica de Villa Adelina, partido de San Isidro, que tiene al menos diez desaparecidos

 entre sus trabajadores.


«MI PAPÁ SE IBA A DORMIR AL TECHO POR SI VENÍAN LOS MILITARES A SACARLO»: BRUTAL RELATO DE HERNÁN DE MALA FAMA


«Mi papá pertenecía a un sindicato.. la dictadura hizo desaparecer al presidente del sindicato, al otro, y como que se venía él»


«Me imagino él, lo que es estar ahí durmiendo en esa carpa, si entran y matan a mi familia o si matan a mí, mi familia se queda sin el sostén»


#PodemosHablar


— Revolución Popular (@RPN_Oficial)

November 15, 2026


Al otro día, la

Comisión Provincial por la Memoria

 dio a conocer que esa persecución está registrada en el archivo

DIPPBA

, la Dirección de Inteligencia de la Policía de la Provincia de Buenos Aires.


“En 1975 los ceramistas reclamaban mejoras salariales pese a los intentos del gobierno de Isabel Perón de congelar los salarios. La represión en Lozadur se sintió antes del golpe: el 13 de febrero de 1976 fue asesinado Juan Pablo Lobos, delegado gremial de fábrica y vocal suplente de la Federación de Obreros Ceramistas”, comenzó narrando el organismo de derechos humanos.


“Posiblemente, esta sea la historia detrás de lo que contó Hernán sobre su padre”.


Lozadur fue una fábrica de cerámicos instalada en Villa Adelina en 1939. Llegó a tener una planta de 1.200 trabajadores, en su mayoría mujeres.


“Las condiciones de trabajo –pago por pieza terminada y no por tiempo de trabajo, altas temperaturas y enfermedades respiratorias por falta de extractores de polvillo- fueron algunos de los factores que llevaron al movimiento obrero ceramista a impulsar ocupaciones fabriles”, siguió describiendo la CPM.


“Ya en la dictadura –continúa el relato-,

los primeros informes de inteligencia sobre la actividad fabril comienzan con un legajo de la serie “Huelgas y conflictos” donde se comunica que los trabajadores de la planta realizan trabajo a desgano como medida de fuerza

. Según la DIPPBA, el conflicto comenzó durante los primeros días de octubre de 1977”.


“El 3 de noviembre de 1977 la dictadura secuestró trabajadoras y trabajadores de Lozadur: Dominga Abadía Crespo, Felicidad Abadía Crespo, Sofía Cardozo, Elba Puente, Ismael Notaliberto, Francisco Palavecino y Ramón Pablo Villanueva. Todavía continúan desaparecidos”.

author: Gladys Stagno
title: Donde hay un trabajador precarizado, nace un moroso
content:
Un relevamiento provincia por provincia muestra la superposición entre precariedad laboral y endeudamiento familiar. Seis millones de personas acumulan atrasos en sus pagos y casi cuatro de cada diez jóvenes menores de 25 años están en situación de mora.


Ilustración: Marcelo Spotti


Por Gladys Stagno


En un escenario de alto endeudamiento familiar y morosidad récord, un estudio aporta un dato nuevo que surge de analizar las condiciones laborales de los endeudados.


En su último informe, el Mirador de la Actualidad del Trabajo y la Economía (MATE) realizó un mapeo de la caída del empleo formal y del aumento de la precariedad, provincia por provincia, en base a datos de la Secretaría de Trabajo, Empleo y Seguridad Social.


De igual manera, y sobre cifras del Banco Central (BCRA), el centro de investigación construyó un “mapa de la mora”, donde se evidencia en qué provincias el fenómeno se ha vuelto más grave.


Tucumán y San Juan son las dos que se encuentran al tope de ambas categorías: más del 50% de trabajadores en la informalidad, y más del 34% de personas en situación de mora. En situaciones similares se encuentran Catamarca, Corrientes, Chaco, Formosa, La Rioja, Mendoza, Misiones, Salta, San Luis y Santiago del Estero.


Una situación atípica ocurre en Santa Cruz, provincia con la menor tasa de informalidad (-30%) –junto con Neuquén– pero alta tasa de morosidad (entre el 30 y el 34%). La Pampa es la provincia con menos mora del país, con menos del 22%.


Fuente: MATE


Jóvenes y precarizados


En toda la Argentina, la deuda en mora de las familias en el sistema bancario ronda el 18%. El número crece si tenemos en cuenta a los proveedores no financieros y billeteras virtuales, donde la cifra supera el 30%, según informes recientes del Centro de Economía Política Argentina (CEPA). Se trata de los niveles más altos desde la crisis de 2001.


En cantidad de personas, se trata de cerca 6 millones de argentinos con deudas atrasadas, de un total de 20 millones de endeudados, lo que representa 1 de cada 4 en situación de mora.


Fuente: MATE


Según el Mapa de la Deuda publicado por el del Centro de Estudios para la Ciudad junto a la fundación alemana Friedrich-Ebert-Stiftung, la situación se agrava en los más jóvenes, donde casi 4 de cada 10 menores de 25 años registran atrasos en el pago de su deuda. Se trata también del sector poblacional más alcanzado por la informalidad laboral. De acuerdo con MATE, en el sector de 15 a 24 años la informalidad ya alcanza al 39,2%.


“La demografía de la mora y la del empleo se vinculan íntimamente: la precariedad laboral avanza sobre los jóvenes y sobre las provincias olvidadas por este modelo económico y la distribución de la mora refleja esta situación”, analiza el instituto liderado por los economistas Diego Kofman, Lavih Abraham, Marco Kofman, Natalia Pérez Barreda y Sergio Arelovich.


La informalidad crece en línea con la pérdida de empleos formales. Según el relevamiento del MATE, la economía argentina pierde más de 370 empleos formales por día.


“El sector privado ya expulsó a 265.765 trabajadores registrados: la industria y la construcción son los sectores que más puestos de trabajo destruyeron”, detallan. Por su parte, el sector público perdió 89.620 puestos, contabilizados desde diciembre de 2023. Se trata, en total, de 375.016 empleos formales menos desde la asunción de Javier Milei.


Ilustración: Marcelo Spotti

title: I nipotini del fascismo usano l’antisemitismo per mettere il bavaglio sulla Palestina
content:
Gli eredi politici di chi promulgò le leggi razziali del 1938 approvano una legge che confonde antisemitismo e critica a Israele. Un’operazione di potere che protegge il governo responsabile del genocidio a Gaza e punta a reprimere la solidarietà con il popolo palestinese.


da

OsservatorioRepressione


C’è qualcosa di politicamente osceno nel vedere gli eredi del fascismo italiano ergersi a difensori della lotta contro l’antisemitismo. Sono gli eredi di una tradizione politica che nel 1938 trasformò il razzismo antiebraico in legge dello Stato, espulse gli ebrei dalle scuole, dalle università, dagli impieghi pubblici e contribuì, con la Repubblica sociale italiana, alla loro persecuzione e deportazione nei campi di sterminio. Oggi quella stessa tradizione politica, attraverso i suoi discendenti, pretende di stabilire quali critiche allo Stato di Israele siano ammissibili e quali debbano essere considerate manifestazioni di antisemitismo. Non è una contraddizione accidentale. È un’operazione politica che utilizza la memoria della persecuzione antiebraica per legittimare nuove forme di repressione del dissenso.


Con 147 voti favorevoli, 93 contrari e 5 astenuti,

 la Camera ha approvato definitivamente il disegno di legge sull’antisemitismo, già passato al Senato. Il provvedimento recepisce la controversa definizione 

dell’International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA)

, che attraverso i suoi esempi applicativi rischia di 

sovrapporre l’odio antiebraico alla critica politica dello Stato di Israele e del sionismo. 

Non introduce un divieto penale generale di criticare Israele, ma costruisce un dispositivo istituzionale che può essere utilizzato per colpire la libertà di espressione, la ricerca universitaria e le mobilitazioni politiche. Il problema non è dunque soltanto ciò che la legge vieta espressamente, ma ciò che rende possibile attraverso interpretazioni estensive, provvedimenti disciplinari, pressioni amministrative e forme di censura preventiva.


La maggioranza ha respinto tutti gli emendamenti delle opposizioni, compreso quello che chiedeva di impedire l’intitolazione di strade, monumenti ed edifici pubblici a persone che avessero sostenuto o propagandato l’antisemitismo e l’odio razziale. Un passaggio che rivela molto della natura politica dell’operazione. Chi pretende di combattere l’antisemitismo attraverso una legge che rischia di criminalizzare l’antisionismo non ha voluto accogliere neppure una disposizione diretta a contrastare la celebrazione pubblica dei propagandisti dell’odio razziale. E mentre si votava una legge presentata come necessaria per difendere la memoria della persecuzione antiebraica, nell’aula di Montecitorio alcuni deputati della destra riabilitavano Giovanni Gentile e insultavano i partigiani comunisti che lo uccisero. Rossano Sasso li ha definiti «vigliacchi», mentre Alessandro Amorese di Fratelli d’Italia ha parlato di un «commando di assassini». La risposta di Gianni Cuperlo, «State zitti, fascisti!», ha restituito almeno per un momento il significato storico di quella discussione.


Ma sarebbe un errore fermarsi all’ipocrisia dei postfascisti. Il rapporto tra le destre europee e il governo israeliano ha assunto negli ultimi anni una precisa funzione politica. L’adesione alla definizione IHRA permette a formazioni provenienti da tradizioni nazionaliste, razziste e antisemite di presentarsi come difensori delle comunità ebraiche, senza mettere realmente in discussione la propria concezione etnica della nazione. In cambio, il governo Netanyahu trova alleati disponibili a sostenere le sue politiche e a delegittimare chi denuncia l’occupazione, l’apartheid e il genocidio in Palestina. La conferenza internazionale sull’antisemitismo promossa nel 2025 dal ministro israeliano Amichai Chikli, con la partecipazione di esponenti dell’estrema destra, ha reso evidente questa convergenza. Il punto di incontro non è l’universalismo dei diritti, ma un nazionalismo fondato sull’esclusione, sull’individuazione di nemici interni e sulla criminalizzazione di chi contesta il potere.


La nuova legge italiana si inserisce perfettamente in questo disegno. Dopo due anni di mobilitazioni contro il genocidio a Gaza, il governo Meloni ha dovuto fare i conti con manifestazioni di massa, occupazioni universitarie, scioperi, campagne di boicottaggio e iniziative di solidarietà che hanno denunciato anche le responsabilità politiche e materiali dell’Italia nel sostegno a Israele. La risposta non è …

author: Bulatlat Staff
title: ‘No red carpet’ for Trump’s arrival in the Philippines
content:
Kampuhan Kontra Pax Silica, a UP Diliman-based formation, together with progressive groups, students, faculty members, and rights advocates hold an indignation protest along Katipunan Avenue in Quezon City on November 15, 2026. Photo by Carlo Manalansan/Bulatlat

By Aaron Ernest Cruz and Anne Marxze Umil

“The Filipino people will never welcome a warmonger, racist, fascist, misogynist, sexual offender, and corrupt leader like Trump.”

Despite attempts to derail their protest, progressive groups continued with their action as US President Donald Trump arrived in the country on November 17.

“The Filipino people will never welcome a warmonger, racist, fascist, misogynist, sexual offender, and corrupt leader like Trump,” Bagong Alyansang Makabayan (Bayan) said in a statement.

“His war on Iran, support for Israel’s genocide in Gaza, military interventions in Venezuela, Cuba, and the Carribean, tariff wars and brutal trade sanctions, and racist immigration policies have hurt people all over the world, destroyed the global economy, and undermined world peace,” Bayan added.

An estimated 6,000 individuals trooped at Liwasang Bonifacio to express their condemnation of the government’s red carpet welcome for Trump and the Pax Silica deal.

According to Bayan, the police blocked the truck to be used in their program and attempted to get their sound system. But the group managed to bring the sound system to Liwasang Bonifacio. During the early morning, the group reported that there were many police deployed in the area.

“Manila is just like a garrison as police were scattered around the city’s entry point,” Bayan Secretary-General Mong Palatino said in an interview.

Bayan President Renato Reyes Jr. also condemned the police for attempting to tow their vehicle, stressing that police violated the Batas Pambansa Blg. 880 which protects the right to hold protests in designated freedom parks without permits. “We don’t need your [police] here and we won’t allow you to tow our vehicle just like what happened last Sunday [November 15].”

Funa-ay Claver, secretary-general of Indigenous group Katribu described the Marcos Jr. administration as a lapdog of the US government, giving up the country’s land for Pax Silica.

“They say it is for development, but we should always ask: Who will benefit from it? It is clear that Pax Silica serves foreign interests rather than the interests of its own people,” Claver said.

Karapatan said that it is not surprising that Marcos Jr. had an extravagant welcome for Trump. “Trump is a fascist, a warmonger and enabler of brutal, genocidal regimes, making the extravagant welcome prepared for him by his fellow fascist and tyrant Ferdinand Marcos Jr. come as no surprise,” the group said in a statement.

Karapata said that it was under Trump that the Marcos Jr. regime began to transform the Philippines into a manufacturing hub for US armaments.

They said that the country became a cog in the US global supply chain, making parts for weapons now being used in US wars of aggression against countries that have stood up against US hegemony. “Only a fellow fascist and tyrant like Ferdinand Marcos Jr. could be motivated to welcome the likes of Donald Trump to our shores.”

The groups tried to march to the ASEAN Summit venue but were blocked by the police. There are also Special Weapon and Tactics (SWAT) personnel holding rifles at the flyover. Under Batas Pambasa Bldg. 880, law enforcers are prohibited to bring guns in a peaceful protest.

“These guards of Trump are arrogant because they have shields and weapons. But the weapons of the Filipino people are truth, democracy, and militant struggle,” Bayan Chairperson Teddy Casiño said in front of the police. He added that even though they were not able to march through PICC where Trump is, he said, their protest is resonating around the world. (DAA)
