author: Shireen Akram-Boshar
title: Report: Parents Deported Under Trump Have Been Denied Contact With Their Kids
content:
In some cases, mothers being detained or deported were denied information on the whereabouts of their infant children.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

A new report finds that parents deported since the start of President Donald Trump’s second term have been cut off from their children or denied the opportunity to make decisions about their children’s future.

The report, published by legal advocacy group Justice in Motion on Tuesday, shines a light on the Trump administration’s moves to weaken and dismantle policies that previously provided protections for immigrant families — all while rapidly expanding the U.S.’s detention and deportation apparatus.

Justice in Motion, which partners with legal advocates in North and Central America, conducted 122 interviews with parents deported from the U.S. to Honduras, Guatemala, and Mexico since January 2025. They found that parents were repeatedly denied opportunities to contact their children after their arrest, and did not have reliable information about their children’s whereabouts and wellbeing both throughout their detention and after their deportation.

In some cases, mothers were separated from their infant children, and were not told the whereabouts of their babies during their detention or after their deportation.

A Brookings study published in May 2026 estimated that over 205,000 children have experienced the detention or deportation of a parent since the start of Trump’s second term. But little attention has been given to what happens after their deportation.

Dora Isabel Melara, a human rights attorney who spoke with deported parents, said in the Justice in Motion report that “deportation does not simply mean removing a person from one country to another; it means fragmenting a family.”

“When speaking with parents who are returned to Honduras, what I consistently observe is an emotional burden marked by desperation, uncertainty, and anguish,” she said. “Many parents arrive without clear information about their children. In most cases, the separation occurred while the parents were on their way to work or had just dropped their children off at school, without a chance to say goodbye or explain the situation to them.”

“What is not always visible from the United States is the complexity that follows that separation: the barriers to reestablishing communication… and a lack of knowledge about the legal processes necessary for reunification or custody,” she continued. “These realities prolong the separation well beyond the moment of deportation.”

Justice in Motion works to connect parents to attorneys to provide long-term support and assist in their reunification efforts after their deportation.

“Each time a parent loses contact, or a parent is denied the opportunity to make a determination about where their child should be, whether it’s with them or with someone else, it feels like a fundamental violation of the most innate responsibilities that a parent holds towards their child,” Justice in Motion’s Keeli Sorensen told Truthout.

In 2018, Trump’s “Zero Tolerance” family separation policy mandated the criminal prosecution of adults crossing the U.S. border without documentation, separating some 5,000 children from their families. Massive public outcry and nationwide protests pushed Trump to sign an executive order ending family separations in June 2018 — but his zero-tolerance framework remained in place, the report notes.

When President Joe Biden took office in 2021, the administration rescinded the 2018 zero-tolerance policy, the report says, and enacted some safeguards for Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) to consider children and families’ rights to stay together, under a parental rights directive. This was followed by a 10-year high of deportations under Biden, exceeding peak numbers from Trump’s first presidency.

In his second term, Trump has rescinded the majority of the safeguards for deported parents to exercise their parental rights — while ramping up family separation, detention, and deportations across the country.

“I think what we’re seeing now is grossly alarming to us because it’s just so much more widespread, it’s pervasive throughout the country, and it’s affecting families who have been here for a very long time, people who grew up here as children who are now parents,” Sorensen told Truthout.

author: Amy Goodman
title: Fossil Fuel Companies Are Undermining Democracy, Climate Activist Says
content:
A bloc of countries are working on a parallel process to COP to create a binding agreement on fossil fuel phaseout.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

What will it take to bring an end to the fossil fuel era? We speak to Kumi Naidoo, the president of the Fossil Fuel Treaty Initiative, which aims to reach a binding agreement for a global transition away from fossil fuels. Currently backed by over 25 countries from the Global South, the intergovernmental process began earlier this year in Santa Marta, Colombia. Meanwhile, at the United Nations, “for 30 years of negotiations, we don’t have any mention of fossil fuels [in the outcome document]. That’s like Alcoholics Anonymous holding 30 years of conferences and not mentioning alcohol,” says Naidoo. We discuss the Fossil Fuel Treaty Initiative’s goals, how the oil and gas industry drives global conflict, and the Trump administration’s glaring absence from international action on climate change.

This is a rush transcript. Copy may not be in its final form.

AMY GOODMAN: We’re broadcasting from Antalya, Turkey, at the global U.N. climate summit, known as COP31. There are just four days remaining for nearly 200 countries to come to some agreement on the next steps to tackle climate change.

On Monday, negotiators published a wide-ranging 18-page draft document that’s been characterized as a shopping list of language and issues to be debated ahead of a Friday deadline for a final agreement. This is the global policy lead for Oil Change International.

ROMAIN IOUALALEN: So, I think this is a text that was designed to basically please everyone, and they took, you know, the best, the most ambitious demands from each group and put it in there. Obviously, throughout this week, what we’re going to see is a game of massacre in the negotiations. We’re going to see a lot of these — a lot of these recommendations or this language going to be cut by parties that don’t agree with any of this. And so, as the president of negotiations, Chris Bowen, just said, the text that we’re going to end up with is going to look very different.

AMY GOODMAN: Agreements here at COP are made by consensus, meaning every country essentially has veto power over the final text. Rich countries and fossil fuel-producing countries have historically thwarted the most ambitious climate goals.

These negotiations, of course, are happening as the Iran war has also drawn global attention to the world’s dependence on fossil fuels. So, what will it take to bring an end to the fossil fuel era? A bloc of nearly 30 countries from the Global South have started a parallel process that’s aiming for a binding agreement to transition away from fossil fuels — a fossil fuel treaty. The first official conference on transitioning away from fossil fuels was held in Santa Marta, Colombia, earlier this year. Nearly 60 countries attended. A follow-up conference is scheduled to take place next year in Tuvalu.

To talk more about what can be achieved at this U.N. climate summit and what makes the process that began in Santa Marta different, we’re joined here in Turkey by Kumi Naidoo, longtime climate justice activist from South Africa, president of the Fossil Fuel Treaty Initiative.

It’s nice to have you back, to see you again, Kumi. Let’s talk about what’s happened so far at this climate summit. In a moment, we’re going to be talking to the former ambassador from Nepal. They just suffered a calamitous glacier melting that led to at least 7,000 people dead and missing. That’s just one example of thousands. What has to happen here? And what is happening?

KUMI NAIDOO: We need to get serious about addressing the root cause of climate change. Eighty-six percent of what’s driving the crisis is our addiction and dependency on oil, coal and gas, what we call fossil fuels. The difficulty we have is that for 30 years of negotiations, we don’t have any mention of fossil fuels. That’s like Alcoholics Anonymous holding 30 years of conferences and not mentioning alcohol in the outcome document.

Now, there are important things that we are pushing here on to get clarity on what a just transition would look like, trying to get resources to go in the Loss and Damage Fund and so on. title: AFT-MI Stand In Solidarity With Your Members (Graduate Employees’ Organization, AFT 3550)
content:
At the University of Michigan Faculty Senate’s November 9, 2026 meeting, AFT-MI Secretary-Treasurer Kirsten Herold publicly opposed a faculty-sponsored motion calling on the University of Michigan to bargain in good faith with the Graduate Employees’ Organization AFT Local 3550, which represents 4,000 graduate workers at the University. Herold questioned GEO’s good faith in negotiations, made inaccurate statements about the union’s bargaining process—including incorrectly claiming that GEO had begun negotiations without written proposals and has no bargaining team—and publicly criticized the union’s bargaining priorities while faculty attempted to express solidarity. Herold explicitly leveraged her position within AFT-MI to give credence to her criticisms.

It is inappropriate and deeply damaging for a high-ranking member of our parent union to use their power to disparage a member union.

author: Clare Hymer
title: New UK Sanctions on Israeli Groups Will Have No Material Impact, Critics Say
content:
Foreign secretary Ed Miliband has announced UK sanctions against Israeli firms involved in building illegal settlements in the West Bank, as well as an activist group that blocks aid from entering Gaza.


But the Israeli authorities driving settlement expansion and the denial of aid have not been targeted in the new measures, critics noted.


The

government said the measures

 against eight construction and property development firms would “disrupt their flows of finance and ability to support further construction in the West Bank”. 


It said that the Tsav 9 group, which has blocked aid crossings into Gaza and set trucks on fire, would also be subject to an asset freeze and ban on its members becoming directors of UK companies. 


Miliband said those who obstruct aid “must be prepared to face the consequences”.


But human rights groups said the sanctions were inadequate and did not target the primary cause of the violations: the Israeli government. 


“Sanctioning a handful of firms involved in illegal settlements is a fraction of what is needed – and targeting one activist group, rather than the Israeli authorities who continue to mastermind the denial of aid to Gaza, is not a serious response to a genocide,” said Kristyan Benedict, Amnesty International UK’s crisis response manager.


Benedict also noted that the

US already sanctioned Tsav 9 in June 2024, adding that the UK was just “playing catch-up”.

While the new measures were “a step in the right direction”, they fell “far short of the action international law demands”, he said.


“The UK must impose trade sanctions banning all services, investment and financial assistance linked to Israel’s unlawful occupation, impose targeted sanctions against Israeli officials most implicated in crimes against Palestinians – and ban, with immediate effect, all arms transfers to Israel.”


Huda Ammori, co-founder of banned direct action group Palestine Action, said Miliband was “sanctioning Israeli companies with little to no presence in Britain”, and so it would have “no material impact”. 


“He isn’t sanctioning JCB,

a British firm

 which destroys Palestinian homes and builds illegal settlements,

or Elbit [Systems]

, which makes weapons used to enforce the occupation,” she added.


Thomas Bell, acting UK director at Human Rights Watch, said: “The UK should take immediate steps to hold Israeli officials responsible for violations of international law by suspending arms transfers to Israel, suspending the UK-Israel Trade and Partnership Agreement,” and by supporting International Criminal Court cases against Israeli officials.   


The UK’s announcement comes just days before the deadline for tender for the construction of thousands of housing units in the E1 project, which threatens to cut East Jerusalem off from the rest of the West Bank and thereby make a contiguous Palestinian state impossible. 


Miliband said: “My message on E1 is clear: do not bid, do not build, and do not profit from the destruction of the two-state solution.”

title: Klimagipfel der Völker in Antalya zur UN-Klimakonferenz COP31 fordert gemeinsame – soziale – Front gegen ökologische Zerstörung
content:
„

Beim Klimagipfel der Völker in Antalya diskutieren internationale Bewegungen über Naturrechte, Klimagerechtigkeit und Widerstand gegen ökologische Zerstörung. Zum Auftakt wurde auch eine Verbindung zwischen Friedenspolitik und Umweltschutz gefordert.  Als Gegenveranstaltung zur UN-Klimakonferenz COP31 hat am Sonntag im Mimar-Sinan-Kongresszentrum in Antalya der Klimagipfel der Völker begonnen. Bis zum 18. November beraten dort Ökologiebewegungen, Menschenrechtsaktivist:innen und Vertreter:innen gesellschaftlicher Initiativen aus verschiedenen Ländern über gemeinsame Strategien gegen die Klimakrise und die fortschreitende Zerstörung natürlicher Lebensgrundlagen

…“

ANF-Meldung vom 15 November 2026


 mit Fotos – siehe mehr Informationen:


Klimagipfel der Völker ruft zu gemeinsamem Widerstand gegen Autoritarismus auf


„

Beim Klimagipfel der Völker in Antalya diskutierten Aktivist:innen über politische Repression, akademische Freiheit und autoritäre Entwicklungen. Die Teilnehmenden forderten eine gemeinsame demokratische Gegenbewegung. Der Kampf gegen die Klimakrise lässt sich nicht von der Verteidigung demokratischer Rechte und Freiheiten trennen. Diese Verbindung stand am dritten Tag des Klimagipfels der Völker in Antalya im Mittelpunkt einer Diskussionsveranstaltung über autoritäre Politik, staatliche Repression und gesellschaftlichen Widerstand. author: Alex Nguyen
title: Texas Attorney General Drops Lawsuit Aiming to Ban Muslim Civil Rights Group
content:
The Council on American-Islamic Relations, which has been targeted by Gov. Greg Abbott, called the news “a huge relief.”

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

Attorney General Ken Paxton has dropped a lawsuit that sought to ban the country’s largest Muslim civil rights group from operating in Texas, state court records show.

The lawsuit, filed in February, had asked a Collin County judge to declare the Council on American-Islamic Relations a foreign terrorist and transnational criminal organization. It alleged that CAIR was working with the Muslim Brotherhood, an international Sunni Muslim group, to “usurp governmental power and establish dominion through Sharia law.” At the time, CAIR said it was being punished for its opposition to Israel’s war in Gaza.

The petition came after Gov. Greg Abbott slapped the same designation against the two groups and urged Paxton to take legal action against CAIR amid a surge in Republican candidates running anti-Islam campaigns.

Paxton’s office filed a notice of nonsuit Monday, voiding the lawsuit nearly two weeks after a blue wave sunk Paxton’s U.S. Senate bid and swept Abbott out of office. Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa has said she will remove the “foreign terrorist organization” label against CAIR.

Shaimaa Zayan, the Austin director of CAIR-Texas, called the lawsuit’s end — which was first reported by Bloomberg Law — a “huge relief.”

“CAIR-Texas faced a huge injustice and continued to operate despite the threats,” Zayan said Tuesday. “We are looking forward to a new chapter in Texas, hopefully where civic life will be flourishing and every voice will be heard in Texas.”

CAIR and its Texas chapter have also cheered Hinojosa’s pledge, which she announced during an interview with The Washington Post.

“Greg Abbott, Ken Paxton, Bo French, and Mayes Middleton staked their political campaigns on shredding the First Amendment to target Texas Muslims, but the people of Texas rejected this un-American bigotry,” the groups added in a statement. “Anti-Muslim hate is no longer an effective political weapon in Texas, and it must no longer have any place in state governance.”

The dropped lawsuit follows a flurry of other lawsuits Paxton’s office has abandoned since the election, including cases against immigrant rights groups as well as the NCAA over transgender athletes.

The Texas Tribune is a nonprofit, nonpartisan media organization that informs Texans — and engages with them — about public policy, politics, government and statewide issues.

Donations are down for Truthout at a time when media is under immense pressure. Google’s AI search has driven our traffic down by 15 percent, Trump is arresting journalists, and many independent media organizations face heartbreaking cutbacks and closures.

At the same time, movement media is vital in the fight against Trump’s authoritarian reign. Our mandate to tell the truth, share strategies for resistance, and speak against fascism is ever more urgent in this deluge of political censorship and misinformation. Yet, we are struggling to meet our publishing costs when our work is so urgently needed.

We are fundraising right now for those basic operating expenses — we need $23,000 in the next 48 hours. If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work. Anything you can do makes a difference.

author: David Venn
title: RCMP conducts ‘largest drug seizure destined for Nunavut’
content:
In what the RCMP calls “the largest drug seizure destined for Nunavut,” police seized five kilograms of cocaine in southern Canada in August, a news release issued Tuesday says.


As a result, an estimated 50,000 doses (measuring one-tenth of a gram) were prevented from entering the territory, the release said.


“This seizure represents far more than the removal of drugs from the supply chain,” Chief Supt. Kent Pike said in the release. “It represents lives protected, families spared from harm and fewer opportunities for organized crime to profit at the expense of Nunavummiut.”


In February 2026, the police force began investigating an alleged money-laundering and drug-trafficking operation.


In August, officers from Nunavut and the federal Arctic unit executed a search warrant in Ottawa, where they seized the drugs.


The federal Arctic unit works under the Federal Policing Northwest Region, which co-ordinates resources to investigate organized crime in Alberta, Manitoba, the Northwest Territories, Saskatchewan and Nunavut.


The release did not say if any charges have been laid. It said the investigation is ongoing and that the RCMP will not provide further comment.

author: Daron Letts
title: Two children killed in sliding tragedy in Kimmirut
content:
Kimmirut is in mourning after two young sisters were killed while sliding Sunday afternoon.


Holly Lyta, 8, and Melanie Pootoogook, 5, were struck by a water truck as it was reversing, said Elisapie Pootoogook, the girls’ great aunt Tuesday in a phone interview.


Their father Charlie Pootoogook witnessed the incident, she said.


“I’m having trouble sleeping,” Elisapie Pootoogook said of how she’s handling the tragedy.

She added that she is very close to her nephew Charlie Pootoogook, who grew up with her in Kinngait.


The girls’ grandparents are planning to head to Kimmirut Friday from Kinngait to support the parents, Elisapie Pootoogook said.


Kimmirut has a population of approximately 400 people.


The community’s school and daycare were closed Monday out of respect for those affected by the girls’ deaths.


South Baffin MLA David Joanasie, whose riding includes Kimmirut and Kinngait, shared his support for the family Monday in a Facebook post.


“My sincere condolences [go] out to the people of Kimmirut during this difficult time of grief after a sudden tragedy,” he said.

“We feel for all those who are most impacted by their loss and hope that love and grace surrounds the families and community as a whole. I thank all the responders who help during this hardship.”


The Education Department, in partnership with the Canadian Red Cross, will provide supports,

 he added.


Elisapie Pootoogook and others in the community are holding various fundraisers for the family.


“Donations to the family are also welcome,” she said. “No family should ever have to experience such heartbreaking loss.”


The RCMP did not respond to an interview request as of noon on Tuesday.

author: Clara Saliba
title: Está na hora de falar da pobreza de tempo
content:
Chegamos em novembro. As lojas e praças já estão decoradas para o Natal. No ar, a sensação de que o tempo passa rápido demais, de que nos atropela… Em meio às reflexões de quase fim de ano, reparei que o tempo, desta vez, esteve mais em pauta do que nunca. Afinal, reduzimos a jornada de trabalho e acabamos com a escala 6×1. 


Ainda este ano, em 16 de dezembro, os trabalhadores e trabalhadoras sob o regime CLT terão direito a duas folgas semanais. Também na mesma data, 60 dias após a aprovação da Emenda Constitucional 141, começará a valer o limite de jornada de 42h semanais, que cairá para 40h em dezembro de 2027. A única exceção à lei são os portadores de diploma de ensino superior que recebam mais de duas vezes e meia o teto do Regime Geral da Previdência Social (RGPS) – cerca de R$21 mil mensais. 


Uma conquista e tanto, que colocou no centro do debate público um número que não é monetário. Talvez pela primeira vez na história, falou-se tanto sobre um valor que não vem sempre acompanhado de um cifrão: o tempo das pessoas. 


Sim, tempo é, em certa medida, dinheiro. Sobretudo para a classe trabalhadora, as horas de vida que se gasta trabalhando têm uma relação importante com a possibilidade de pagar as contas ao fim do mês. 


Frequentemente, terceirizamos algumas tarefas porque é mais fácil pagar por elas do que dispor das horas para fazê-las. 


Quem nunca escolheu comer um salgado pronto, no caminho para o trabalho, apenas para poder dormir mais meia hora, e não se preocupar em preparar o café da manhã? Ou contratou uma diarista, para dar conta da faxina que acumulava para o fim de semana? 


Mas essas duas variáveis não são a mesma coisa: ainda que ter tempo nos economize dinheiro – permitindo que nós mesmas realizemos uma série de tarefas em vez de pagar por elas – e que ter dinheiro nos economize tempo – permitindo que contratemos – nem todo o dinheiro do mundo substitui a necessidade de tempo para comer, dormir, ter higiene e socializar, por exemplo. E nem todo o tempo, se não virar dinheiro, nos torna autossuficientes materialmente.


Esse é o raciocínio por trás de uma medida econômica pouco conhecida, e que tem sido explorada pela economia feminista: a pobreza de tempo.  


A economista estadunidense Clair Vickery escreveu sobre isso nos anos 1977. Ela definiu como pobres de tempo as famílias que não teriam uma combinação mínima de tempo para realizar as tarefas de cuidado pessoal e doméstico e dinheiro para comprar bens essenciais. Nessa linha, quem tem menos dinheiro precisa compensar com tempo, e quem tem menos tempo, com dinheiro. Quem não consegue nenhuma combinação suficiente de dinheiro e tempo com o salário que recebe é pobre, mesmo que ganhe mais do que o mínimo da linha de pobreza monetária. 


Nessa pesquisa, ela identificou as mães e pais “solo” como a população mais vulnerável à pobreza de tempo, ainda que essa situação seja mais comum entre as mulheres. Muitas vezes, elas estão sobrecarregadas pelo cuidado dos filhos, acumulando a jornada de trabalho fora com a responsabilidade total por outra(s) pessoa(s). 


Aqui no Brasil, ainda é difícil mensurar a pobreza de tempo, porque nos falta uma variável indispensável dessa equação: saber quantas horas as pessoas gastam por dia em cada atividade, o que é conhecido como pesquisa de “Uso do Tempo”. O que sabemos são quantas horas as pessoas passam trabalhando fora de casa por semana. Sabemos também, em alguma medida, quanto tempo elas gastam em cuidados e afazeres domésticos: 21 horas para as mulheres e 11 para os homens, de acordo com o IBGE, em 2022, ainda que haja fortes indícios de que essa pesquisa erre para baixo. As médias dos outros países da América Latina para mulheres, por exemplo, ficam sempre acima das 30h (para saber mais, vale ler a

Nota de Política Econômica 64 do Made-USP

). 


Mas, mesmo que seja difícil de medir,

a pobreza de tempo certamente é experienciada por muitos brasileiros e brasileiras. 


Longas horas no transporte público e jornadas elevadas de trabalho dentro e fora de casa se traduzem em uma qualidade de vida que despenca. 


Soma-se a isso todos os problemas de elevação do custo de vida percebidos desde a pandemia, e o resultado é que nem a renda nem o tempo tem sido suficientes para muitas pessoas, especialmente para as mulheres.


O tamanho da mobilização pela redução da jornada de trabalho foi uma prova disso.

 A aprovação da PEC com unanimidade na Câmara e no Senado não deixou dúvidas:

no debate público …

author: Chris Walker
title: Largest Data Centers in US Emit as Much Carbon as Denmark, Study Finds
content:
The largest US data centers use almost 2 percent of US electricity, more than New York City and Los Angeles combined.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

A new study published this week suggests that the combined yearly output of carbon dioxide from the largest data centers in the U.S. rivals that of some countries.

The study, which appeared in the journal Nature Sustainability on Monday, finds that the largest data centers in the country release a combined total of 25.7 million metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions per year. That accounts for about 2 percent of all electricity use in the U.S. — an amount that is greater than the yearly electricity use of Los Angeles and New York City combined.

The study examined 403 facilities in total, finding that their combined carbon emissions were comparable to those of countries the size of Bolivia or Denmark.

Some states’ data centers had larger carbon outputs than others. Virginia, Iowa, and Ohio account for half of emissions alone, while other states, such as Oregon, have much smaller carbon emissions, due to a larger portion of electricity being generated through means other than fossil fuels.

According to reporting from The New York Times, much of the researchers’ work amounted to “detective work” due to the lack of federal requirements on public disclosure by these facilities.

“Communities shouldn’t need a team of Harvard researchers to analyze satellite images to understand their environmental impact,” said Gianluca Guidi, the Harvard scientist who led the research team.

Indeed, safeguards against pollution from data centers are limited, in large part due to workarounds that are being allowed by the Trump administration’s Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), including the use of “islanded” power plants, which are built solely to power data centers and are not part of the electrical grid.

Data centers are also undoing recent progress in reducing pollution in states with larger carbon emissions. In Texas, for example, years of work to lower those rates could be undone if a plan to build hundreds of new data centers (in addition to those that have already been constructed) goes through in the next few years.

Americans appear aware of the problems posed by data centers, including rising electricity prices and environmental concerns. Earlier this month, in midterm elections across the country, voters overwhelmingly passed referenda to bar or regulate the rapid expansion of data centers in their communities.

“Tuesday’s election was a historically bad night for the Republican Party. It might have been even worse for big tech and their plans to spend trillions of dollars building AI data centers,” read one analysis of the election outcomes.

Public opposition to data center expansion likely played a role in Democrats’ “blue wave.” Exit poll data from NBC News found that 56 percent of voters described data centers and artificial intelligence (AI) as “crucial or major factor[s]” in determining their vote.

author: Labor Notes Staff
title: Stewards Corner: Laying the Foundation for Change in Your Union
content:
Revitalizing a local union may require electing new officers with a different vision. But running for office should not be your first step.


Successful campaigns for union office usually start by organizing against management first, often years in advance of any eventual run.


A group of workers wants to accomplish something—better pay, more control over their conditions on the job, an end to tiered wages or benefits—but their officials, or something about the way their union operates, is in the way. So they begin to change the culture of the union, getting more members involved in building power on the shop floor.


Your ultimate goal, after all, is not just electing new leaders, but building a stronger union. And doing that means involving as many members as possible.


WHERE TO START


The good news is you can begin organizing for change in your union any time.


“Your campaign should start with workplace fights that involve your co-workers,” says John Pearson, a nurse at Highland Hospital in Oakland, California, and former president of the SEIU Local 1021 chapter there. “You need that type of credibility and trust from people to be able to lead successfully.”


Before running for office, Pearson helped lead a campaign to defend breaks, involving nurses throughout the Alameda County hospital system, which resulted in a big back pay settlement. He also led an effort to save a substance abuse clinic from defunding.


“The word spreads if you’re effective at fighting in the workplace—people know to ask you for help,” says Pearson.


This type of organizing shows members that you have a track record, and that collectively members can make a difference.


The Caucus of Rank-and-File Educators (CORE), which won leadership in the Chicago Teachers Union in 2010, built up strength in campaigns like a fight to stop the school district from closing dozens of neighborhood schools and replacing them with privately run charters.


“So much of our caucus was really forged in the fight against school closings,” says Norine Gutekanst, who was a third-grade teacher at the time. Caucus members attended school closing hearings and teamed up with community activists to camp out all night in front of threatened schools. The leadership of the union, meanwhile, was absent from the fight.


CORE was already “doing what the union should have been doing,” said Chicago social studies teacher Bill Lamme. “So when the election came, [CORE activists] didn’t say ‘Elect me and I’ll do this.’ They said, ‘This is what we’ve been doing and we’ll keep doing it.’”


ATTEND MEETINGS


If you’re serious about getting involved in and transforming your union, you should be regularly attending union meetings, even if the meetings don’t allow for much debate. Bring other members who share your views. By participating, your group can shake things up.


“The first time you attend a meeting, just listen,” says Ken Paff, longtime national organizer with Teamsters for a Democratic Union.


“Later on,” Paff says, “you can make a proposal, and organize your group to present it. Talk to members before the meeting; draw them in. Get things out to the members, not only to make your group transparent, but also to make union meetings that way.


“Tell people there will be a motion on the pension plan, or another burning topic. Ask them to come support the motion. Put it out in writing. Get them to sign a petition in support of it.”


In Letter Carriers (NALC) Branch 9 in Minneapolis, a group of members started meeting to talk about how to change the culture of their branch, including its meeting agendas. “We had a president of over 30 years who would just use Robert’s Rules to keep people down,” says letter carrier Chris Pennock.


But the group of reformers kept bringing more members to meetings. Eventually their motions started winning. Pennock got 10 minutes on the agenda to talk about fighting post office closures. It was a small step, but a co-worker told him: “I don’t know if you know how historic that is—I’ve never seen a motion pass that the executive board not only didn’t support but were actively opposed to.”


Their organizing helped lay the basis to run a reform slate; Pennock is now vice president of Branch 9. “Have faith that you can change the culture,” he says.


At the same time, “it’s a mistake to think that meetings are the important thing,” says SEIU Local 1021’s Pearson—especially since most members won’t attend meetings. You want to find other …

author: Sarah van Gelder
title: Democrats Face First Test Post-Midterms: Fund or Oppose Forever Wars?
content:
The Democrats should use their midterm momentum to stop writing a blank check for the Pentagon.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

The historic Democratic Party midterm victories were fueled in large part by deep opposition to the war on Iran, according to polling. Every Democrat who won in a competitive congressional race, except for one, opposed the war, including 13 in the Senate and 48 in the House, according to post-election analysis by the Progressive Change Institute.

New members won’t take office until January 3, when control of both houses shifts to Democrats. But the first test of whether Democrats in Congress will heed voters’ mandate for the end of the war on Iran, and respond to widespread opposition to “forever wars” more broadly, could occur much sooner. Although Democrats remain in the minority until January, they still have powerful leverage to block excessive Pentagon funding and stop the war in Iran during the current lame-duck session.

The National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) is key. The bill authorizes $1.15 trillion in military spending — along with dangerous policies to move toward integration of U.S. and Israeli military technology development, to build a destabilizing new generation of nuclear weapons, and to accelerate deployment of AI in weaponry.

The Trump administration is requesting an additional $350 billion just for the Iran War, bringing the total spending to a breathtaking $1.5 trillion dollars.

But Congress could just say no. The message delivered by the midterm elections could finally flip the script on the conventional wisdom that Congress will grant any level of Pentagon funding in the name of national security. Democrats must use their midterm momentum to stop destabilizing policies and sky-high defense spending, and finally take a stand for spending that meets the needs of families and communities.

The 2027 NDAA was passed by the House in July. But in the Senate, 60 votes are required to allow a measure to come to the floor for a vote, and Senate Democrats were able to stop the bill from progressing. They can do that again, with or without Republican support, and the midterm election results make clear that is what voters want them to do.

Opposing the massive increase in military spending and the war in Iran should be an easy call — especially at a time when so many Americans are struggling to get the food, housing, medical care, and education they need. But giant defense corporations invest heavily in lobbying to influence defense policy, with nearly $164 million spent on lobbying in just the first three quarters of 2026, according to OpenSecrets. Defense expenditures are distributed nationwide, so members of Congress are often reluctant to reduce budgets that could impact their districts. Funding the Pentagon is also conflated with support for U.S. service members and considered a signal of patriotism. It is time to put that falsehood to rest.

Neither the NDAA nor the Pentagon appropriations bill is truly a must-pass measure. The two bills serve different purposes: the NDAA authorizes military programs and establishes defense policies, while the appropriations bill actually provides the money to fund them. If an appropriation bill doesn’t pass, Congress can keep the Pentagon operating through a continuing resolution. And the programs and policies included in the NDAA do not have to be bundled into one massive annual bill; Congress can address them through separate legislation.

If either bill stalls, the incoming Congress, with its new Democratic majorities, could write new versions after members take office in January 2027. They could use these bills to end the war in Iran, to halt destructive new nuclear weapons development, to stop military technology integration with Israel, and to force a reduction in Pentagon spending.

Congress could redirect our taxpayer dollars toward unmet needs of families and communities, beginning by reversing cuts to Medicaid funding scheduled to take effect in the new year.

Only Congress has the Constitutional power to determine federal government funding, and it should use that power. Here are seven things it could do instead of rubber-stamping the Pentagon’s requests:

End the deeply unpopular war in Iran. The Iran war was a “crucial” or a “major factor” for 74 percent of voters, according to an NBC exit poll …

author: Dana DiFilippo
title: New Jersey Cops Are Using Opioid Settlement Funds For Drones, Cars, and Gym Gear
content:
A new bill would restrict police use of the funds, which are meant to cover addiction treatment and support services.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

In Ocean County, a day’s work might mean Elizabeth Burke Beaty, a harm reductionist, helps someone struggling with drug addiction by getting them a ride to treatment, connecting them with a food pantry or housing assistance, or even traipsing into the woods to bring them a new tent.

Law enforcement agencies in Ocean County, though, have decided that helping people beat addiction means splurging on new police cars, canines, surveillance cameras, street signs, body armor, and more.

Police across New Jersey have commandeered millions of dollars that pharmaceutical companies have paid New Jersey, its 21 counties, and 241 of its largest municipalities since 2022 to settle lawsuits over the deadly opioid epidemic.

With the state set to receive over $1.1 billion in settlement funds through 2038, advocates now are demanding that lawmakers tighten oversight of spending to ensure it meets approved uses — addiction prevention, treatment, and support services for people in recovery.

“The police have been well-funded for very, very long, and they’re not recovery specialists,” said Burke Beaty, founder and CEO of Sea Change Recovery Community and Harm Reduction Center. “The money that they’re taking is not in the spirit of repairing all the harms caused by Big Pharma.”

A New Jersey Monitor analysis of municipalities’ spending reports and records on the watchdog site Opioid Audit shows that police spent opioid funds in all sorts of ways that don’t directly help people harmed by addiction.

Seventeen agencies spent more than $1.5 million on cars, lights, lettering, vehicle wraps, and related expenses. Eleven departments spent more than a half-million dollars on police canines, kennels, canine training, and veterinary care. Seven bought surveillance cameras and automated license plate reader systems.

At least 20 spent money on technology including drones, digital roadside billboards and radar systems, e-bikes, vape detectors for schools, police radios, mapping software and investigative databases, drug analyzers and breathalyzers, and defibrillators.

Scores more used settlement funds to pay for officer training, salaries and overtime, staff wellness programs, bicycles, gym equipment, subscription renewals, body armor, clothing, National Night Out costs, junior police academies, school assemblies, and associated promotional materials.

The departments typically characterized the spending as prevention, harm reduction, community engagement and education, and recovery support.

But officials often stretched the definition of those terms.

Wall Township explained spending more than $30,000 of opioid funds on treadmills, weights, and other gym equipment as an investment in the “mental health of first responders.” Garfield police cited public awareness as the chief goal of $5,450 they paid for a vehicle wrap and thousands more spent on a “Let’s Knock Out Opioid Use Together” festival that featured a live DJ, several inflatable bounce houses, food vendors, a pop-up party area, and a helicopter landing display.

While the settlement requires officials to invest in evidence-based strategies to reduce addiction and repair harms, some police spending seems to flout that rule. In Highland Park, police bought 10 anti-choking devices for $605 last year even though state health officials issued a cautionary statement about the devices and the federal Food and Drug Administration has warned that using them carries risks.

In many cases, police invested opioid funds in things that have historically been paid for out of their budgets, such as police salaries, vehicles, and safety gear. Watchdogs have long warned against using opioid money as “slush funds” or to plug budget gaps.

Much of such spending would be barred under new legislation Assemblywoman Maureen Rowan (D-Atlantic) introduced Monday.

Rowan’s bill would prohibit police and public officials from using opioid funds on any activities, equipment, or technology that normally would be paid out of municipal, county, or state budgets. It also would forbid spending the funds on police training and salaries not specifically tied to addiction remediation, drug takeback programs, and anything related to surveillance, crime …

author: Nehaa Bimal
title: GN, University of Ottawa partner to train doctors in Iqaluit
content:
The Government of Nunavut is partnering with the University of Ottawa to train family medicine residents in Iqaluit, in an effort to improve access to primary care and encourage more doctors to practise in the territory.


Health Minister Janet Pitsiulaaq Brewster announced the five-year agreement Monday at the university’s Faculty of Medicine.


The new Nunavut-uOttawa Family Medicine Residency Stream will bring four medical residents to Iqaluit in 2027, with another four expected to join in 2028, said a University of Ottawa news release.


The program will reach a capacity of eight residents in its second year, the release said.


Residents complete two months of clinical rotations in Iqaluit during their first year of residency and five months during their second year.

The GN will fund the residency positions.


“The valued knowledge, expertise, and collaborations that medical residents will experience in Iqaluit will be shared within our community of learners to open broader perspectives on training, care, and research,” University of Ottawa president and vice-chancellor Marie-Eve Sylvestre said in the news release.

title: Statement — IOF OFF REKOGNITION (Amazon Worker Intifada)
content:

These included photographs from Rolling Stone, the IOF’s central database of Palestinians stored on AWS, which has amassed millions of photographs taken from identity cards issued to every Palestinian resident when they turn 16.

Following the ground invasion of Gaza, the IOF deployed facial recognition systems at checkpoints where Palestinians were being forcibly displaced and fleeing the IOF’s bombardment. IOF used AWS infrastructure to support the processing of images collected at these checkpoints, matching people against photographs held in Rolling Stone.

Any suggestion that Amazon is merely a passive or neutral technology provider, detached from the military operations its infrastructure supports, is impossible to reconcile with these revelations. Amazon is the digital arms manufacturer of the “israeli” genocide in Gaza.

In 2018, the ACLU demonstrated that Rekognition misidentified Black and Brown members of Congress as criminal suspects. Washington County, Oregon, and the Orlando Police Department ran pilots. Federal agencies piloted it too.

author: Josh Richman
title: Privacy's Defenders Podcast: Snowden Exposes NSA’s Lies
content:
By 2013, EFF had spent seven years arguing in court that the National Security Agency was sweeping up ordinary Americans’ communications, including through the secret room that whistleblower Mark Klein had exposed. The government would neither confirm nor deny it, and outside the courtroom the public seemed to have moved on.

Then, in early June, documentary filmmaker Laura Poitras and journalist Glenn Greenwald mysteriously missed a Freedom of the Press Foundation board meeting at EFF’s offices. It turned out they were in Hong Kong, meeting an NSA contractor who had been secretly writing to Laura for months. His name was Edward Snowden, he had thousands of secret documents proving the government had in fact been spying on millions of Americans. When he subsequently revealed himself, a photo of him sitting behind his laptop – emblazoned with a big red EFF sticker – went worldwide.

Welcome to the fourth episode of “Privacy’s Defenders,” a podcast about the people – lawyers, journalists, hackers, and others – who’ve fought to secure your digital liberties since before most people even knew what the internet was.

(You can also find this episode on the Internet Archive and on YouTube.)

In this episode, former EFF Executive Director Cindy Cohn talks with Laura Poitras about how she got to that historic moment, including her years of expertise in communicating via encrypted channels. Freedom of the Press Foundation Executive Director Trevor Timm – a former EFF activist – shares his recollection of the day the first Snowden story broke. For EFF and its clients in Jewel v. NSA, Snowden’s documents were proof of what the government had spent years refusing to confirm. As Cindy puts it, “We were struggling along in the mud, and we felt like somebody gave us wings.”

It's the story of the lawyers who fought for your privacy, the government that lied about spying on you, and the whistleblower who blew it all wide open.

The “Privacy’s Defenders” podcast is a follow-up to Cindy’s book, “Privacy’s Defender: My Thirty-Year Fight Against Digital Surveillance,” bringing to life pivotal moments in the voices of those who fought for your rights. Sales of “Privacy’s Defender” benefit EFF, so pick up your copy today!

Joanne Elgart Jennings co-produced and created this podcast.

Jarrod Sport co-produced, mixed, and mastered it.

Corinne Ruff is our story editor.

We had additional help from Rachel Estabrook and Alison Broverman.

The original music was composed and performed by Nat Keefe of Hot Buttered Rum with Ben Andrews on the fiddle.

content:
Romulos “Mulong” Robiños, a 24-year-old tricycle driver was abducted from his home in Angeles city, Pampanga on November 17, 2006 by suspected state forces. author: By Sean Summers, Unicorn Riot
title: Two Palestine Solidarity Activists Refuse to Testify Before a Grand Jury
content:
Merrimack County, NH — In November 2023, Sophie Ross and Bridget Shergalis approached a large industrial building in Merrimack, New Hampshire. The structure houses Elbit Systems of America, the domestic branch of an Israeli weapons manufacturer that’s a key supplier of drones and ground equipment used in the country’s ongoing

genocide in Palestine

.


The two were participating in an action organized by Palestine Action U.S. Some blockaded the road leading to the facility while Shergalis and Ross, along with others, continued to the building.


A few protesters stayed on the ground and sprayed the facade with red paint, sealed doors shut with a bike lock, and broke windows. Shergalis and Ross made their ways to the building’s roof and lit flares to announce their presence while attempting to damage the building’s HVAC system.


Both women were arrested that day, along with Calla Walsh. Paige Belanger, another participant, was arrested days later. All four were

charged with multiple felonies

 that could have brought decades in prison if convicted. After a legal battle, and a series of victories, Shergalis, Ross, Belanger and Walsh were

sentenced to 60 days jail time

 for misdemeanor convictions.


See all of our Palestine coverage


Nearly three years after that action, Shergalis and Ross have been subpoenaed to testify in front of a federal grand jury. The reason for the subpoena isn’t clear, but one thing is: both women are refusing to cooperate.


On October 5, Bridget woke up to strangers knocking on her window. When her partner answered, he found people dressed in unassuming clothes. Only after he asked what they wanted did the couple realize what was happening. The strangers were FBI agents there to serve her a subpoena to testify before a grand jury.


She told the agents to leave their contact info and expect to hear from her attorney, Kira Kelly. Ross was spared the door knock after agents delivered a subpoena to Kelly, the attorney representing both of the women.


The document simply ordered both women, individually, to appear in the U.S. District Court in Concord, New Hampshire on October 21, only 16 days out from the delivery of the subpoena.


No other details that clarify the target or goals of the investigation appear in the subpoena, and both Shergalis and Ross, along with their lawyer, are unclear about the reason behind the order. While Kelly told Unicorn Riot an assistant U.S. attorney told them it’s in relation to the 2023 action, no more information was made available to them, leaving everyone but prosecutors to speculate about the motivation behind the investigation.


While details are sparse, reporting from the time of the action and recent developments suggest the grand jury may be related to the Cox Media heir and controversial left-wing benefactor James Cox “Fergie” Chambers Jr.


Chambers participated in the November 2023 Elbit protest where Shergalis and Ross were arrested. In a 2024

profile in Rolling Stone

, Chambers told a reporter he had fled the country after the action for fear that he may be implicated in a racketeering case for his involvement. Chambers insisted in that interview that he wasn’t doing anything wrong by moving to Tunisia, but that he was scared of facing RICO charges.


In July, Chambers was arrested in Ibiza, Spain and he’s been held in the country since while awaiting the

outcome of an extradition order under consideration

 by the Spanish government. The U.S. has asked authorities in Spain to send Chambers back to this country to face charges on a still-sealed indictment.


Related:

Anarchist Hacker Jeremy Hammond Summoned to Testify in Front of Grand Jury


More important to Shergalis and Ross than the who or why of the grand jury’s convening, though, is the principle behind the practice and the pair’s moral objection to the process. The thought of betraying a political movement both say they’re committed to is unacceptable to them.


“I would like to be able to, like, look other people in the eye and sleep at night and all of that good stuff,” Shergalis told Unicorn Riot. “And that’s, that isn’t possible with testifying. It just isn’t, it wouldn’t be.”


By openly opposing the subpoena from the start, both hope to establish that they cannot be coerced into testifying. That’s a key distinction in how things may play out.

law

, people who refuse to testify after being subpoenaed to a

grand jury

author: Jake Johnson
title: 21 Dem Senators Join GOP to Move Forward Bill to Speed Up Data Center Permits
content:
The bill, which will change federal approval processes for fossil fuel projects, is backed by Big Oil and tech giants.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

US senators, including 21 members of the Democratic caucus, voted late Monday to end debate on permitting reform legislation that would weaken critical environmental safeguards to speed up the federal approval process for energy projects, including fossil fuel infrastructure and data centers.

One Democratic senator, Catherine Cortez Masto of Nevada, opposed the cloture motion on Monday after previously voting to advance the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), legislation backed by the oil lobby, tech giants, and the climate-wrecking Trump White House, as well as major labor unions. Cortez Masto said after last week’s procedural vote that she would vote against advancing the bill to final passage if its changes to the National Historic Preservation Act were not removed.

The Senate Democratic caucus members who supported the cloture motion, which sets the stage for final passage, were: Richard Blumenthal (Conn.), Chris Coons (Del.), John Fetterman (Pa.), Ruben Gallego (Ariz.), Kirsten Gillibrand (D-NY), Martin Heinrich (NM), John Hickenlooper (Colo.), Andy Kim (NJ), Angus King (Maine), Amy Klobuchar (Minn.), Jon Ossoff (Ga.), Gary Peters (Mich.), Jack Reed (RI), Jacky Rosen (Nev.), Brian Schatz (Hawaii), Chuck Schumer (NY), Jeanne Shaheen (NH), Elissa Slotkin (Mich.), Mark Warner (Va.), Raphael Warnock (Ga.), and Sheldon Whitehouse (RI).

“The senators who voted to advance BAAJA just betrayed the voters who turned out en masse to demand that Congress rein in data center development, stop corruption, and bring down electricity costs,” said Elizabeth Bast, executive director of the advocacy group Oil Change International. “BAAJA would double down on Trump’s failed energy policies, which enrich Big Oil and his own stock portfolio at the expense of communities and our climate. Even analysis from the American Petroleum Institute, a major BAAJA backer, shows that the bill doesn’t stop energy prices from rising.”

“BAAJA would act as a kill switch for future climate action without offering any meaningful emissions reductions,” Bast warned. “At best, this bill leaves US emissions over 2.1 billion tons short in 2040 of even a modest climate goal. Big Oil and Big Tech have spent millions lobbying for this backroom deal, which has not had a single hearing, and are urging Congress to ram through the bill before the incoming Congress is sworn in.”

If, as expected, the Senate votes for final passage of BAAJA, the bill would move to the narrowly GOP-controlled House, where it has drawn significant opposition from Democratic lawmakers, including the Congressional Progressive Caucus (CPC). Environmental groups and other opponents have urged lawmakers in both chambers to press pause on the bill until Democrats take control of Congress in January.

“BAAJA includes important policies for which the CPC has advocated, including stronger federal authority to approve much-needed transmission lines to accelerate the clean energy transition,” the caucus said in a statement last week. “However, it also contains provisions that would undermine Tribal sovereignty and roll back key environmental laws, such as the National Environmental Policy Act, the Clean Water Act, the Endangered Species Act, and the National Historic Preservation Act. As a result, the public would lose key tools used to protect the environment and hold the administration accountable against ICE detention centers, Trump vanity projects, and more.”

The Senate’s cloture vote came days after around 100 environmental and energy law scholars warned in a letter to the chamber’s Democratic leadership that BAAJA “would inflict permanent, sweeping damage on the nation’s core environmental laws (and on the people and environment they are designed to protect).”

“Whatever modest emissions reductions its transmission reforms may deliver cannot justify the rollback that comes with them,” the letter reads. “And the threat posed by this lame-duck initiative provides a template and momentum for rollbacks far beyond environmental protections — potentially undercutting enforcement of public health protections, civil rights, public education, consumer finance, and more.”

author: Clare Hymer
title: The Workers Who Made GTA 6 Are Voting on Whether to Form a Union
content:
UK-based workers at Rockstar Games are voting on whether to recognise a union in their workplace, as the release of Grand Theft Auto 6 is set to break records.


The ballot of around 1,600 workers runs from 12 to 26 November and could lead to the creation of the Rockstar Game Workers Union, which would be the biggest in the UK video games sector.


Nestor Uriarte, an animation programmer at Rockstar, told Novara Media that game workers were being dragged into “a future of uncertainty”, and that the ballot was their chance to regain some control.


“As Rockstar workers we build games that set the industry standard. It’s time for us to build a workplace that does the same,” he said

.


The vote comes as the games giant faces an employment tribunal over the dismissal of dozens of workers.


Rockstar sacked 31 UK-based union members without warning in October 2025, in a move the Independent Workers’ Union of Great Britain (IWGB) called “the most blatant and ruthless act of union busting in the history of the games industry”. 


The firm denied this allegation, claiming the workers were dismissed for leaking confidential information. The IWGB insists workers “only communicated in private and legally-protected trade union channels”. 


In June,

Rockstar lost a legal battle

 to stop fired workers from pursuing claims that the firm blacklisted them. Closing submissions for the employment tribunal are scheduled for 17 and 18 November – although a ruling could take weeks.


Jack Hoxby, a sacked worker and claimant in the tribunal, told Novara Media that he and other colleagues had been organising to try and give Rockstar workers a say over their working conditions. “We never imagined that doing so would cost us our jobs,” he said.  


GTA 6, which will be released on Thursday, is the first new game in the GTA franchise in 13 years and is set to be the biggest video game blockbuster of all time. Anticipation is so high that researchers expect another outbreak of

“GTA flu”

, whereby workers take time off to play the game. 


The UK video games sector has historically had few trade unions. If unionisation efforts are successful, Rockstar would become the second UK games studio with a recognised union – following ZA/UM in October 2025 – in a breakthrough workers hope could boost unionisation efforts across the rest of the industry.


Hoxby said that regardless of the outcome of the tribunal, “more and more people across the sector are building unions… Whilst a ruling in our favour would be a form of justice for us, that wave of organisation is a victory for everyone.”

author: Karina Shedrofsky
title: Documentos do Deutsche Bank ligam empresas de Trump a esquemas de lavagem de dinheiro
content:
Vazamento mostra escândalos de um dos maiores bancos do mundo. A

 Pública

 é o único parceiro no Brasil. Leia o especial

Inside Deutsche Bank


aqui.


Vazamento mostra escândalos de um dos maiores bancos do mundo. A

 Pública

 é o único parceiro no Brasil. Leia o especial

Inside Deutsche Bank


aqui.


Durante anos, as relações de Donald Trump com a Rússia despertaram uma suspeita: que interesses financeiros o ligam ao país cujo presidente, Vladimir Putin, ele elogia repetidamente?


O ex-chefe da campanha de Trump, Paul Manafort, foi acusado, em uma investigação do governo dos Estados Unidos, de ter repassado informações internas da campanha a um homem que as autoridades americanas acreditam ter ligações com o serviço secreto russo. Até hoje, não haviam surgido provas de que o próprio Trump tenha sido de alguma forma comprometido por suas relações comerciais com a Rússia.


Mas

documentos vazados

 do

Inside Deutsche Bank

 mostram agora que a instituição financeira há muito tempo mantém em seu poder evidências potencialmente comprometedoras envolvendo Trump e a Rússia.


Os arquivos mostram que, ao processar pagamentos feitos a algumas das muitas empresas de Trump,

o banco confirmou, em um memorando de maio de 2020, que duas delas estavam envolvidas em transações com entidades supostamente ligadas a redes de lavagem de dinheiro — ou

lavanderias financeiras

 — tanto na Rússia quanto no vizinho Azerbaijão.


Isso ocorreu apesar de um advogado sênior do banco ter afirmado antes, em uma resposta enviada internamente às autoridades americanas, que, até abril de 2019,

a instituição não tinha conhecimento de nenhuma ligação entre Trump e a Rússia “relacionada aos negócios do sr. Trump com o Deutsche Bank”.


O material é parte do

Inside Deutsche Bank

, investigação transnacional da qual a

Pública

 faz parte, baseada no vazamento de mais de 15 milhões de documentos do banco, obtido pelos jornalistas sul-africanos Josy Joseph e Khadija Sharife. O projeto tem coordenação global da Barracuda Media e do Centro Latinoamericano de Periodismo de Investigación (CLIP) na região. A

Pública

 é a única representante do Brasil.


Os documentos vazados para o projeto mostram,

segundo detalhado em diversas reportagens

, como o banco alemão repetidamente ignorou sinais de alerta de possível lavagem de dinheiro e violações de sanções e como descumpriu suas próprias regras para clientes poderosos.


As lavanderias


Na chamada Lavanderia Russa (

Russian Laundromat

), uma gigantesca estrutura financeira criminosa foi utilizada para transferir bilhões de dólares para fora da antiga União Soviética entre 2011 e 2014. O esquema foi

revelado

 pela primeira vez pelo Organized Crime and Corruption Reporting Project (OCCRP).


Já a Lavanderia Azerbaijana (

Azerbaijani Laundromat

), que operou entre 2012 e 2014, movimentou bilhões de dólares por uma rede de empresas de fachada e contas bancárias. Os recursos eram frequentemente utilizados para influenciar políticos europeus, a mando do regime repressivo do Azerbaijão.


Muitas das transações da Lavanderia Azerbaijana passaram pela filial estoniana do maior banco da Dinamarca, o Danske Bank, que se tornaria um elemento indissociável do escândalo.


Como esses pagamentos chegavam a figuras influentes em toda a União Europeia, o veículo de comunicação dinamarquês Berlingske e o OCCRP noticiaram que

uma empresa de fachada britânica chamada Faberlex ocupava uma posição central no esquema.


Agora, jornalistas que trabalham com o vazamento do

Inside Deutsche Bank

 descobriram que a

Faberlex aparentemente realizou transações com pelo menos uma empresa de Trump.


Um extrato bancário da Faberlex obtido pelos jornalistas mostra que quase 1 bilhão de dólares foi depositado na empresa em centenas de transações diferentes entre maio de 2013 e maio de 2015.

author: Unknown
title: Ji bo girtiyên nexweş ben berdan çalakiya nobetê hat destpêkirin
content:
Malbatên Girtiyên Nexweş, Komeleya Piştgirî û Piştevaniyê ya Malbatên Girtî û Hikumxwaran re (TUAY-DER), DEM Partî, Komeleya Hiqûqnasên Ji bo Azadiyê (OHD), Komeleya Mafê Mirovan (ÎHD) gelek kes bi daxwaza girtiyên nexweş bên berdan û gihîştina mafê tenduristiyê li ber Wezareta Dadê çalakiya nobetê ya bêdem dan destpêkirin.


Li gorî nûçeya Ajansa Welat parlamenterên DEM Partiyê û gelek kes jî ji bo piştgiriyê tevlî daxuyaniyê bûn.


Di daxuyaniyê de pankarta navê girtiyên nexweş li ser bû û li ser, “Em ê deriyên zindanê bi berxwedanê vêbikin” dinivisî hat vekirin. Her wiha girseyê bênavber dirûşmeyên, “Girtiyên siyasî rûmeta me ne”, “Ji girtiyên nexweş re azadî” berz kir.


"Heta girtiyên nexweş bên berdan çalakiya me dê bidome"


Hevberdevkê TUAY-DERa Enqereyê Şîrîn Altay bi lêv kir ew ji bo êdî di girtîgehan de girtî jiyana xwe ji dest nedin dest bi çalakiyê kirinê û wiha axivî:


“Tevî pêvajoya Aştî û Civaka Demokratîk jî hê li girtîgehan girtiyên nexweş jiyana xwe ji dest didin û berdana wan tê asteng kirin. Em ji bo dengê xwe bigihînin berpirsan li vir dest bi çalakiyê dikin. Divê girtiyên nexweş demildest bên berdan. Heta girtiyên nexweş bên berdan çalakiya me dê bidome.”


"Em ji bo kes êdî nemirê têdikoşin"


Parlamenterê DEM Partiyê yê Mersînê Alî Bozan jî destnîşan kir ku bernedana girtiyên nexweş baweriya ji bo pêvajoyê dişkînê û wiha got:


“Em ji bo pêvajoyê têdikoşin. Em ji bo kes êdî nemirê têdikoşin. Lê hê jî li girtî jiyana xwe ji dest didin. Êdî tahamula me nemayê. Hê hefteyê borî girtiyê nexweş Tuncer Sağlam jiyana xwe ji dest da. Baweriya civakê ji bo vê rewşe kêm bû ye. Em ji bo girtiyên nexweş dest bi çalakiya nobeda bê dem dikin. Em li vir bang li Wezareta Dadê û saziyên dewletê dikin ku li gor pêvajoyê tevbigerin û girtiyên nexweş berdin.”


"Divê ev nobet ji berê ve bihata dest pê kirin"


Dayika girtiya nexweş Newroz Bozkurt ku nexweş,ua Losemiya kronîkê lê peyda bûye û li nexweşxaneyê tê derman kirin û rewşa wê xeternek e, Sultan Bozkurt jî diyar kir ku ew ji ber nexweşiya keça xwe ji Stenbolê hatiye û wiha axivî:


“Hê jî min nekariye keça xwe bibînim. Ne nexweşxaneye, ew der jî girtîgeh e. Ez Enqereyê baş nizanim. Heke min baş bizaniba ez ê peya biçûma wir. Divê ev nobet ji berê ve bihata dest pê kirin. Bi vê pêvajoyê re me got êdî dayik nagirîn. Lê dayikên Kurd hê jî digirîn. Tu ferqa hêsirê çavê dayikan tune ye. Divê êdî dayik negirîn û ji bo wê ez li vir careke din bang li saziyên dewletê dikim ku girtiyên nexweş demildest berdin.”


"Mafê tenduristiyê mafekî bingehîn e"


Hevjinê girtiya nexweş Evîn Zapsûyê ku teşhîsa penceşêrê merheleya 4an lê hatibû danîn Mecîd Zapsû jî destnîşan kir ku ew ji bo dengê xwe bigihînin saziyên pêwendîdar dest bi çalakiya nobetê dikin û wiha got: 


“Em ji bo Wezareta Dadê peywîra xwe bi cih bîne li vir in. Mafê tenduristiyê mafekî bingehîn e. Lê ji ber ku ew maf tê binpêkirin îro girtî bi gelek nexweşiyan re rû bi rû dimînin. Hevjina min Evîn jî li girtîgehê nexweş bû û ji ber ku tedawiyeke baş nehat kirin rewşa wê giran bû. Heta girtiyên nexweş werin berdan em ê çalakiya xwe bidomînin.”


Piştî axaftinan girseyê li vir dest bi nobedê kir. Piştî demekê polîsan xwest mudaxileyî çalakiyê bike. Li ser vê yekê girseyê bertek nîşan da û di bin dorpêça polîsan de çalakiya xwe didomîne. Hate gotin ku dê nobet sibê jî li heman cihî berdewam bike.


Li gorî agahiyên fermî yên Parlamentoyê di sala 2025an de li girtîgehan jê 792 hukumxwar, 77 girtî û bi giştî 869 kesan bi awayekî bi guman jiyana xwe ji dest dane. 132 girtî jî di pêvajoyên qeza an destûrê de mirine ku bi hev re 1001 kes mirine. Her wiha di navbera 1ê Kanûna Paşîn û 6ê Gulana 2026an de 26 girtiyan xwe kuştiye û ji van 14 girtî jî dermanên psîkiyatrîk bi kar dianîn.


Li gorî daneyên ÎHDyê hezar û 412

girtiyên nexweş

 hene. 


(AY)

author: David Venn
title: Nunavut coroner schedules inquest into Rankin Inlet man’s death
content:
Nunavut’s chief coroner has scheduled an inquest into the death of a 21-year-old Rankin Inlet man who was shot and killed by police five years ago.


The inquest is set for Nov. 23 to 27 at Siniktarvik Hotel in Rankin Inlet, the Office of the Chief Coroner announced in a public service announcement Monday.


“The purpose of this inquest is to explore the circumstances surrounding the death of Mr. Trey Angootealuk,” the announcement states, “and to consider recommendations to prevent death in similar circumstances.”


On the afternoon

 of Nov. 6, 2021, RCMP officers responded to a call for a disturbance that involved “intoxicated males,” according to a police report at the time.


Angootealuk walked around town with a rifle, shot toward police officers, hijacked a truck at gunpoint and drove to the outskirts of town, where police contained him for several hours before shooting him.


In May 2022, the Ottawa Police Service, which investigates major incidents that involve Nunavut RCMP, found that there were

no grounds

 to believe any officer committed a crime.


Coroner’s inquests are mandatory under Nunavut law for deaths involving an on-duty police officer. They do not determine the guilt or innocence of anyone involved in the incident.


Anyone who would like to participate in the inquest can contact the territory’s coroner’s office at 867-975-6562.

author: Main alba channel
title: La vie d'une fleur.Vostfr
content:
La vie d'une fleur


De Gonzalo Mateos


Titre original : “La vida de una flor”


Catalogne - 2024 – 58'


Version originale sous-titrée en français


Ce documentaire vise à mettre en lumière un épisode peu connu de l’histoire de la Catalogne et de l’État espagnol.


Il s’agit de l’insurrection du Haut Llobregat et du Cardoner, au cours de laquelle le communisme libertaire fut proclamé dans certains villages.


Federica Montseny a évoqué cet événement en ces termes : « Cinq jours d’anarchie… qui n’ont pas duré plus longtemps que la vie d’une fleur. »


L’insurrection libertaire du Haut Llobregat fut la première des trois insurrections générales soutenues par la CNT pendant la période de la République espagnole, avant la Révolution sociale de 1936. Elle s’est déroulée pendant plusieurs jours au cours de la seconde quinzaine de janvier 1932 dans les villages de la région du Berguedà, entre le Llobregat et son affluent, le Cardoner. L’ancrage des sociétés ouvrières catalanes affiliées à l’Association internationale des travailleurs s’appuyait déjà sur plusieurs décennies d’activité de nombreuses associations prônant l’anti-étatisme et une société sans classes. Le capitalisme s’était implanté dans cette région sous la forme d’une exploitation menant principalement à la création de colonies ouvrières textiles et dans l’industrie minière. Dans ces colonies ouvrières, les patrons tentaient de contrôler les relations sociales de leurs travailleurs et d’empêcher leur syndicalisation en les menaçant de perdre leur emploi, et donc les logements où ils vivaient avec leurs familles à proximité des usines.


Le dimanche 17 janvier 1932, une grève est déclenchée dans la commune de Berga, qui s’étendra le lendemain à d’autres localités de la région, parmi lesquelles le village de Fígols, où les ouvrières du textile et les mineurs de Sant Corneli se mettent en grève pour que les accords salariaux conclus soient respectés. La grève fut un succès et entraîna un arrêt total du travail. Mais dans cette commune, la grève avait son propre programme : elle se transforma en une grève révolutionnaire impulsée par des collectifs anarchistes. D’une assemblée réunissant hommes et femmes de la commune naquit l’accord de proclamer le communisme libertaire afin de chasser les patrons industriels de la région. La CNT décide de soutenir l’initiative des travailleurs insurgés ; la Garde civile et le Somatén (milice rurale catalane) sont désarmés, le drapeau rouge et noir est hissé sur la mairie de la localité, la propriété privée est abolie et l’approvisionnement en denrées alimentaires est assuré. Le mercredi 20 janvier 1932, des élections populaires au suffrage universel furent même organisées pour constituer la commune libre de Fígols, au cours desquelles furent élus un délégué général ainsi que huit autres délégués représentatifs. La tendance révolutionnaire de la grève ne triompha toutefois pas complètement à Berga ni à Manresa, mais elle fut un succès dans des villages tels que Sallent, Cardona, Balserany ou Súria. C’est dans ces villages que le communisme libertaire fut proclamé pour la première fois.


À travers des entretiens avec des historiens, des experts, des proches des participants et des habitants de la région, ce documentaire cherche à reconstituer les faits, ainsi qu’à analyser leur contexte et leur importance dans l’imaginaire collectif de la région. Par ailleurs, nous utiliserons comme ressource la voix off des chroniques d’Eduardo de Guzman, un journaliste proche des idées anarchistes, qui fut envoyé spécial par le journal « La Tierra » pendant les jours de l’insurrection. Le documentaire dure environ une heure et utilise des images d’archives ainsi que différents supports graphiques pour reconstituer l’Histoire.

author: Nathaniel Njeru Mugo
title: The names on the ice
content:
Mount Kenya’s glaciers carry names such as Lewis, Gregory, Tyndall, Darwin, Forel and Heim. Within a few years, the ice carrying those names may be gone. Two of the less famous glaciers, Cesar and Josef, tell the story better.

In 1899, Halford Mackinder set out to make the

first recorded ascent of Batian

 with six Europeans, 66 Swahilis, two Maasai guides and 96 Kikuyu. Among the Europeans were César Ollier and Joseph Brocherel, Alpine guides from Courmayeur in Italy. Brocherel was also listed as a porter. Both men left their names on the mountain:

Cesar Glacier and Josef Glacier

.

The 96 Kikuyu did not.

That discrepancy invites an easy story about Europeans overwriting an African map. The mountain is less tidy. Lower down, African names persist:

Kikami

,

from the Kikuyu word for hyrax;


Mbairunyi

,

“Place of Fighting”;


Gacheno

,

“Place of Danger”;


Kethimbui

,

“Place of Rest.”

 They record animals, conflict, fear and respite rather than distant scientists and explorers. The pattern is not absence but altitude. The higher the map goes, the whiter it gets.

Even the summit area complicates that pattern.

Mackinder adopted Batian, Nelion and Lenana, names of Maasai figures, on the suggestion of Sidney Langford Hinde

, a British colonial officer in Maasailand. Africans appear throughout the mountain’s nomenclature — as guides and porters, as informants and sources of names. Europeans were usually the people deciding which names entered the map, and which endured.

At the ice line, the contrast becomes harder to miss. Lewis is named for a geologist; Darwin for Charles Darwin. The ice became an index of European science, honoring men with no particular connection to Mount Kenya. Tyndall is the sharpest case.

His experiments established that gases including carbon dioxide and water vapor absorb radiant heat

. The glacier bearing his name is disappearing in a changing climate.

There is a second imbalance. The industrialized countries from which many of those explorers and scientists came account for a disproportionate share of the emissions changing the planet’s climate. From 1850 to 2019,

the IPCC calculates

, developed countries produced 57% of cumulative fossil fuel and industrial carbon dioxide emissions; Africa, just 3%. The names were assigned here; most of the carbon was emitted elsewhere.

Nor was every European name an act of personal vanity. When J.W. Gregory surveyed Mount Kenya,

he named glaciers after Forel and Heim for a practical reason: glaciers needed names if they were to be described and mapped

.

Useful to whom is a small question, but not an empty one.

The

Mountain Club of Kenya’s guide

 records that in 1924 porters insisted they had seen a lion beside a tarn; Melhuish and Dutton called it Simba Tarn. The porters’ observation survived on the map; their names did not. The same men named another tarn after Gitchini, Melhuish’s personal servant, who accompanied him on mountain journeys.

Another name connects Mount Kenya with Kilimanjaro. The missionary

Johannes Rebmann joined Johann Ludwig Krapf in Mombasa in 1846

. In 1848, Rebmann reported snow on Kilimanjaro. On

December 3, 1849, Krapf sighted Mount Kenya

, whose name he recorded as Kenia or Kegnia after hearing it from Kamba people. The precise etymology is disputed, but an African name entered the European written record and eventually named the country.

Krapf got a glacier too.

There is precedent for reconsidering what mountains record. At

Tanganyika’s independence in 1961, Kilimanjaro’s Kaiser-Wilhelm-Spitze became Uhuru Peak

. The summit proclaimed freedom; the ice retained a different history.

Rebmann Glacier

 was not renamed. Kenya became independent two years later, and Krapf Glacier kept its name too.

In 1963,

twelve of Mount Kenya’s named glaciers still survived

: Northey, Krapf, Gregory, Lewis, Melhuish, Diamond, Darwin, Forel, Heim, Tyndall, Cesar and Josef. Their names did not change. Kenya nonetheless

renamed Lake Rudolf as Lake Turkana in 1975

. The machinery existed. It simply never reached the ice.

Lewis Glacier

lost 90 % of its volume between 1934 and 2010

.

Prinz and colleagues found

Sharif Jamilenvironmental activist, coordinator of Waterkeepers Bangladesh and board member of the Waterkeeper Alliance.

Bangladesh’s first riverkeeper, Sharif Jamil, shares how poor countries in the Global South are struggling to effectively adapt to climate change as rising sea levels, extreme weather patterns, pollution and more are creating an escalating “humanitarian catastrophe,” while the wealthy impede efforts to reallocate financial resources for adaptation and mitigation. “If you want to protect the planet, if you want to save the planet from global warming, you need climate finance to make all this transition,” says Jamil.

Sharif Jamilenvironmental activist, coordinator of Waterkeepers Bangladesh and board member of the Waterkeeper Alliance.

AMY GOODMAN: This is Democracy Now!, democracynow.org, The War and Peace Report. I’m Amy Goodman. We’re broadcasting from COP31, the U.N. climate summit, in Antalya, Turkey.

We turn now to how Global South countries at the frontlines of climate change-fueled disasters are demanding more funding and accountability from rich countries during the negotiations here at COP31.

In August, catastrophic floods in mountainous Nepal washed away entire villages, left nearly 7,000 people dead or missing, triggered by the collapse of a Himalayan glacier. Meanwhile, in low-lying Bangladesh, rising sea levels pose an existential threat to tens of millions of Bangladeshis living along the coast. Bangladesh and Nepal are among the most vulnerable to climate change-related disasters, yet together they contribute less than half a percent of global carbon emissions. They’re also among the poorest countries in the world.

The U.N. Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage was created in 2022 to provide financial support to developing nations on the frontlines of climate-fueled disasters, but the fund has fallen far short of what’s needed. In total, the fund already has over 175 requests from developing countries for nearly $3 billion, but rich countries, the most responsible for climate change, have only pledged $820 million to the fund.

For more, we’re joined by Sharif Jamil, environmental activist, coordinator of Waterkeepers Bangladesh, board member of the Waterkeeper Alliance.

It’s great to have you with us.

SHARIF JAMIL: Thank you for having me.

AMY GOODMAN: Why don’t you pick that mic right …
